agenda_note: This is the time for the public to come forward with any comments they may have. Citizen comments relating to any agenda matter may be made at the time the matter is before Council. Please state your name and address, and please limit your comments to three (3) minutes or less.
minutes_note:
Jean Clark, 1520 Monroe Drive, requested a saturation law to limit how many of the same businesses are allowed to be in one area, citing several laundromats near South Ridgewood Avenue. She also had concerns about standing water at Mike's Tires causing a palmetto bug infestation for neighboring properties.
Danny Robbins, 2041 Taylor Road, Port Orange, the Volusia County District 3 representative, addressed the Council to offer County support on flooding, economic recovery, and grants. He referenced the Transform 386 initiative at Volusia.org, over $100 million in dedicated stormwater funds, and encouraged attendance at the following day's Volusia County Legislative delegation meeting in DeLand.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, recounted that during pre-flood communication, he was assured via text that Duck Lake Pond would be completely drained, yet it was only partially pumped down. Expressing discontent with Interim City Manager Thurman's absence of actual monitoring, he criticized the City's inadequate flood response and urged corrective measures.
Jay Magrane, 2114 Pine Tree Drive, stated that during a flood, his paraplegic partner was left without evacuation help after no response from the Fire Department. He also expressed concerns regarding Police conduct, noting that officers observed rather than stopped vehicles creating wakes on flooded streets, and criticized the use of multiple patrol units for single traffic stops.
Claudia Adkins, 3230 Woodland Drive, addressed concerns regarding: high water bills, ineffective stormwater fee use, three (3) minute speaking limits, mandatory recycling fees, the need for alternative revenue sources like pay-to-park systems, and insufficient canal maintenance compared to nearby municipalities like South Daytona.
Mary Wells, 2011 Mango Tree Drive, echoed concerns about a debris-filled, poorly draining retention pond on Mango Tree Drive. Her house suffered complete flooding in one storm and garage water intrusion in another. She opposed fee hikes lacking a maintenance or improvement plan.
Mandi Bullard, 1417 Needle Palm, requested speed bumps or speed tables in Florida Shores, citing constant speeding in residential areas, the absence of sidewalks and streetlights, and near-miss incidents involving pedestrians and cyclists.
Mayor Depew acknowledged the streetlight issue, noting that FPL had initiated an underground utility program that would allow the City to add streetlights in Florida Shores and that an update had been requested from FPL.
Eric Rainbird, addressed the Planning & Zoning process, emphasizing that developers are legally required to manage stormwater and prevent runoff onto adjacent properties. He claimed the City failed in enforcement, specifically monitoring Woodbridge Lakes as a major source of flooding on his property. He urged the Council to enforce regulations on developers and consider raising impact fees.
Terry Roberts, 2114 Mango Tree Drive, reported that the retention pond across the street had been poorly managed for two (2) years, with a blocked outflow and overgrown vegetation. After Hurricane Ian, he spent $120,000 and another $70,000 after Hurricane Milton, with a pending FEMA claim. He suggested adding check valves on pumps and elevating the pond's berm.
Kim Long, 3312 Mango Tree Drive, observed the new subdivision on Volco Road was four to five feet higher than Florida Shores, resulting in stormwater visibly flowing across 35th street into Mango Lake. She provided photos.
Mary Forrester, 1937 Edgewater Canal Road, raised concerns about fill being deposited behind the octagonal house on Volco Road, potentially worsening flooding in Florida Shores. She announced a new eight-unit transitional shelter for at-risk families in Edgewater, managed by the Edgewater Alliance Church. Volunteers and contractors are invited to contact the Church for more information.
David Patrick, 2729 Needle Palm Drive, identified a severely undersized catch basin at Needle Palm Drive's intersection, serving three (3) western streets. He reported frequent clogging from debris and spanish moss. He urged the Council to outline maintenance plans before the hurricane season, adding that the City lacks a forward-looking schedule on social media.
Daniel Crooker, 2218 Orange Tree Drive, reported a neighbor dumped concrete into a drainage swale and easement, including approximately three (3) truckloads in a two-foot-wide ditch, blocking drainage. He noted the neighbor had an existing code violation for adding fill and questioned the permitting process.
Mike Wellendorf, 1850 Kumquat Drive, stated that he and his wife had lived in a severely damaged home for over two (2) years after Hurricane Ian, delaying repairs because Hurricane Milton confirmed his belief that new developments are causing flooding. He urged the City Attorney to pursue legal action, alleging developers violated federal law by disrupting natural water flow to the detriment of neighboring properties.
Unnamed Resident, 3425 Willow Oak Drive, described creating swales for about six (6) homes to prevent flooding, which worked. A month later, she claimed the City filled in her work without notice. After contacting Mr. Thurman, he admitted failure. She felt it was retaliatory and asked for that to stop against proactive residents.
Lisa Delaney, 2228 Kumquat Drive, stated that she had been requesting the City dig a drainage ditch in front of her home but had not gotten any response and expressed frustration with Mr. Thurman's lack of action. She threatened legal action if the issue remained unsolved.
Brian O'Koniewski, 139 W Connecticut Avenue, seconded the prior speakers' flooding concerns, raised the condition of the damaged dock at Menard Park (which he noted had been in disrepair since Hurricane Ian), and asked about the possibility of a pay-to-park system at Menard Park to fund repairs.
Councilwoman Gillis requested biweekly reports from Environmental Services on completed work. Mayor Depew concurred and suggested public projection. Interim City Manager Thurman noted an existing map online. He reported that seven (7) out of 120 miles of work had been completed, improving the timeline to about four (4) year, a 2.5 times increase in efficiency.
Mayor Depew suggested a special public meeting on January 27th at 4:00pm for Public Works to discuss their 2025 goals and resources, which the Council agreed to. Interim City Manager Thurman mentioned the search for two (2) CDL Class A operators for the VAC truck program.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilman Thomas, second by Councilwoman Gillis, to approve Ordinance No. 2024-O-62: request for approval for a City wide Moratorium regarding annexations, rezoning’s, comprehensive plan amendments, site plans, preliminary plats, and final plats. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, provided a staff report and recommendation. The Planning & Zoning Board gave an unanimous favorable recommendation while the Economic Development Board gave a unanimous unfavorable recommendation.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Mayor Depew noted for the record that the CRA redevelopment and infill lots, as well as the major commercial and largest industrial corridor in Volusia County, were excluded. He stated he had received no complaints about those areas during his tenure as Mayor.
Donna McDavid, 1201 Bond Street, expressed support for the moratorium.
Stephanie Ford, President and CEO of the Southeast Volusia Chamber of Commerce, spoke in opposition of the moratorium.
Teresa David, 1015 Regent Street, expressed support for the moratorium.
Bob Perry, 608 Midfield Loop, representing Habitat for Humanity, requested the Council exempt affordable housing from the moratorium.
Candace Cecil, President of the New Smyrna Beach Board of Realtors, representing over 700 members in Southeast Volusia, expressed opposition to the moratorium.
Bliss Jamison, 635 Air Park Road, urged a vote against the moratorium.
Kelsey Bauer, Chief Operating Officer of Advent Health New Smyrna Beach, felt a moratorium could negatively impact the local economy and health care capacity.
Rebecca Crews, 2139 S Riverside Drive, asked the Council to pause on the second reading pending further information.
Robin Regacho, 3425 Willow Oak Drive, spoke in support of the moratorium.
Dina Brown, 3006 Silver Palm Drive, clarified what she felt were misconceptions about the moratorium and expressed support for it.
Brittany Arnold, representing Southeast Volusia Habitat for Humanity, asked Council to consider exempting affordable housing from the moratorium.
Mark Billings, 240 N Ridgewood Avenue, representing Habitat for Humanity and serving as Chamber Chair, questioned if the moratorium would stop flooding and urged council to make decisions based on data and accountability.
Greg Matthews, 2825 Victory Palm Drive, spoke in favor of the moratorium.
Mary Forrester, 1937 Edgewater Canal Road, spoke in support of the moratorium and asked for clarification on the Supreme Court's ruling on public comment restriction.
Suzanne Shiver, 548 Sandy Oaks Boulevard, representing Dream Green Volusia, spoke in support of the moratorium.
Patrick Fisher, 2100 S Air Park Road, spoke in support of the moratorium.
Claudia Adkins, 3230 Woodland Drive, reiterated her support of the moratorium.
Tory Kidder, 3314 Pine Tree Drive, spoke in support of the moratorium.
Tim London, 2632 Woodland Drive, expressed support for the moratorium.
Jack Travis, representing Habitat for Humanity, asked for an exemption for Habitat for Humanity homes.
Bernard Barry, representing Southeast Volusia County Habitat for Humanity, thanked the Council and Interim City Manager for their support of Habitat's work.
Mary Wells, 2011 Mango Tree Drive, spoke in support of the moratorium.
Jeff Brower, De Leon Springs, Volusia County Chair, expressed support for the moratorium.
Rachel Phillips, Habitat for Humanity, urged Council to vote no or step back from the decision to consider the employment impact on Habitat and the families they serve.
Gina Holt, 1798 Hideaway Lane, expressed support for the moratorium.
Mayor Depew expressed disappointment that this point had been reached due to unaddressed land development codes and neglected infrastructure. He noted that despite the moratorium, over 11,000 homes are still approved for construction. This moratorium aims to reassess the City's comprehensive plan, codes, and review capabilities.
Councilman Thomas displayed a map that had been created prior to Hurricane Milton showing 22 proposed new subdivisions with orange dots. Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, confirmed that approximately 8-10 entitlements with approximately 2500 units were currently in process at various stages of review. Councilman Thomas had concerns about the cumulative infrastructure impact of the upcoming population and vehicle traffic, stating the City had to catch up before adding more.
Councilwoman Gillis clarified that many items do not come before Council because they can proceed under straight zoning. She also noted that Habitat for Humanity had been advised prior to the moratorium's adoption that they may submit applications during the window before adoption. She stated that she hears from flood affected residents constantly and that the Council had to respond even without absolute proof the moratorium would stop flooding.
Councilwoman Dolbow asked about a financial risk analysis for the period after the moratorium and plans to generate revenue for anticipated infrastructure improvements. Mr. Solstice explained that while the housing cycle was already slowing down exemptions for commercial and industrial areas would help mitigate revenue impacts. However, future costs might necessitate increases in ad valorem taxes or utility raises. Councilwoman Dolbow raised concerns about the potential lack of funds for future councils to address necessary repairs. She noted objections and support from constituents and likened it to a restaurant staying open during a redesign. Despite recognizing the need for flood-related updates, she was hesitant to move forward without a full-time City Manager and a solid financial strategy.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance 2024-O-62: Request for approval for a City wide Moratorium regarding annexations, rezoning’s, comprehensive plan amendments, site plans, preliminary plats, and final plats.

minutes_note:

Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Applicant Brad Hansen, 26969 S Meridian Road, Aurora, Oregon, identified himself as the owner and applicant.

Mayor Depew expressed concern about the commercial parcels fronting the street remaining undeveloped and the possibility of future commercial construction creating the same type of stormwater and residential compatibility issues seen elsewhere in the City.
Councilman Thomas noted that residents on the street would likely prefer residential use over a commercial businesses bringing additional traffic, and expressed support for the rezoning.
Councilwoman Dolbow indicated that it was likely the application costs, rather than opposition, that led northern properties to decline participation.
Mr. Solstice confirmed that the lot is about 8,000 square feet, with current B-3 zoning potentially allowing commercial use amid residential homes.

Interim City Manager Thurman summarized activities from January 6-12, noting attendance at the 2025 Volusia County Legislative Delegation meeting, a coffee event with the Mayor, and the Volusia County Elected Officials Roundtable in Daytona Beach. He was selected to present at Florida's APWA Expo 2025 in Orlando on April 30th and invited to join the Florida APWA Speakers Bureau.
Mr. Thurman provided an update on the Delta Group's third-party flooding investigation. A 300-page report, along with a 4-page executive summary was submitted to City Hall and distributed to the Mayor, Council, and City Manager. Key Findings addressed three (3) main allegations:
1. Duck Lake pump allegation: No evidence was found that any City employee intentionally failed to use pumps in order to cause retaliatory flooding.
2. Kumquat Drive drain blocking allegation: No evidence was found that City employees intentionally blocked outfall drains to cause retaliatory flooding. The rapid recession of floodwaters observed was attributed to tidal action, not any employee action with a T-handle tool.
3. Edgewater Preserve elevation allegation: No evidence was found that the City Engineer or any Public Works employee intentionally approved the development to cause retaliatory flooding. All employees interviewed held City Engineer Randy Coslow in the highest regard and vehemently denied any intentional misconduct.
Mr. Thurman announced that the City Engineer position had been posted to the City website, LinkedIn, and several industry sources.
Interim Environmental Services Director Sean Maroney gave a stormwater maintenance update, highlighting routine activities, inlet work on Yule Street, and the use of vac trucks over the weekend to compensate for utility-related delays on Friday. He mentioned Phase 1 of the G2-G11 project would finish design by month's end, with permitting and bids by March's end. Phase 2 design is set for May, with bids thereafter. Milligan also discussed the initiative to showcase stormwater maintenance photos and maps at Council meetings, aiming to include location labels in future displays.
Development Services Director Ryan Solstice provided an update on the comprehensive plan's progress. Scheduled public education seminars, in partnership with VCARD, will precede a workshop focusing on Future Land Use, Transportation, and Housing. A draft plan is aimed for May, with Planning and Zoning review in June. A 90-day review process by the State agency is anticipated, targeting final adoption in December. Work on the Land Development Code rewrite will commence during the plan's State review.
Councilwoman Dolbow thanked Mr. Thurman for reading portions of the investigation report and emphasized the importance of transparency regarding the findings related to City Engineer Randy Coslow.
Mayor Depew thanked staff for their responsiveness to residents, including a canal fence issue that had been resolved.

The MOTION FAILED due to lack of SECOND.
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, presented the staff report, indicating that Edgewater Preserve Phase 2's final plat was initially reviewed on April 18, 2024. The Technical Review Committee, along with contracted City surveyor CPH and engineers (Mead & Hunt), evaluated the plans and confirmed compliance with the preliminary plat, Land Development Code, and residential planned unit development agreement. Staff recommended approval and the Planning & Zoning unanimously endorsed the plat.
City Attorney Wolfe clarified that this is a quasi-judicial, administrative decision. Once an applicant demonstrates that their application meets City criteria, the burden shifts to the City to show by competent substantial evidence that the applicant does not meet standards. If denied, reasons must be stated in writing and the applicant may resubmit.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Harry Newkirk, Newkirk Engineering, 1230 North US Highway 1, Ormond Beach, appeared on behalf of the property owner, concurred with the staff report, and offered to answer any technical questions.
Agnes Witter, 223 Flagler Avenue, asked whether all St. Johns River Water Management District requirements had been met. Mr. Solstice confirmed that SJRWMD permits had been issued and that all third-party engineering reviews had been completed.
Eric Rainbird, stated that the Planning and Zoning Board had reviewed the plat and found it well laid out with adequate drainage and retention. However he highlighted that despite engineers claiming stormwater issues are managed. flooding still occurs near developments. He emphasized the importance of holding developers accountable within the two-year post-Certificate of Occupancy period, pointing out that unresolved drainage issues from past construction near his property despite several complaints.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, expressed strong opposition, noting that building up fill leads to stormwater runoff, causing neighbor flooding. He claimed that Code Enforcement targeted flood victims attempting repairs, while developers proceeded with projects contributing to the flooding. He urged Council to halt the project.
Mayor Depew expressed discomfort proceeding without a written explanation of a previous berm or dam failure during heavy rainfall, its cause, and the preventative measures taken. He inquired if the post-approval two-year period would address impacts beyond the subdivision, including near 35th street.
Councilman Thomas opposed the application, citing loss of trust by both the Council and the residents due to the previous flooding. Video evidence showing stormwater issues was proof of their failure. He would only endorse the project with a canal between the subdivision and Florida Shores.
Councilwoman Gillis agreed, stating that she had been present during the flooding and that the City had received nothing in writing from the developer acknowledging what occurred or what was done to fix it.
title: FP-2400: Request for Final Plat approval for Edgewater Preserve Phase Two generally located West of Volco Road.

minutes_note:
Interim Environmental Services Director Sean Maroney introduced the presentation, noting that the City had received a grant to conduct a vulnerability study and engaged the East Central Florida Regional Planning Council (ECFRPC) to carry out the work. The ECFRPC presenter along with their GIS Director Josh, delivered the second of two (2) public meetings on the vulnerability assessment that included the project overview, the exposure analysis, sensitivity analysis, and adaptive planning.
The key takeaways are that the sea level is expected to rise by about 1 foot over the next 25 years, pushing tides and storm surges further inland. Future development must consider flood risks. Elevating structures is a costly yet effective adaptation strategy when combined with other solutions. The presenter mentioned that the ECFRPC is carrying out about 7-8 vulnerability assessments, with three (3) already pursuing funding, and an adaptation plan is the grant's next phase.
A resident inquired if NOAA 2021 or 2017 data was used, and Josh from ECFRPC confirmed that the 2017 NOAA curves were applied, per Florida State requirements for projects started before July 2024. He mentioned that the 2017 curves are slightly more aggressive than the 202 curves.
title: East Central Florida Regional Planning Council to give a presentation on the status of the Vulnerability Assessment Study.

Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, specified that Edgewater Preserve's PUD agreement allows for 50-and 60-foot lots, and noted that Councilman Thomas might be confusing it with Edgewater Lakes, where lot sizes increased across phases. He confirmed the site includes 16-17 acres of wetlands and 8-9 acres for the St. Johns River Management District. Mr. Solstice acknowledged that the City's code lacks restrictions on fill, which Councilman Thomas found concerning due to potential flooding impacts.
Councilman Thomas responded to Mr. Rainbird's inquiry about water management west of I-95, noting that the City planned a reclaimed water lagoon project, to create a wildlife habitat and handle excess reclaimed water during the wet season, instead of discharging it into the Indian River Lagoon.
Councilwoman Dolbow raised concern about an investigation involving former director Randy Coslow. Bobby Copeland, a City Employee, claimed witness Kimberly Penny falsely attributed statements to him, and his supervisor lacked a chance to respond, potentially suggesting slander. Councilwoman Dolbow inquired about the liability for the City or the investigators. City Attorney Wolfe explained the investigation company was quoting a witness, probably without liability, and any defamation claim against the witness would hinge on whether the statements were knowingly false.

City Attorney Wolfe instructed the Council to document and provide written reasons for the recent denial of a final plat, as mandated by the Land Development Code. action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, to approve Ordinance No. 2024-O-47. The MOTION FAILED for lack of second.
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Staff confirmed no changes since the first reading and recommended approval.
Mark Watts, representing the Edgewater River Oaks project, requested the annexation of a 0.683-acre shoreline parcel inadvertently left out of the initial annexation. They want to ensure the entire hotel and marina are under the same jurisdiction. The applicant plans to remove invasive species, plant additional mangroves, and restore the shoreline in line with the Marine Discovery Center's guidance.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, was concerned that annexing the shoreline parcel may empower the developer to alter a historically shellfish-rich riverbank. He implied the County may enforce stricter shoreline protections than the City, urging Council to weigh the environmental effects of marina development on water quality and shellfish habitat.
Teresa David, 1015 Regent Street, representing the Riverside Conservancy, praised the applicant's intention to remove invasive species and maintain mangroves but urged for strong, enforceable shoreline protections and emphasized the necessity of involving the Riverside Conservancy throughout the process.
Councilwoman Gillis preferred input from the Riverside Conservancy before approval. The applicant's representative stated that detailed shoreline plans and restoration commitments occur at the site plan and development stages, which follow zoning and annexation.
Councilwoman Dolbow highlighted the economic impact of the overall project, including an estimated 368 jobs, significant impact fee contributions, a $35 million tax base increase estimated to yield approximately $266,000 annually in tax revenue, and contributions to the Volusia County manatee fund.
Councilman Thomas raised concerns about developers not keeping promises, pointing to previous tree removal along Jones Fish Camp Road. He requested the applicant to show where vegetative buffer was maintained, to which the applicant affirmed its inclusion in the approved PUD plan.

minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, provided a staff report and recommendation.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, asked for clarification on feather flag allowances and raised the ongoing topic of backyard chickens. Council confirmed that was not part of this item.
Mayor Depew clarified that the Ordinance allows one (1) feather flag per business annually and also permits a 4-by-8 professional banner near the roadway.
Councilwoman Dolbow expressed some concern about having both a feather flag and a banner on the same property creating visual clutter on US 1 and suggested businesses might best be served by choosing one or the other.
Councilman Thomas stated that he had no objection to allowing businesses to advertise, emphasizing that Edgewater has a reputation for being unfriendly to small businesses and that removing advertising barriers may be helpful.
Councilwoman Gillis and Mayor Depew noted that cost alone would likely deter most businesses from utilizing both options simultaneously.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilman Thomas, second by Councilwoman Gillis, to approve Ordinance No. 2025-O-06: Requesting to amend the Florida Shores Drainage Basin Building Permit Moratorium excluding pools. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, read the Ordinance into the record.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, asked for clarification on whether subdivisions that excavate material on-site rather than importing fill would be affected. Mayor Depew confirmed that this moratorium only applies to the Florida Shores Basin and does not affect the separate moratorium on PUDs and annexations.
Heather Bendl, 1709 Queen Palm Drive, stated that she was a geologist and objected the amendment. She argued that pools were impermeable and stop water absorption into soil, stressing that with more severe storms, easing the moratorium is unwise. She felt the amendment weakens established protections.
Robin Cassessee, 3425 Willow Oak Drive, thanked Mr. Solstice and staff for resolving the fencing issue, stating that fencing should never have been included.
Council discussion centered on excluding pools from the amendment to stay true to the original intent of focusing on fencing and sheds, pending clearer stormwater impact studies. The Council decided to approve the amendment while excluding pools until the final reading.
title: 1st Reading - Ordinance No. 2025-O-06: Request to amend the Florida Shores Drainage Basin Building Permit Moratorium.

minutes_note: City Attorney Wolfe reported that the case of Lawrence Garrett v. City of Edgewater and State Farm was settled during mediation. The incident on April 19, 2022, involved the plaintiff, on a bicycle without a light, being hit by an Edgewater Police vehicle near McDonald's on US 1. The plaintiff suffered a fractured femur requiring surgery and treatment, with medical expenses totaling $104,303. The City's expert validated the injury's permanence. The settlement entails State Farm paying $25,000 to the plaintiff, while the City's insurer covers $50,000 and mediation costs.

minutes_note:
Chairwoman Jamison went over the position brochure published by SGR and then turned the meeting over to Mr. Knutson to provide discuss the responsibilities of the Committee, expectations, and process.
Mr. Knutson introduced himself and provided an overview of his team and the company. He advised the Committee that the position was posted on February 12, 2014. He and his team would be doing candidate outreach; and advised where they advertised the position; he stated the goal was to have15-20 candidates for the committee to evaluate.
He advised the Committee that his team's first review of the candidates would start on March 16, 2024 to assess the field and determine if the position should remain open for an additional two (2) weeks).
Mr. Knutson stated they would like to meet with the Committee the week of March 24th to review the applications. The candidates would be discussed in detail at that meeting and the semifinalists will be picked. Once the semifinalists are determined SGR will do a more in-depth review of those finalists; as well as on-line interviews.
He then advised that the committee should meeting during the week of April 14th to go over the in-depth review of the semi-finalists and narrow the pool of candidates down to four (4) or (5) for Council to meet with in May. From the time the finalists are selected and the meeting with Council, the Committee and the public SGR will do a second, more in-depth, review and analysis as well as background checks of those candidates.
Chairwoman Jamison asked if they would meet the candidates in May and narrow down the group. Mr. Knutson clarified that the group would be narrowed down on two (2) occasions, the first would be in March to pick the semifinalists; the second would be in April when the finalists are chosen.
Mr. Ward asked what the percentage was of those hired in the past having to relocate. Mr. Knutson was unsure, but stated that it was relatively high, likely in the high 90's. Mr. Ward then asked if relocation costs would be part of the offer, Mr. Knutson stated that would be part of the negotiation.
Mr. Resheidat requested the Committee be provided the background on the semifinalists; Mr. Knutson confirmed that would be provided and the amount of information provided will build with each step.
Mr. Resheidat then asked if SGR was provided criteria from City Council as to what they are looking for in a City Manager. Mr. Knutson confirmed he met with each Council member and Senior Staff to develop that criteria. Chairwoman Jamison referred to the "Ideal Candidate" page in the position brochure. Mr. Resheidat responded that he was looking for something more specific to Edgewater and provided his view of the issues Edgewater is currently facing. Mr. Ward felt that would beneficial to discuss during the interview's. Mr. Knutson stated they will be asking the finalists specific questions related to the challenges and opportunities identified in the position brochure.
Ms. McDavid asked if the Committee would be able to preview the questionnaire that will be sent to the finalists. Mr. Knutson replied that the Committee will review and sign off on the questionnaire.
The Committee set the next meetings for March 26, 2025 at 4:00 pm and April 17, 2025 at 4:00 pm.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilman Thomas, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to approve Resolution No. 2025-R-03. The motion failed by the following vote:
attachments: 2025-R-03 Budget Adjustments - Mar. FY25 with Exhibit A
Additional detail 2025-R-03 Budget Adjustments - Mar. FY25
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Resolution into the record.
Bridgette Vaissiere, Finance Director, provided a staff report and recommendation.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Mayor Depew asked when the budget was typically approved; Ms. Vaissiere said September.
Mayor suggested that a motion be made to hold a special meeting regarding the budget amendment as he felt he didn’t have sufficient time to ask questions and felt there hadn't been enough transparency.
Ms. Vaissiere and Interim City Manager Thurman pointed out that if they tabled this; they would be unable to move forward with the other items pertaining to the budget amendment.
Councilwoman Dolbow said she had met with Interim City Manager Thurman; Ms. Vaissiere and Development Services Director Ryan Solstice regarding the budget amendment and they had answered all her questions and stressed the necessity to meet with Staff.
Councilman Thomas felt that employee morale was low and he did not want to deny the employees the 2% wage increase when it was needed. He had been working with Ms. Vaissiere and felt she does an excellent job.
Mayor Depew asked Ms. Vaissiere to provide the total amount in the ARPA fund; Ms. Vaissiere asked to go get the information from her desk.
Meeting went into a brief recess at 7:01pm.
Meeting reconvened at 7:07pm
Ms. Vaissiere informed Council that currently there was $3,922,339 available in the ARPA fund; the budget amendment provided would be using $2,042,941; that would leave a remaining balance of $1.8 million in ARPA funds. She added that Council had approved the terms for the Union contracts last September.
Mayor Depew asked for citizens comments and received none.
Councilman Thomas made a motion but Councilwoman Gillis asked to make further comments.
Councilwoman Gillis asked if they could move forward only approving a portion of the amendment; City Attorney Wolfe said it was legally possible but Ms. Vaissiere stated that it would be messy. She suggested if they did do that, they would have to allow a recess for her to be able to bring forth the corrected numbers.
Councilwoman Gillis felt there did need to be more discussion; Ms. Vaissiere said they typically try to meet with Mayor and Council before the meetings and that the agenda is posted publicly.
Councilwoman Dolbow's issue was that the entire Council was given the opportunity to meet with staff and ask questions; she felt Council was not responsible and didn't do their due diligence to learn the information that was readily available.
Mayor Depew said he asked plenty of questions and had a great working relationship with Mr. Thurman; he just felt that this should be a special meeting.
Councilman Thomas suggested approving the ratification of the Police Benevolent Association; the ratification for the Edgewater Fire Fighters and the mid-year wage adjustment. The Mayor felt approving the Police and Fire items were a given. Councilman Thomas emphasized the importance of the rest of the employees and felt they deserved it.
Ms. Vaissiere clarified that certain things could not be approved without this mid-year budget amendment per Florida Statute.
Further discussion ensued over the importance of utilizing staff beforehand to ask questions.
Ms. Vaissiere offered to go through each line item with Council.
Councilwoman Gillis felt there should be more public participation but was not against the wage increases for the general employees.
Mayor Depew reiterated that he would like to approve the wage increases and the ratification for Police and Fire. Ms. Vaissiere explained the process and asked for a short recess in order to do so.
Meeting went into recess at 7:26
Meeting reconvened at 7:47
After the recess and further discussion, Mayor Depew stated that he had reconsidered his position, acknowledging that the amendment was funded entirely through ARPA funds, impact fees, and grant revenues with no tax increase to residents, and that much of it had already been effectively committed through prior approvals. He apologized for his earlier questions and expressed full support.
title: Resolution 2025-R-03; March Amended Budget for Fiscal Year 2024-2025

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to approve the second reading of Ordinance No. 2025-O-05 with the consensus that we will have a workshop in six (6) months. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, gave a brief recap of the Ordinance but noted that nothing had changed since the first reading.
City Attorney Wolfe advised that the City Charter requires three (3) votes to pass an Ordinance or Resolution and as there are only three (3) Councilmembers present, they have to vote unanimously.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Councilwoman Dolbow asked if there were any restrictions on the amount of flags or banners per business if the Ordinance passes; Mr. Solstice explained that you were allowed one (1) per business and they had to follow regulations but there were no spacing requirements.
Councilwoman Dolbow said she had concerns over the lack of regulations regarding the banners and the possibility of them being a distraction.
Mayor Depew noted that they have discussed this three (3) times and felt that not every business will get banners or follow the code so it may be a non-issue; he proposed that maybe if there were more than a certain number of businesses in a plaza, they have to choose one or the other.
Mr. Solstice told Council that they could schedule a workshop in six (6) months to change the Ordinance or add regulations if there are issues.
Further discussion ensued over the number of businesses in the City and revisiting the Ordinance in six (6) months.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance No. 2025-O-05: Request for approval for amendments to Article III, Article VI and Article XX of the Land Development Code.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to table Ordinance No. 2025-O-06. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, advised that this was a second reading but a text amendment change had been done as Staff had erred in the first submittal with the exclusion of pools.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Agnes Witter, 223 Flagler Avenue, discussed her issues with the moratorium regarding fill dirt and suggested ways to add more infrastructure in the future to prevent flooding.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, referenced previously approved subdivisions and stormwater issues; Mayor Depew said that this was just related to Florida Shores, not to any subdivisions.
Dan Knight, 2290 Elegant Manor Circle, had issues with the pools not being permitted while detached garages were. He believes this Ordinance could open the City up for litigation if approved as written.
Billy Dove, representative for the Edgewater Preserve Development, felt that the revised proposal is an inappropriate way for the City to deflect the responsibility for preventing flooding, stated responsibilities of the City regarding stormwater infrastructure; said that the City is using Edgewater Preserve as a scapegoat; and discussed previous flooding issues.
Eric Rainbird, 118 San Remo Drive, agreed with the previous commenter and said subdivisions should be required to put in stormwater first.
Mayor Depew asked for Council comments.
Councilwoman Dolbow asked Council how they felt about allowing pools as she had received concerns from residents who felt it wasn't right that they could pull a permit for a detached garage but not a pool that may be less impervious surface.
Councilwoman Gillis noted that pools were banned from the original moratorium; Councilwoman Dolbow was concerned it could be a legal problem.
City Attorney Wolfe acknowledged that there was a risk for the moratorium to be challenged for equal protection or not treating people equally and it may lead to litigation.
Mayor Depew suggested the item be tabled until the next Council meeting.
After the motion, Mr. Solstice asked for direction. Mayor Depew said he did not have to do anything as they tabled the item for future discussion.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance No. 2025-O-06: Request to amend the Florida Shores Drainage Basin Building Permit Moratorium.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilwoman Gillis, to approve FP-2401, request for Final Plat approval for Smyrna Creek Preserve. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:

Matt Stoles, representative for DR Horton, offered to answer any questions or concerns regarding the project. The development team is present as well if there are any specific questions.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Mayor Depew expressed his opinion on not building until the stormwater master plan is completed but advised that this was the only subdivision he had not received a single complaint about. He had walked the development and made note of the large buffer and how the mobile home park behind it has been completely unaffected. He felt it was a subdivision that meets quality expectations and suggests other developers take note.
City Attorney Wolfe advised Council that if the Final Plat complies with the comprehensive plan, the land Development code, the zoning and the RPUD; then the application should be granted approval.
Mayor Depew asked who will be responsible to maintain the stormwater of the subdivision and around the property; Mr. Solstice explained the flow of the runoff and stated that County maintains the ditch along Old Mission for the project. The City part of the comp plan states that they have to either dedicate the wetlands and areas in conservation to St. Johns or the City. However the HOA will maintain the stormwater system on the specific site.
Councilwoman Dolbow liked that out of the 21 acres for this project, 15 are going to be conservation and that it flows north into wetlands.
Mayor Depew asked for a motion to approve.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilwoman Gillis, to approve Ordinance No. 2025-O-06; deleting the sentence "no pools shall be permitted". The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, provided a staff report and recommendation.
Council debated if banning pools specifically posed an equal protection issue. City Attorney Wolfe warned that allowing concrete-slab structures like sheds but not pools might lead to such a legal challenge, as it treats similar property owners differently. Mr. Solstice explained that with a "no fill" standard, residents may still build fences, driveways, pools, and sheds on a slab-on-grade, provided no fill dirt is used. He noted the moratorium has led to the denial of 15 to 30 pool permits.
Council also discussed the unintended impacts of the moratorium, noting residents' difficulties in obtaining permits for propane tank slabs and routine improvements. Councilwoman Gillis voiced frustration over repeated amendments needed to address these unforeseen issues. Both Councilwoman Dolbow and City Attorney Wolfe supported the proposal to remove the pool restriction as a straightforward solution.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Cindy Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, cautioned that pools with decks can cover as much impervious area as a house, and noted homeowners often fail to drain pools before storms. She said her neighbor's undrained pool led to flooding and caused her yard to collapse into the canal.
Art Slack, 3031 Umbrella Tree Drive, cautioned that pre-storm draining is impractical and stressed that the core issue is poor canal maintenance.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, shared his experience managing pool water levels before Hurricane Milton, noting a pool can serve as a personal retention pond when maintained properly. He supported allowing pools.
Corrie Sapp, 2630 Travelers Palm, expressed frustration that the moratorium has been amended repeatedly since its adoption and questioned whether it had been fully thought through before being initiated.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance No. 2025-O-06: Request to amend the Florida Shores Drainage Basin Building Permit Moratorium.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve FP-2400: Request for Final Plat approval for the Edgewater Phase Two. The motion failed by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, provided a staff report and recommendation.
Billy Dove, Attorney at Gray Robinson, appearing on behalf of the developer, addressed the Council. He stated that the final plat application is compliant and meets all City requirements. The Planning & Zoning Board had approved it and City Code mandates its acceptance. The developer filed a petition to protect appellate rights pending reconsideration, agreeing to withdraw if it is approved by May 21st. The emergency access road near 36th street will be gated for emergency use only. The stormwater ponds, designed for 100-year storms, are now stabilized and operational. The developer also reduced planned homes by about 34% and increased stormwater capacity.
The project engineer confirmed that the stormwater ponds failed during the September 2024 construction-phase rain events but said the berm is now redesigned and stabilized. He noted Florida Shores' drainage has flowed north since at least 1996, with prior flooding concerns. Planned units on Volco Road's west side decreased from 436 to 225, and on the east side, from 338 to 254 lots.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Ashley Applegate, 3422 Woodland Drive, noted ongoing runoff from Edgewater Preserve into Florida Shores and mentioned a neighbor using a pump to redirect development water. She pointed out that filled wetlands, elevated about five (5) feet above Florida Shores, create runoff that overwhelms the canal system.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, had observed water flowing from Edgewater Preserve into Florida Shores during rain events and suggested drainage solutions.
Cindy Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, spoke about the projects previous plans for being a golf course and expressed concern about future phase approvals, as ponds are built for regular rainfall, not hurricanes.
Mandi Bullard, 1417 Needle Palm Drive, had personally witnessed water flowing from the Edgewater Preserve property onto Umbrella Tree a few days before the recent election, and stated that the stormwater system's efficacy has not been proven under actual storm conditions.
Alan Rathbun, 131 Highland Avenue, has viewed video evidence of water flowing from the development into Florida Shores following pond failures, and characterized the failure during construction as constituting neglect regardless of whether the ponds were completed.
Mayor Depew stated on the record that he has also personally observed water coming off the property on three (3) separate occasions. Councilwoman Gillis stated she has stood knee-deep in water flowing off the property.
City Attorney Wolfe advised the Council that this is a quasi-judicial proceeding and that denial requires competent substantial evidence in the record demonstrating the application does not meet published criteria. He cited relevant sections of the Comprehensive Plan and Land Development Code referenced in the prior denial letter, including Policy 1.2.2 of the stormwater sub-element, and code sections addressing minimization of flood damage and limitations on fill placement.
Councilman Thomas stated that he would be willing to support the plat if the developer agreed to construct a canal or ditch between the development and Florida Shores as a mitigation measure, and indicated that he was otherwise planning to vote no. Attorney Dove declined, asserting that the application is fully compliant and approval is non-discretionary.
Councilwoman Dolbow noted that the preliminary plat phase is key for setting new conditions and confirmed that the application meets current code and plan criteria. Despite this, she was worried about continued runoff, highlighting that Florida Shores' converted swales to driveways over time have worsened drainage issues.
Councilman Rainbird stated that he could not in good conscience assure residents that the development will not produce runoff, and expressed skepticism based on years of experience on the Planning and Zoning Board.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed that residents rights are equally important as developers' appellate rights and stated emphatically that Florida Shores should not serve as the developments stormwater pond
Motion to deny FP-2400, the request for Final Plat approval for Edgewater Preserve Phase Two, was made by Councilman Rainbird and seconded by Mayor Depew. Upon roll call, the motion carried 4-1, with Councilwoman Dolbow voting no.
title: FP-2400: Request for Final Plat approval for Edgewater Preserve Phase Two generally located West of Volco Road.

action_text: A motion was made by Mayor DePew, second by Councilman Rainbird, to open that up for discussion. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Mayor Depew attended a Florida League of Mayors meeting and had spoken with the CRA Director from Sanford about opportunities.
Mayor Depew felt that residents were concerned with the performance of City Attorney Wolfe and had lost their trust in his abilities. He had read Mr. Wolfe's contract and would like to put out an RFQ for the position to have him reapply.
Mayor Depew passed the gavel to open up the discussion.
Mayor Depew spoke of the City Attorney's evaluation; Councilwoman Dolbow said she felt City Attorney Wolfe kept City Council informed and protected the City as per his contract. Councilwoman Gillis said she had also received complaints and felt that Mr. Wolfe was not pro-active enough.
Discussion ensued regarding the purpose of putting it out for bid; the content of the current contract and the possibilities of restructuring it and the public's perception of the City Attorney's role.
Councilwoman Dolbow had concerns about certain residents urging Councilmembers to go after employees jobs; she felt if there was a problem with an employee, it should be addressed privately. Mayor Depew pointed out that the Council only has jurisdiction over the City Manager; the City Clerk and the City Attorney. Councilwoman Dolbow acknowledged that but stated that employees are being attacked by residents and there are no repercussions.
Councilman Thomas expressed concern over the timing of the discussion and bringing in someone new who doesn't have the time or experience that Mr. Wolfe has as the City Attorney. He felt Mr. Wolfe does an excellent job and had kept the City from being sued up until recently. He had ultimately not participated in the evaluation process as he felt he was not qualified to do so.
Councilman Rainbird spoke of the number of interim positions currently in place; encouraged any residents who had issues to come forward and discuss it; and acknowledged that the employees were under a lot of pressure and could find opportunities elsewhere.
Councilman Thomas reiterated that he felt it was a bad time.
City Attorney Wolfe informed Council that his contract expires in January of 2026. Mayor Depew felt that City Attorney Wolfe does represent the City well but the public trust is not there.
Discussion ensued regarding when to discuss the contract; the terms of the former City Manager's contract; and how the termination of a City Manager should be handled. Councilman Thomas suggested that they wait until the City Attorney's contract is up; Mayor Depew said he felt they should wait until they hire a permanent City Manager.
Mayor Depew asked for an explanation of the minutes; City Attorney Wolfe advised that per the Sunshine Law chapter 286, minutes are required to be promptly recorded and kept of public meetings. Councilman Rainbird detailed his personal experiences with minutes and expressed displeasure over the state of them.
City Clerk Zlotnik explained that it was a lack of staff and time. For Planning and Zoning; the minutes done were not up to professional standards. Councilman Thomas believed there needs to be a Deputy City Clerk; Ms. Zlotnik said they were in need of both a Deputy City Clerk and an additional administrative assistant.
Councilwoman Gillis felt they should give consensus to allow the Deputy City Clerk position but Mayor Depew felt it should be discussed at budget time.
Councilman Thomas had received several phone calls, including one from Councilwoman Gillis about the drainage situation on Sea Gull Court. Sean Maroney, Interim Public Works Director, provided an explanation and plan to resolve the issue.
Councilman Thomas detailed a conversation with Robbie Lee from the Miami Corporation regarding the canal on Silver Palm Drive and asked about the plans regarding it; Mr. Maroney gave a detailed explanation.
Further discussion ensued regarding the maintenance/cost of clearing of the land donated by the County and possibly receiving some kind of assistance to do so.
Councilman Thomas shared plans of a ride along with Tommy Smith, Public Works Superintendent, and of his upcoming vacation.
Mayor Depew brought up an issue with an easement located at Fisherman's Cove and asked staff to reach out to them.
Councilwoman Dolbow discussed two (2) senate bills she had concerns with the school pick up situation at Indian River Elementary on 30th Street. Police Chief Joe Mahoney addressed her concerns.
Councilman Rainbird discussed his conversation with County Chair Jeff Brower; expressed gratitude for the Police Departments high water rescue vehicle; urged residents to be prepared for the worst when a hurricane comes; had toured and was impressed by the Edgewater portion of Deering Park; and attended the Edgefest Festival.
Councilwoman Gillis commended Parks and Recreation for their building capabilities; attended the Habitat Earth Day celebration; two (2) Florida League of Cities regional events; the Edgefest Earthday event; the second annual FDOT District 5 Safety Summit; the City's Hurricane Preparedness Seminar; the State of the State at the Brannon Center; the Volusia County Quarterly breakfast; the Florida Metropolitan Planning Organizations weekend institute. She met with various residents; delivered a proclamation celebrating John Stearns in New Smyrna Beach; she thanked numerous staff members from Public Works, Parks and Recreation, Development Services; and Code Enforcement for their efforts to resolve various issues. She participated in a ride along with the Police Department and spoke with Interim City Manager Thurman about the agenda and City Clerk Zlotnik regarding various issues.
Councilwoman Gillis discussed the possibility of buying pumps instead of renting them; Mayor Depew said he was all for it but wanted to check if a grant was possibly available.
Sean Maroney, Interim Public Works Director, advised that Florida Department of Emergency Management will provide the pumps for free. He felt it wasn't necessary to purchase them and have them on standby all year from a maintenance standpoint when they may only be used for two (2) months out of the year. If the City does have to rent pumps; it is reimbursed through FEMA if it's a declared event. He felt it was not fiscally responsible to purchase them and would rather use that grant money for other necessities. Mayor Depew discussed a previous event where pumps were not delivered as they were supposed to be.
Councilwoman Gillis mentioned Mango Tree Lake becoming a passive park for the community; Jason O'Keefe, Parks and Recreation Director acknowledged that it had been previously discussed but was not sure of all the details. Mayor Depew knew there were concerns about the depth of the lake; Mr. Maroney said that the banks were also too steep to have docks.
Council gave consensus to have further discussions on the matter.
Councilwoman Gillis felt that the amount of overtime that the Police Department uses a year would more than pay for four (4) additional officers to alleviate the amount of overtime needed and wanted to make sure that was reflected in the upcoming budget discussions.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve the first reading of Ordinance No. 2024-O-55. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, provided a staff report and recommendation.
Mr. Solstice explained why they could not put any language in regarding the mangroves if the Ordinance does not move forward to the second reading.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Mark Watts of Cobb Cole, 231 N Woodland Boulevard, representative for the applicant, acknowledged the multiple moving parts of the project and said they were asking Council to let everything be scheduled and heard on one agenda. He clarified that approving this wouldn't approve any final action; it would allow them to come back June 2nd with the annexation, the land use amendment, the PUD rezoning Ordinance and then the actual amendment to the PUD document to incorporate language Council had requested at prior meetings with regard to mangrove and shoreline protection.
Mayor Depew stated he was glad the applicant was working with the Riverside Conservancy and discussed the applicant entering into a contract to allow the conservancy to maintain the national shoreline. Mr. Watts acknowledged that language had been put into the agreement for the next meeting to coordinate through the Riverside Conservancy for the design of the shoreline. They had also discussed working together on grant opportunities; allowing some space in the ship store for the Conservancy to promote themselves and have parts of the proceeds from the sales of materials go towards the supporting of the Conservancy.
Councilwoman Dolbow appreciated that the project was moving forward in a positive manner and thanked them for partnering with Kelly McGee of the Riverside Conservancy.
Councilman Rainbird felt it didn't make sense to have the parcel be under someone else's control.
Mayor Depew inquired with City Attorney Wolfe and Mr. Solstice that the City has the ability to dictate how the shoreline is moving forward and that it could be put into the contract that the applicant had to work with the Riverside Conservancy.
Mr. Solstice advised that the current language stated that they are going to work and coordinate with Riverside Conservancy but they could request it be put into a contract in the PUD itself. The developer may not agree. Mayor Depew said he would only support it if that was done.
Mr. Watts said they would reach out to the Riverside Conservancy to confirm that they were okay with a contract being put in place.
Councilman Rainbird confirmed with Mr. Watts that the main intention was to add a vision barrier; add more mangroves and native species while removing some invasive plants. That is what they want to coordinate with the Riverside Conservancy to design.
Councilwoman Gillis asked if there was any other reason they wanted this annexed in; Mr. Watts said no, they just didn't want to have to split permitting between the City and the County. This streamlines the process.
Mr. Solstice advised that there were only three (3) things in the PUD amendment; increased dry stack storage parking, increase in dry stack storage and then what staff has added regarding the wetland plantings and mangroves.
Mayor Depew asked why the height increase of the dry stack storage; Mr. Watts clarified that they are not increasing the capacity or the amount of boats that can be stored, it's so they can design the building to withstand the 180 mile an hour wind loads as that requires additional structural mechanics and so they can have individual fire suppression equipment above each of the slips.
Councilwoman Gillis requested a sign falsely advertising the project be taken down; Mr. Watts agreed.
Mr. Solstice assured Council that this motion does not give the developer the right to do anything, it simply moves the item onto a second reading to add all contingencies; it remains under control of the County until after the second reading.
Councilman Rainbird and Councilwoman Dolbow agreed that residents would trust their own City rather than trust the County.
Mayor Depew closed the public hearing.

attachments: 2025-R-11 Budget Adjustments - June FY25 w Exhibit
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Resolution into the record.
Bridgette Vaissiere, Finance Director, provided a staff report and recommendation.
Mayor Depew stated that they normally don't do middle of the year budget adjustments; Ms. Vaissiere clarified that typically at minimum they do one mid-year and one final budget amendment for various things that may occur throughout the year such as various grant opportunities. The original operating budget is a fluid document.
Mayor Depew noted that they did not raise taxes or do a utility study this year; Ms. Vaissiere said that both were correct. Those things are done during the original budgeting process. The mid year or additional budget amendments are funded by either grants; impact fees or the CRA funds.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Councilman Rainbird inquired over the amendment to the City Manager search cost; Ms. Vaissiere confirmed that per the contract, the City would pay the cost of flying the candidates in to interview them. Ms. Vaissiere further explained that $10,000 was originally set aside when they believed there were five (5) candidates, not the remaining two (2) and that it is a high estimate. Anything that wasn't used would go back into the general fund.
Mayor Depew asked how many quotes they had gotten for the City Hall mitigation and remodeling; Jason O'Keefe, Parks and Recreation Director said they had gone with the original quote from the vendor who had done the mold study; he had gotten two (2) other quotes as well and they were all close and competitive.
Mayor Depew discussed the plans for the portion of City Hall being remodeled; the previous plans for the City Clerks office; the need to fix the mold problem and the additional cost for the City Manager search.
Ms. Vaissiere reiterated for Mayor Depew that the $10,000 was based on five (5) candidates and that they had estimated high. City Clerk Zlotnik explained that it was a direct reimbursement so they would not know the exact costs until the candidates provided receipts.
Mayor Depew commended staff for their efforts towards the budget and asked if there were additional comments.
Councilwoman Gillis felt unimpressed by the remaining City Manager candidates and felt they should go back out for more applicants, possibly without SGR. City Clerk Zlotnik informed Council that she isn't sure of the exact details of the contract but that the interviews were scheduled for the following week.
Mayor Depew wanted consensus to hold a workshop to discuss the contract and figure out what Council wanted to do.
Councilwoman Dolbow felt they should approve the budget with the $10,000 just in case it was needed; if it wasn't, it would simply go back into the general fund.
Further discussion ensued on how Council felt they should handle the City Manager Search; the cost of the candidates travel and the SGR contract.
City Attorney Wolfe said he would have to review the contract before giving legal advice.
City Clerk Zlotnik said it would be up to Council to see if there is a penalty to not move forward with SGR and do an independent search. City Attorney Wolfe recommended a public meeting so the residents can participate.
City Clerk Zlotnik said she would not be comfortable heading an independent search as she is not Human Resources but she would figure it out if she had to do so.
Council agreed to hold a special meeting and planned to schedule it during the City Clerks report.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to accept interviewing the two applicants. The motion failed by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Prior to the main agenda item, Mayor Depew invited Interim City Manager Mahoney to deliver a 96-hour update. Mr. Mahoney reported the following actions taken since assuming the role:
• Authorization to purchase two pumps: one for post-storm continuous flow at the 18th Street Canal, and one for pre-storm capacity at Duck Lake to address flooding in the Gaslight Subdivision. A budget amendment will be presented at the July 7th Council meeting.
• Public Works will develop a written policy for pump operation and maintenance.
• Three (3) building inspectors will be sent to a stormwater certification training scheduled for late July, granting them authority to issue stop work orders for construction violations such as improper silt fencing, erosion controls, and dewatering.
• Code Enforcement reviewed all previous private stormwater violations; three (3) locations were found out of compliance and enforcement action has been initiated.
• A more consistent schedule for the vac truck and concrete catch basin repairs is being developed, with an update to follow at the July 7th meeting.
• The City Hall remodel, previously halted, has been restarted.
• An offer to purchase 104 N Park Place has been submitted.
• Meetings with all department directors are underway, with progress on budget and flood prevention matters.
Councilwoman Gillis noted that the building inspectors' certification classes are scheduled for the following week, meaning they would be licensed by the end of that week.
Councilman Thomas inquired about the status of negotiations with Lennar. Mr. Mahoney confirmed he is still working through notes from his predecessor and will be reaching out to Councilman Thomas for clarification before making formal contact.
Contract Review and Council Discussion
City Attorney Wolfe explained the SGR contract's key points, noting a fixed fee of $27,009 paid in four (4) parts: 30% at contract start, 30% after presenting applicants, 30% post-interviews, and 10% upon employment acceptance. The contract offers a placement guarantee to redo the search at no extra fee, though the City covers costs like background checks. Utilizing New Smyrna Beach's contract, there's a termination clause needing 30 days' notice and fair payment for work done. Options for Council include: (1) ending the contract now to save 40% of the fees; (2) using the performance guarantee to restart; (3) conducting finalist interviews to save 10%. The shift from 5 to 2 candidates could justify invoking the performance guarantee.
Mayor Depew acknowledged that SGR fulfilled their contractual duties by presenting five (5) candidates, though three (3) withdrew. He voiced dissatisfaction with the remaining candidates based on his research into their backgrounds. He highlighted the challenge of hiring a City Manager amid hurricane season and budget cycle but expressed strong support for maintaining a national search. He affirmed full confidence in Interim City Manager Mahoney's leadership during this interim phase.
Councilwoman Dolbow stated her desire to interview the remaining two (2) candidates, noting the six-month investment and the City's commitment. She welcomed the idea of an outsider with a new perspective. However, she recognized the need to reopen the search if the candidates were unsatisfactory and warned that further delays might lead to losing qualified candidates to other opportunities.
Councilman Thomas stated he was not comfortable with the reported travel costs to bring candidates in, expressing the view that a candidate sufficiently motivated to serve the City would fund their own travel. He stated a preference for more time to evaluate options and expressed strong confidence in Mr. Mahoney, citing his institutional knowledge of the City, its budget process and its hurricane history.
Councilwoman Gillis supported moving forward by interviewing the two (2) candidates before deciding to reopen the search, expressing confidence in the Search Committee and a preference to complete the current process first.
Councilman Rainbird worried about losing the two (2) remaining candidates to other jobs due to delays but recognized the limited pool and time needed for more interviews. He was unsure which path to take.
Councilwoman Gillis added that if the search was reopened, the two (2) existing candidates could reapply along with new applicants.
Councilwoman Dolbow suggested pausing the search until after hurricane season and then reopening with SGR, expressing confidence in Mr. Mahoney to carry the City through hurricane and budget season in the interim.
Councilman Rainbird questioned the effectiveness of immediately reopening the search, noting the previous search resulted in about 15 video interviewees, reducing to two (final) finalists. He inquired about how swiftly SGR could gather more applicants.
Interim City Manager Mahoney informed the Council that starting a hybrid in-house search before October or November is unfeasible to hurricane season and the budget cycle. He cautioned against immediately reopening the SGR search, as it might not draw significantly more applicants shortly after the previous round. He mentioned the option of considering alternate search firms.
Councilwoman Gillis suggested that if the Council wished to provide updated parameters to SGR, this could be done via email or Zoom rather than requiring an in-person visit, at less cost to the city.
Mayor DePew emphasized the need for a unifying city manager with effective team-building skills, acknowledging the continued community interest. He expressed willingness to either continue or pause the search, depending on Council consensus, and underscored the need to retain the current City Manager Search Committee if the search is relaunched.
SGR Representative Kevin clarified via phone that reopening the search is part of the original service and won't activate the performance guarantee, meant for replacement post-hire. Only incremental candidate expenses, like background checks, would incur charges. He mentioned that around two months have passed since the last search concluded and new candidates are expected. Additionally, one of the current finalists is a Florida resident with hurricane experience, which addresses Council concerns.
An unnamed member of the audience advised the Council to complete the current process as it had already been paid for, allowing for a repeat without extra fees, and emphasized a guarantee for further attempts if needed. She urged the Council to meet the candidates within 60 days and consider reopening the search if the candidates proved unsatisfactory.
Art Slack, 3031 Umbrella Tree Drive, expressed confidence in Interim City Manager Mahoney's readiness and urged prioritizing hurricane preparedness, suggesting the City Manager search resume after addressing storm season threats.
Donna McDavid, 1201 Bond Street, urged the Council to cut ties with SGR due to communication issues, noting that the committees information requests were unmet. She suggested waiting until the season's end to reassess the approach.
Tim London, 2632 Woodland Drive, encouraged Council to follow through and interview the two (2) remaining candidates. He stated that doing so would either confirm or rule out their suitability, and that the process would be a learning experience regardless of the outcome.
A second public comment was offered by the gentleman who had spoken earlier, who noted that a stormwater master plan had been anticipated. Mayor DePew confirmed that the stormwater master plan will not be completed until November.
Following citizens' comments, the Council returned to deliberation. Councilwoman Dolbow moved to proceed with interviewing the two candidates.
Following the failed motion, Mayor DePew discussed pausing the search for six months due to hurricane and budget season, with Interim City Manager Mahoney continuing in his role. The Council agreed to later reopen the search with SGR, using the existing vetted City Manager Search Committee. SGR's representative Kevin confirmed there would be no extra professional fee to restart, only incremental costs for candidates.
title: City Manager Search - Review of SGR Contract and determine whether or not to reopen position for new applicants.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve item 8a; Ordinance No. 2024-O-47. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Interim City Manager Mahoney provided a staff report and recommendation.
Mark Watts of Cobb Cole, 231 N Woodland Boulevard, representative for the applicant, discussed the history of the project; the different items before Council; residents concerns and suggestions; and the future of the development.
Jim Lovgren, 182 Jones Fish Camp Road, thanked Council and Interim City Manager Mahoney for reaching out in response to a letter he had sent; presented a petition signed by residents of Jones Fish Camp Road regarding road improvements and access ways and shared his disapproval of the annexation.
Extensive Council discussion followed regarding: road design sequencing, whether the road must be built first, the developer's responsibility for the majority of the road costs, the possibility of accessing adjacent property owned by Ralph Richardson for a secondary entrance, the developers prior unsuccessful attempts to purchase the Richardson property, the applicant's commitment to hold a public workshop with Jones Fish Camp Road residents before finalizing the road design, the City's performance bond protections, and that no construction can begin without a road agreement coming back to Council for approval.
Mr. Watts offered to add language to paragraph F (road agreement) and paragraph G (entrance to project) in the development agreement requiring: (1) a public workshop with the community prior to finalizing the road agreement, and (2) evaluation of the Richardson property as a possible secondary or construction access point, with results reported back to Council.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, explained that City staff recommends the road be built at the end of construction rather than at the beginning, to avoid damage from heavy construction vehicles, and that the City has approximately $775,000 in impact fee obligations toward the road from prior development (Riverfront Estates). He noted apartments under construction on Jones Fish Camp Road are already required to repave their section when done.
Councilman Rainbird noted the development would allocate approximately 43% of the City's available boat slips.
Mayor Depew confirmed that the public boat ramp project is a separate issue not affected by this development, and that any final road design and site plan must return to Council for approval before construction begins.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilman Thomas, second by Councilwoman Dolbow. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe advised the Council to reconsider its vote from the June 2nd meeting about the All Florida Plumbing appeal. The property owner was not properly informed beforehand and only found out about the hearing from a public member on the day itself, leaving them unable to attend. He mentioned that City protocol normally includes notifying the applicants, but staff had failed to do so in this instance. City policy permits any Councilmember from the prevailing side of the four-to-one vote to request a reconsideration within a year.
Mayor Depew expressed disagreement, noting the agenda is publicly posted and property owners bear responsibility for monitoring it, particularly when they know there is an issue with their property.
Councilwoman Dolbow and Councilman Thomas argued that business owners cannot be expected to constantly monitor agendas and that the CIty has an obligation to notify when a property is on the agenda.
On the Gottlieb Case, City Attorney Wolfe reported that the plaintiff failed to respond to discovery despite a court order, the plaintiff's attorney withdrew, and the plaintiff failed to either hire new counsel or proceed pro se within 30 days. A motion to dismiss was filed and granted. The case had been dismissed against the City.
title: b. City Attorney

minutes_note:
Interim City Manager Mahoney explained that the K9 in question earlier had been placed with former Police Officer Rippeon's family due to the cost/extended time they would have to board the dog; the lack of staffing to train a new handler; the length of time to train and the age of the dog at that point. They had done what they felt was best for the Department and the dog; it was a humane decision and a business decision. There was a contract in place stating the dog could never be used for Law Enforcement services and could never be gifted or sold to any other entity or person.
In reference to the Form 61; Mr. Mahoney explained that it's all under the Florida Police's Bill of Rights. The Officer was the subject of an internal investigation that the Police Department had issued. Acting Chief Geiger concluded the investigation and sustained the policy violations; at that point, the officer was no longer under investigation. In between the conclusion of the investigation and the mandatory statutory required disciplinary hearing, the officer resigned. The Florida statute pertaining to the officer Bill of Rights required a disciplined hearing. Mr. Mahoney then explained the process an agency goes through to hire a new employee and said that everything was done above board.
Councilman Thomas wasn't thrilled that the former Officer kept the dog but understood their choices were limited; Mayor Depew agreed that none of Council is thrilled about the situation but wanted people to understand that it was out of Council's hands.
Mr. Mahoney confirmed that the dog was still alive.
Mr. Mahoney gave a brief introduction and recap over his accomplishments in his first few weeks as Interim involving Building Inspectors; Stormwater; Code Enforcement; Public Works; City Hall remodel; a possible program to utilize inmates; the purchase of a property located near City Hall; and the open positions at the City.
He informed Council of the new lobby and parking lot conduct policy put in place to protect employees who may face harassment. He had met with all Directors to determine their needs and share his expectations for them as well and was coordinating with HR to determine which positions they could potentially alter the education requirements for; so someone without a high school diploma or GED would qualify. He announced that Chris Love had been promoted to Deputy Director of Parks and Recreation.
Mr. Mahoney advised that he was working to set up a team building for the Council and whomever is in the City Managers seat as he believes it will foster cohesion.
He shared that he had attended the Police Academy graduation and congratulated Officer Feliciano as he is the first Officer they have sponsored through the Academy; Transform 386; the Fourth of July event; the new Public Works groundbreaking; had met with the Boys and Girls Club Youth Civic session at Habitat for Humanity and several residents to try to resolves their issues.
