minutes_note:
Bliss Jamison, 635 Air Park Road, addressed the Council regarding an upcoming Disaster Preparedness and Business Continuity Webinar to be held on August 12, 2025. The seminar is hosted by the Southeast Volusia Manufacturing and Technology Coalition and will feature presentations by the Small Business Administration and the Small Business Development Center at Daytona State College.
Art Slack, 3031 Umbrella Tree Drive, discussed an unresolved issue with water lettuce in a canal. He explained that although he previously brought this to the City's attention and some work began, it was not completed. Upon following up, Public Works staff claimed the water lettuce was completely removed, but Mr. Slack argued that it had merely shifted to a different part of the canal. He expressed concerns about these inaccurate claims and requested further action.
Cindy Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, spoke on the budget workshop and water rate increases, stating that the rate for 0-2,000 gallons rose by 68.1%, from $2.79 to $4.69. She felt that the increase burdens seniors and low-income residents who use less. She also asked Council to explore solutions like an opt-out option for recycling during the budget workshop.
Carmine Wallace, 2331 Mango Tree Drive, discussed the flooding on Mango Tree Drive post July 15th rain event, detailing issues with a culvert. A crack had been filled with concrete and it was causing drainage problems.
Frank Potemski, 3331 Mango Tree Drive, corroborated Ms. Wallace's account as he has the same drainage issue due to a notch in the back of the catch basin being concreted over and an abundance of debris. He discussed an unproductive conversation with the City engineer who had not been helpful and stated that no one had ever come out to inspect the catch basin until the most recent flood. He urged Council to take action.
Carmen Arana, 2403 Mango Tree Drive, also complained about the concrete being used to fill in the opening on the catch basins as it was causing water to back up. She provided photographs and video and offered to share them with the Council. Ms. Arana urged that the situation needed urgent attention heading into hurricane season.
Nelson Rivera, 1723 Willow Oak Drive, raised two concerns. First, he observed that many swales throughout Edgewater are too shallow to hold water, causing overflow onto streets and contributing to broader flooding. He noted that the entire drainage infrastructure must function as a coordinated system to be effective. Second, he raised a traffic concern regarding SR 442 between US 1 and Air Park Road and cars going well over the speed limit. He felt a traffic signal in that corridor between the two points could help regulate traffic flow in addition to enforcement efforts.
title: CITIZEN COMMENTS

minutes_note:
Councilwoman Gillis shared that she had met with numerous residents and addressed many concerns, particularly in the aftermath of the rain event, going out to meet people, taking notes, and photographing issues to relay to Interim City Manager Mahoney and appropriate staff. She encouraged residents experiencing issues to reach out to Councilmembers so that matters can be directed to the correct people.
Councilman Thomas reported that he had driven during the rain event to assess conditions, acknowledging that while the City still has work to do, there has been considerable improvement. He had ridden with Tommy Smith that day along the road leading into the hammock and was impressed to see water flowing south down the ditch behind Silver Palm Drive and into the cypress swamp, where he said it naturally belongs. He noted that the canal behind Florida Shores is large, approximately 25-30 feet wide, and that City workers were actively digging out culverts throughout. He commended Interim City Manager Mahoney for the performance of City staff, noting workers had cleared roughly a mile of that road. He added that with continued work to dig out that ditch, a significant volume of water from the back side of Florida Shores will be directed into the hammock where it belongs. Regarding traffic concerns raised by Mr. Rivera, Councilman Thomas noted that Police enforcement is underway.
Councilwoman Dolbow thanked all City workers for their response during the rain event. She stated that every issue she had brought to Interim City Manager Mahoney had been taken care of, that responses to residents were prompt, and that residents were very impressed and thankful. She described seeing the pump deployed at Lime Tree and spoke with a worker who explained that the equipment was being used to move water more quickly from Pine Tree toward a canal behind her home. She had taken a tour of the upcoming industrial business coming to Edgewater, INCERTEC. She noted that they had purchased a 36,000-square-foot building in January and received its renovation permit in July, with an anticipated opening in mid-to-late October. The company has already invested $2,000,000 in equipment in the existing facility and plans to invest an additional $4,000,000 in an expansion, which is a total of $6,000,000 in taxable equipment, in addition to regular property taxes. She noted the company will have 50 to 60 high-quality, good-paying jobs at opening and anticipates 150 jobs following the expansion within approximately two years. She emphasized the importance of preserving the adjacent 137 acres of vacant industrial land for future industrial development, and expressed enthusiasm that Intersect's presence would likely attract other manufacturers who need its services.
Mayor Depew echoed Councilwoman Dolbow's comments, noting that INCERTEC is located at the former Factory Direct building across from Boston Whaler. He felt it was a perfect match for the City. He thanked Bliss Jamison and the Volusia Manufacturing organization as well as Development Services Director Ryan Solstive for helping facilitate the businesses arrival.
Councilman Rainbird had attended a budget workshop and was surprised that the City holds $4 million in reserves. He suggested redirecting $1 million for infrastructure improvements like Queen Palm Drive instead of increasing water rates, which are a common resident complaint. During a flood event while he was in North Carolina, he kept in touch with City leadership, ensuring quick response and action. He urged residents to report issues to City staff. Councilman Rainbird criticized SB 180 for limiting local government authority, and proposed joining the legal challenge against it. He also recommended explaining drainage systems to residents at a future meeting.
Councilwoman Gillis interjected with her support of challenging SB 180, suggesting that the topic be discussed further at the following day's workshop. She referenced City Attorney Wolfe being in contact with an attorney experienced in challenging similar State preemption measures.Councilman Thomas also expressed support, noting that multiple cities were expected to join together in a legal challenge. Mayor Depew stated that all Councilmembers appear mutually aligned in opposition to SB 180, and referenced the consensus given at a previous meeting for City Attorney Wolfe to reach out to an attorney who had previously been successful in eliminating form 6 requirements.
Mayor Depew addressed the flooding and box culvert concerns raised by multiple citizens during public comment. He stated he received 41 calls regarding water retention areas following the July 15th event.
He commended City staff for their response, recognizing Interim City Manager Mahoney, Tommy Smith, Sean Maroney, and others. Two (2) homes were saved from flooding and the deployment of pumps on Queen Palm Drive was notably successful, transforming a barely passable road to completely dry in two (2) hours.
Regarding box culverts, Mayor Depew stated that residents contacted the State, leading the St. Johns Water Management District to direct the City's Public Works to concrete over the culverts by a deadline. He expressed frustration, noting this action contributed to flooding. He has been having ongoing discussions with State Representative Chase Tramont, who is setting a meeting to address it. In the interim, He and Interim City Manager Mahoney are considering a short term fix that adheres to St. Johns Water Management standards, for emergencies. Mayor Depew is looking forward to finding a permanent solution.
Interim City Manager Mahoney added that, without stating it as official City policy with respect to regulatory compliance, if that City were under a declared state of emergency and residents were in danger of flooding, the City would open the box culverts and deal with the regulatory consequence afterward.
At Mayor Depew's request, Sean Maroney, Interim Deputy Director of Public Works, provided an updat on drainage work near 30th Street, commonly referred to as the Silver Palm Canal.
Mr. Maroney reported that the City has cleared and opened the west-running canal, removing trees to enhance access and water flow. Out of seven (7) crossing restrictions; at least three (3) had been removed to improve water flow, with only two (2) crossings kept for essential access. Mayor Depew thanked Mr. Milligan for the update and expressed enthusiasm about the progress.
Mayor Depew requested, based on Councilman Rainbird's earlier suggestion, that Interim City Manager Mahoney or his designee present an explanation at the next Council meeting of what a box culvert is, how it functions, why retention areas hold water by design, and what happens when debris enters a box culvert. Council gave consensus.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve Resolution No. 2025-R-28 Authorization for the City Manager to enter into agreements with Volusia County for acceptance of properties acquired through the Housing and Urban Development Community Disaster Block Program (CBDG-DR) for funding the single family homeowner repair and replacement program and the homeowner recovery program buyout pathway. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Resolution into the record.
Interim City Manager Mahoney explained that Volusia County received CBDG-DR funding from HUD for disaster recovery after Hurricane Ian and Milton. The Office of Recovery and Resiliency, called Transform 386, manages programs for Single-Family Homeowner Repair and the Hurricane Milton Homeowner Recovery. These programs offer voluntary buyouts for properties in flood areas. Local governments can receive titles to these properties, with land use restricted to open space, floodplain, or wetlands management. The City will handle ongoing maintenance. Approval was recommended for the City Manager to execute necessary documents with Volusia County for property acquisition
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Councilwoman Dolbow stated that she had researched the program and confirmed that approximately $20,0000 is available for buyouts. She noted that the buyout portion of the program is anticipated to open by the end of July and is administered through the County. She clarified that there is no City-maintained list of interested residents; residents interested in a potential buyout should contact the County or watch the City's newsletter and social media for further information. She noted that the City can also assist in connecting residents with the appropriate County contacts.
Mayor Depew asked for clarification on whether the City has any monetary obligations under this program. Interim City Manager Mahoney confirmed that the City would only be responsible for maintaining properties once ownership is transferred, and that the City is not contributing to the purchase price. The funding is federal and administered through the County.
Councilwoman Gillis clarified for public record that this is an entirely voluntary program for residents who may be interested, and is not the City seeking to acquire properties. Residents could apply on their own if interested.
Councilman Rainbird got confirmation that it was aimed at acquiring flood prone properties for potential demolition and conversion to water retention areas. He raised several questions about the logistics, including potential costs for demolition and hauling, and environmental compliance concerns if the City were to demolish structures. He expressed hope that the program would not become more complex or costly than anticipated, and asked that staff obtain more detailed answers on these points for future discussion.
Mayor Depew noted that resident with more questions may contact Donna DeMarsh at Volusia County, who oversees the program.
Mayor Depew closed the public hearing.
title: Resolution No. 2025-R-28: Authorization for the City Manager to enter into agreements with Volusia County for the acceptance of properties acquired through the Housing and Urban Development’s (HUD) Community Disaster Block Grant-Disaster Recovery (CBDG-DR) program of funding the single-family homeowner repair and replacement program and the homeowner recovery program buyout pathway.

attachments: 2025 Preliminary Tax Rolll with Roll Back Calculaiton for FY26
minutes_note:
Bridgette Vaissiere, Finance Director, advised that pursuant to Florida Statute 200.069, the Council must authorize the advertisement of the maximum millage rate for the upcoming budget year as part of the TRIM notice. The current operating millage rate is 6.33 per $1,000 of assessed value. The current taxable value is $2,222,709,693. The current year rollback millage rate is 5.9161 per $1,000 of assessed value. At the rollback rate, preliminary ad valorem taxes for FY26 would be $12,492,284 at 95% collection rate. At the current 6.33 millage rate, estimated preliminary ad valorem taxes would be $13,149,773. Staff noted the FY26 proposed budget was presented at the July 8th budget workshop and is based on the 6.33 millage rate. Staff sought authorization to advertise the Edgewater Operating maximum millage as part of the 2025 TRIM notice.

Mayor Depew noted for the public record that this action is not approving a millage rate, but rather authorizing the rate to be advertised on the TRIM notice, which notifies property owners of the proposed maximum. He clarified that the rate can be reduced after this point but cannot be increased beyond the maximum without extraordinary re-noticing requirements. He confirmed that the rate is held flat from the prior year, though under Florida Statute it is still considered and advertised as a tax increase due to rising property values.
Mayor Depew closed the public hearing.

title: a. City Clerk

action_text: A motion was made by Councilman Thomas, second by Councilman Rainbird, to discuss the termination of the City Clerk without cause. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe reported two (2) new lawsuits:
Bristol West Insurance company related to a car accident with a City Police Officer. Mr. Wolfe had filed a motion to dismiss because (1) proper pre-suit notice was not given to the City, and (2) the City employee was improperly named as a defendant, having individual immunity. After the plaintiff filed an amended complaint, Mr. Wolfe filed another motion to dismiss, leading the plaintiff to dismiss the case voluntarily. He anticipates the plaintiff will send proper notice, wait six (6) months, and then possibly refile. The case is currently dismissed without prejudice.
Mr. Patel v. City of Edgewater and a City employee: The case involves an automobile accident and was recently served. City Attorney Wolfe stated the he has not yet filed a response but intends to do so within the following week.
Councilman Thomas raised concerns regarding City Clerk Zlotnik. He outlined several concerns he had accumulated and stated that he would like to move to terminate the City Clerk without cause.
Mayor Depew asked if a second Councilmember would like to bring the motion forward for discussion and requested a roll call to open said discussion.
Councilman Rainbird stated that he had also received phone calls from residents regarding the City Clerk. He cited concerns about how meeting minutes would be completed, and noted a specific remark made at the previous meeting that he characterized as very unprofessional.
Councilwoman Gillis stated that she personally had not had problems with the City Clerk. She noted that Ms. Zlotnik is always professional, answers her questions promptly, and completes tasks that she is asked to perform. She acknowledged that concerns raised may be valid but suggested that some issues may be attributable to staffing shortages and workload. She suggested the situation may benefit from a conversation about how the Clerk's office can better serve all members of Council, particularly Councilman Thomas, and whether adaptations could be made to his communication preferences.
Councilwoman Dolbow stated that she has also never had issues with the City Clerk and finds Ms. Zlotnik to be professional, prompt and responsive to her requests. She offered that perhaps a constructive conversation was in order rather than termination but acknowledged that Councilmembers should not miss meetings and should be held to the same accountability standard regardless of communication method. She had difficulty understanding how the remark alleged to have been made in Chambers could have been heard by residents seated 15 feet away, behind a screen. Mayor Depew noted that Ms. Zlotnik herself acknowledged that the comment had been made, which he admitted was the right thing to do.
Councilman Thomas reiterated his position, noting that when he was previously Mayor, City Clerk Zlotnik had printed his emails and placed them in his inbox and questioned why she could not do the same now.
Mayor Depew believes that City Clerk Zlotnik has done a tremendous job overall but echoed concerns about follow-through on certain agenda-related communications he had requested and about public records issues brought to his attention by community members.
City Attorney Wolfe advised that the City Clerk's contract does allow for termination with or without cause with 30 days' notice. He confirmed that termination without cause constitutes a termination for convenience and does not require a stated reason. He noted that upon termination without cause, the City Clerk would be entitled to 20 weeks of severance pay and other benefits set forth in the contract.
After the motion was made, City Attorney Wolfe confirmed that the 30-day notice period commences immediately, that City Clerk Zlotnik is expected to continue performing her regular duties throughout the 30-day period and will be compensated accordingly, and that severance pay and other contractual benefits will commence upon the conclusion of the notice period.
City Attorney Wolfe noted that a special meeting may need to be scheduled to appoint a new City Clerk as the City Charter requires the City Clerk to be appointed by the City Council and this function cannot be delegated to the City Manager. He noted than an interim may need to be identified.
Interim City Manager Mahoney stated that he would provide an update at the following day's workshop regarding available options, either in-house or external, for an interim City Clerk appointment.
title: b. City Attorney

minutes_note:
Interim City Manager presented the following updates to Mayor and Council:
Council Chamber Sound System: the lapel microphones and additional sound system capacity have been ordered. An installation date in late August is anticipated.
Duck Lake Project: The contract was awarded to THADCON. Field survey work commenced during the week of the meeting to locate utilities prior to construction. Construction is scheduled to begin the week of July 28th. The project included 72 feet of pipe underneath Needle Palm Drive at 17th Street, installation of a control structure at the northeast corner of Needle Palm and 17th Street that will pump into an outfall, and a concrete pad installed on 17th Street near the southwest corner of Duck Lake to place the pump. The project is expected to take a couple of weeks.
Strategic CRA Acquisitions: The City is looking to acquire 123 W Park Avenue and 114 N Riverside Drive, which aligns with the long-term plan for Park Avenue.
Traffic and Speeding at Jones Fish Camp Road: The Police Department conducted a speed survey between July 7th and July 14th, recording 904 vehicles during that period. The department is continuing to study the location to determine the appropriate speed limit and has increased enforcement in the area.
Rain Event - Invest 93: The system affected the City on July 15th, with the majority of rain falling between 8am and noon. Approximately 4-6 inches of rain fell depending on location, with total rain saturation for the 48-hour period at approximately 10 inches. Interim City Manager Mahoney stated the City fared very well overall with a robust, all-hands-on-deck response. New pumps were deployed to move water in the Queen Palm and Lime Tree Drive area, and both VAC trucks were utilized to prevent water intrusion at specific homes. action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Councilman Rainbird, to appoint Monique Toupin as the Interim City Clerk, effective August 21, while the City opens up for taking applications. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Interim City Manager Mahoney presented three (3) options to the Council for filling the City Clerk vacancy. He explained that outgoing City Clerk Zlotnik had decided to utilize vacation time and will remain technically in her role until August 20th, although she will not return to the office. Assistant to the City Clerk Toupin will be acting in the City Clerk capacity during the 30 days, without an official interim title.
Three options were presented:
1. Appoint Monique Toupin as Interim City Clerk effective August 21st, immediately advertise the position, and allow the City Manager and HR to conduct interviews and vet candidates, with Council making the final selection. Interim City Manager noted that Ms. Toupin had indicated that she did not wish to hold the position permanently.
2. Consider external applicant Kelly McQuillan, whose resume and qualifications had been placed on the agenda. Interim City Manager Mahoney disclosed that on the morning of the meeting, at approximately 10am, he received an investigative report from the City of New Smyrna Beach indicating sustained policy violations. He stated that staff would need more time to review the report before making a recommendation, but that the Council was welcome to review it and make a determination.
3. Pause the process and allow the Interim City Manager to return with additional recommendations at the August 18th City Council meeting.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Councilwoman Gillis stated that she would like to see multiple candidates, not just a single recommendation finalist, and expressed support for advertising the position.
Mayor Depew preferred that the position be advertised, that he gets to view every applicant submitted, and expressed full confidence in Mr. Mahoney and HR to conduct the interviews. City Council will retain the hiring authority.
Councilwoman Dolbow only wanted to meet qualified candidates with the proper accreditations and certifications, rather than all applicants, noting the importance of candidates who are ready to serve upon hiring. She indicated that she would support seeing at least five (5) finalists rather than three (3).
Councilman Thomas emphasized that the City Clerk's office is a critical function and stressed the need to move expeditiously. He supported advertising the position and having HR and the Interim City Manager handle vetting, and inquired whether a college degree was a formal requirement. He expressed support for preferred rather than required college education, noting that the position should not discriminate against otherwise qualified candidates.
Mayor Depew noted that the previous City Clerk did not hold a college degree when first appointed and pursued her education while serving. He recommended that a college degree be preferred but not required, and that State Clerk certification be the baseline qualification. Council reached consensus that a bachelor’s degree would be preferred, not required.
City Attorney Wolfe and Interim City Manager Mahoney confirmed that neither the City Charter nor State law mandates a college degree for the City Clerk position. Interim City Manager noted that the current job description lists a bachelor’s degree in public administration, business or a related field as required, but indicated this could be adjusted per Council direction.
Julie Christine, HR Director, confirmed the direction and asked whether an associate's degree should be required. Council consensus was that college education would be preferred but not required, with State Clerk certification being the key qualifying credential. Interim City Manager Mahoney noted that educational requirements could be incorporated as contract stipulations for the selected candidate.
Interim City Manager confirmed that he was aware of at least two (2) internal employees who had expressed interest in the position as of that morning. Councilwoman Gillis expressed support for promoting from within to maintain staff morale.
Council reached the following consensus on the hiring process: advertise the position for 30 days beginning July 29th through approximately August 29th-30th; HR and the Interim City Manager will vet applicants; all applications will be sent to Councilmembers for review; the Interim City Manager and HR will conduct interviews and recommend the top five (5) finalists; a special meeting will be held for Council to discuss applicants and conduct interviews. Councilwoman Gillis noted the importance of Council retaining the option to request interviews with applicants beyond the top five (5) if desired.
Assistant to the City Clerk noted that the Florida Association of City Clerks maintains a job posting page that could be utilized for statewide outreach. Interim City Manager Mahoney indicated the position would also be posted on Indeed, the League of Cities platform, and clerk-specific outlets.
Councilman Thomas inquired about the anticipation salary range for the position. Interim City Manager Mahoney stated that the salary is not formally set as the position reports directly to the Council, but that the anticipated range would be $85,000-$100,000 based on the qualifications.
Ms. Toupin expressed her willingness to serve as Interim City Clerk until a permanent hire is made. She had received consistent training from Ms. Zlotnik over four (4) years and is close to completing her CMC. While she is currently most comfortable in her Assistant role, she does not dismiss the possibility of eventually pursuing the permanent City Clerk position.
Councilman Thomas emphasized the issue of Tallahassee contacting him about a financial disclosure filing via email, which he did not receive. This oversight, linked to the City Clerk's responsibilities, led to potential fines. He highlighted the need for timely and reliable communication from the Clerk’s office.
Kelly McQuillan, 2021 India Palm Drive, expressed her interest in the City Clerk position. She shared decades of municipal experience, including eight (8) years as the New Smyrna Beach City Clerk and a year at Port Orange. She resides in Edgewater and shared her favorite role as City Clerk. She confidently felt she was a suitable candidate for the City of Edgewater and requested consideration upon the opening of formal applications. Mayor DePew acknowledged that Ms. McQuillan has a strong resume and that he received mostly positive feedback from New Smyrna Beach residents, along with some questions regarding matters that arose during her tenure there.
After the vote to appoint Ms. Toupin as Interim, City Manager Mahoney raised the matter of her compensation as she serves in the interim capacity. He noted that her current annual salary is approximately $47,000 and recommended a salary of $65,000. City Attorney Wolfe advised that a formal motion was required. .
Additional Business - Small Business Spotlight Program:
Mayor Depew proposed that the City consider adopting a monthly small business spotlight program, similar to what other municipalities have implemented. The spotlighted business could rotate monthly between the four council districts and the Mayor. Council members expressed support, and Mayor DePew noted that the chosen business doesn't have to be in the nominating member's district.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow to approve 2025-O-09. The motion failed for a lack of second.
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Interim City Manager Mahoney presented the staff report, explaining that the Ordinance prohibits the operation of motor assisted electric bicycles in any City park, sidewalk, trail, or green space unless powered solely by human effort through pedaling. He emphasized the Ordinance applies only to City parks, not City-wide, and is intended to protect pedestrians, particularly children and seniors. If a rider is pedaling like a conventional bicycle, the Ordinance would not apply.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Danielle Bailey, 2107 Tatum Boulevard, New Smyrna Beach, expressed strong opposition to the Ordinance. Identifying as handicapped, she relies on a three-wheeled electric bicycle for her 20-mile daily commute. She expressed ADA compliance concerns, asserting it's a HIPAA violation for Police to question her disability status. Furthermore, she warned of possible legal action if banned from riding in the City.
Jamie Graves, 2114 Pine Tree Drive, opposed the Ordinance and expressed concern that it would effectively prohibit e-bikes anywhere pedestrians walk.
Interim City Manager Mahoney interjected to clarify for the record and for the public that this Ordinance pertains only to City parks, not to sidewalks or open areas throughout the City.
Dean, 3422 Victory Palm Drive, opposed the Ordinance and stated that senior communities are gated and their residents can remain there if they are concerned about safety. He argued that children's parents are responsible for teaching them how to behave on bikes, and expressed frustration that taxpayers fund the parks and should be able to use e-bikes within them.
Mandi Bullard, 1417 Needle Palm Drive, expressed concerns that the specifics of the Ordinance needed to be more clearly stated before a vote. She noted that many Edgewater children have no bus routes and rely on e-bikes to get to school, and that placing them on roadways rather than sidewalks creates serious safety risks.
Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Avenue, acknowledged that some of the e-bike issues stem from parental responsibility and respect for others. He supported the idea that in a park setting, riders should simply pedal. He felt parents needed to teach children to ride respectfully.
Gina Holt, 1798 Hideaway Lane, described the Ordinance as an enforcement nightmare. She suggested that handicapped riders could be issued a visible permit tag similar to a disabled parking placard. She further proposed requiring a safety course for children riding electric bikes, and suggested that if an e-bike is considered a motorized vehicle, riders should be required to have a license.
Katrina Gray, 1500 Tatum Boulevard, has used e-bikes for three (3) years now and opposed the park ban, emphasizing her taxpayers rights to access them.
Mayor Depew noted several citizens had time remaining and offered them the opportunity to use it.
Mayor Depew expressed reservations about the Ordinance, noting he had personally observed e-bike riders throughout the City and that all were behaving respectfully. He acknowledged the importance of child safety but felt the Ordinance was premature and that he would rather see young people on sidewalks than on the side of US 1. He also referenced his own history using a three-wheeled bicycle for his lawn care business and expressed empathy for those who rely on e-bike for transportation.
Councilwoman Dolbow expressed support for the Ordinance, stating that park goers should be able to pedal through. She raised issues with 35-mph e-bikes in areas used by the elderly and kids, who often do not use helmets or eye protections. She supported banning motor-assist in parks but supported the use of pedal power.
Councilman Thomas expressed a general philosophical concern about enacting too many laws, stating that every new law takes away a degree of freedom. He said he was the one who had previously suggested that if a new law is passed, an old law should be repealed to provide balance.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed concern about enforcement, particularly handling ADA exemptions without infringing on rights. She questioned if complaints were mainly about Whistle Stop Park instead of all City parks, and proposed limiting the Ordinance to specific locations. She also inquired about the possibility of a temporary Ordinance to assess enforcement effectiveness before making a permanent decision.
Interim City Manager responded that the intent was always to have a lengthy education period before any citations would be issued, and that the Ordinance is primarily meant to give law enforcement a tool to address the small number of individuals creating safety hazards, rather than to broadly penalize e-bike users. He confirmed that complaints had been received about e-bikes traveling at 35-mph through parks.
Interim Police Chief Geiger confirmed that park-related bicycle incidents occur five to six times per week during summer months, with roughly 25 such incidents per year across the City. City Attorney Wolfe clarified that liability for any injury caused by an e-bike rider would rest with that rider, not the City.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance 2025-O-09 - Amending Section 12.5.1 Parks Use Ordinance

action_text: There was no motion made.
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read Ordinance 2025-O-10 into the record.
Interim City Manager Mahoney provided the staff report, explaining that this is a City wide Ordinance that would prohibit motor-powered e-bike use on all public City sidewalks throughout Edgewater.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Jenny Roesch, 811 Old Mission Road, explained that due to bus driver shortages at Volusia County Schools, middle schoolers get home as late as 6:30pm, leading parents to use e-bikes as a solution. She insisted that banning e-bikes from sidewalks won't deter reckless riders; she felt they would still ride wherever they choose, while forcing responsible ones onto unsafe roads. She cautioned that such an Ordinance could risk children's lives and urged a focus on education for parents and kids before penalizing responsible riders.
Adrian Arnie, 811 Old Mission Road, a teenager advocated for e-bikes on sidewalks as crucial for commuting to school and visiting friends, citing limited bus access. He admitted some riders act irresponsibly, but believed they will defy any Ordinance, leaving responsible riders needing safer pathways.
Roger Cole, 599 Beta Vista, spoke for seniors, explaining he bought an e-bike after heart surgery to help with pedaling and rides at 12-15 mph. He's scared of riding on US 1 with traffic at 55 mph and noted that sidewalks in Hacienda, extending to Oak Hill, are mainly used by seniors with minimal pedestrian or vehicle issues. He urged the Council to consider solutions other than a blanket ban on all sidewalks.
Danielle Bailey, 2017 Tatum Boulevard, returned to describe how her three-wheeled e-bike restored her freedom and mobility after she became unable to drive long distances due to a disability. She rides to Oak Hill on sidewalks and would never attempt US 1. She urged the Council not to restrict her rights or those of children relying on e-bikes for safe school travel.
Jay Magrane, 2114 Pine Tree Drive, expressed strong opposition to granting Police additional authority to enforce the Ordinance.
Deborah, 302 S Ridgewood Avenue, discussed the removal of Votran's Route 41 bus service in January 2025 has led Edgewater's low-income, carless residents to rely on e-bikes for transportation. Banning e-bikes from sidewalks could significantly limit their travel options, impacting those who struggle financially. She requested a follow-up meeting with Mayor Depew to discuss restoring the bus route.
Todd Smith, 126 E Turgot Avenue, shared a personal anecdote about nearly colliding with an e-bike rider traveling the wrong way against traffic at an intersection. He suggested that State-level regulation, including defined speed limits for e-bikes on sidewalks, would be a more appropriate and enforceable solution than a City Ordinance.
Dean, 3422 Victory Palm Drive, returned to praise Councilman Rainbird and argued that restricting e-bikes would negatively affect his wife, who has MS, as she should be able to ride through Parks. He expressed frustration with rising water bills and flooding, questioning the Council's focus on bicycles when more urgent infrastructure issues need attention.
Mary Forrester, 1937 Edgewater Canal Road, expressed opposition to increased regulation, arguing the City should focus on the 25 individuals annually causing issues rather than all e-bike riders. As someone who drives 500-700 miles weekly, she is more concerned about children riding next to cars than on sidewalks with e-bikes. She questioned if parents would be responsible for minors' citations and suggested the Ordinance lacked sufficient consideration before being proposed for a vote.
Katrina Gray, 1500 Tatum Boulevard, returned briefly to urge any Councilmember skeptical of the danger of riding alongside traffic to try riding an e-bike next to cars at 15-20mph before voting.
Councilman Thomas felt that education and safety, not new law, was the right approach, echoing the comments of a speaker earlier in the evening.
Mayor Depew agreed that the Ordinance was premature, reiterating what he had seen around Edgewater in regards to e-bike riders. He expressed a preference for young individuals using sidewalks over roads like US 1. He committed to arrange a meeting with the City Manager and County representatives regarding the Votran route 41 issue, raised by a resident, and acknowledged the City's insufficient sidewalk infrastructure to accommodate redirected riders.
Councilwoman Dolbow echoed support for education as a solution, suggesting a program where Fire and Police visit schools at year's end to discuss bicycle and e-bike safety. She stated she is uncomfortable putting children on the road with distracted and elderly drivers on narrow streets, and emphasized that enforcement would be a challenge under this Ordinance as well.
Councilwoman Gillis was in agreement with the direction the Council was heading. She thanked Danielle Bailey for the pothole and infrastructure reports she regularly provides by phone. She also praised Adrian Arnie for his courage in speaking before the Council and expressed hope for a youth Council program. She voiced concern about enforcement and stated her concerns had only grown since the first item was considered.
Councilman Rainbird observed that while bike lanes exist, they are rarely used by actual cyclists. He noted the only e-bike problem he had personally witnessed involved riders in the middle of the road at night, not where they should be. He also noted the City's lack of adequate sidewalk infrastructure as a broader issue that needs addressing.
Councilman Thomas raised a point about a state-funded $50 million bike trail that runs through the area, noting it could not be redirected for road improvements because the federal funds were earmarked specifically for bicycle infrastructure.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance 2025-O-10: Amending Section 17-46. Traffic, Electric Bicycles; Enforcement

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Thomas, to approve Ordinance No. 2025-O-08. The motion failed by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Ordinance into the record.
Interim City Manager Mahoney delivered the staff report, prefacing his comment by acknowledging that stormwater management and flood mitigation remain his top priority during his tenure. He stated that the sole reason for the staff recommendation to approve the Ordinance is to comply with Florida State Law.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Patrick Fisher, 2100 Air Park Road, the newest member of the Planning and Zoning board, felt the Ordinance lacks the Board's recommended language to clarify the repeal is state-mandated and not in Edgewater's best interest. He emphasized this addition is crucial for maintaining legal grounds to potentially challenge SB 180, urging Council to express protest in the Ordinance and consider joining a challenge coalition.
Suzanne Scheiber, representing Green Volusia, reminded Council of the January moratorium vote aimed at comprehensive plan review, stormwater study amid slowing development, stormwater maintenance plan creation, funding pursuit, project implementation and City Charter review. She emphasized unchanged circumstances and potential City flooding post-rain events. Following a meeting with Representative Tramont, she proposed three (3) motions: retain the moratorium, mandate Development Services Director Ryan Solstice to expedite the comprehensive plan with Interim City Manager Mahoney's oversight, and join the SB 180 litigation coalition. She stressed their necessity to address flooding issues.
Gina Holt, 1798 Hideaway Lane, noted the court reporters presence, calling it visible pressure from the developers. She read Commissioner Dori Howington of Deltona's statement, which critiqued SB 180 as far-reaching, impacting more than emergencies: altering comprehensive plans, reducing impact fees funding essential services, limiting local livestock regulations, changing Volusia County's rural boundaries, overruling voter initiatives, and risking tree protections. She emphasized municipal authority and duty to counter laws endangering resident welfare, advising the Council to resist developer pressures.
Judy Bourdeau, 2916 Oak Trail, recalled hearing Councilman Rainbird tell a news reporter that SB 180 may work in some communities but is not a good fit for Edgewater. She agreed with that sentiment and urged Council to resist pressure to repeal the moratorium.
Teresa David, 1015 Regent Street, urged the Council not to cave to the pressure of SB 180 and to join the coalition.
Tom Holt, 1798 Hideaway Lane, urged the Council to stand firm against the pressures from Tallahassee, stating that State legislators can't understand local community needs. He clarified the moratorium's purpose: fostering informed growth planning, not hindering development. Without amending the Future Land Use map, issues remain stagnant and flooding could escalate. He encouraged seizing the current resident consensus, warning that developers might outlast Councilmembers, seeking more agreeable replacements. He emphasized that lifting the moratorium jeopardizes the ongoing $100,000 stormwater study.
Mary Forrester, 1937 Edgewater Canal Road, whose home borders Edgewater, experienced severe flooding tied to development-related canal backwash. After storms, her yard remained flooded for 13 days. She urged the Council and County to work together on solutions. Mayor Depew directed Interim City Manager Mahoney and Development Services Director Ryan Solstice to discuss the issue with County officials.
Mandi Bullard, 1417 Needle Palm Drive, reminded Council of the community's repeated requests for flooding solutions, noting prior responses claimed their hands were tied due to inherited issues. She urged Council to see this vote as a crucial decision for their legacy, emphasizing the importance of extending the moratorium and joining the coalition against SB 180, stressing it as a threat to local stormwater governance and planning.
Douglas Frederick, Edgewater Landing, returned briefly to read from page one of his 59-page document, arguing that the lack of local control under Florida Live Local creates further community risk. He expressed hope that the moratorium would remain in place citywide until a safe and proper path forward for every community exists. He offered praise for the City's Police Department, calling them professional and proactive.
Todd Smith, 126 E Turgot Avenue, urged the Council to keep the moratorium in place until the problem it was created to solve has been resolved. He used the analogy of a house that has been repeatedly expanded until the original sewer pipe can no longer handle the load, arguing that Edgewater's drainage ditches were never designed to handle the volume being pushed into them by successive new developments.
Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Avenue, described how the canal behind his 48-unit complex at Persimmon Place rises to the top within 30 minutes of rain. He asked about the retention pond near McDonald's with silver overflowing boxes and whether it could be pumped out during dry periods to increase its capacity ahead of storms. Mayor Depew confirmed that it is under County jurisdiction and noted that the City is working on a 10th Street overflow acquisition.
Councilman Rainbird asked City Attorney Wolfe to confirm his understanding that SB 180 already nullifies moratoriums as a matter of State law, and asked why the City needs to formally repeal them if the State has already done so.
City Attorney Wolfe confirmed that SB 180 does nullify the moratorium Ordinances, but also provides a mechanism for any City resident or business to file suit to enforce SB 180. If they prevail, they are entitled to attorney's fees and costs. The only way to prevent that liability is to formally repeal the moratorium within the specified pre-suit notice period.
Mayor Depew stated that he was elected by the people and for the people, and that the Council worked hard to reach the moratorium decision. He acknowledged the City is approaching the original purposes of the moratorium, updating the comprehensive plan, but expressed that complying with the law is the most important obligation. He noted he had encouraged working with State legislators to consider tweaking SB 180 going forward. He felt he could not in good conscious vote yes to break the law or no against the moratorium, and announced that his vote would be recorded as "present". He reiterated that he wants to continue the goals of the moratorium regardless of the outcome of tonight's vote.
Councilman Thomas stated his support for the moratorium but mentioned the he couldn't vote against State law due to his oath. He raised concerns about potential risks to future grant funding, like the $1 million secured for canal improvements with Representative Tremont's help, if the State is opposed in court. He noted, unlike the City of Deltona engaged in amendments instead of lawsuits, he favors working with the legislature to amend the law collaboratively.
Councilwoman Dolbow agreed with including the clarifying language in the Ordinance, explicitly stating that the repeal is to comply with State law, not in residents' best interest. She believed the Council must follow State Statutes but valued having this nuance in the record. She proposed proceeding with the first reading, meeting with City Attorney Wolfe individually in the Interim, and reassessing before the second reading.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed her determination to stand up and speak out, despite potential legal challenges. She voiced frustration over State constraints hindering the Council's flood solution efforts and questions the City Attorney's focus on joining an external coalition instead of directly seeking an injunction or legal action. She founded the emphasis on limitations instead of potential solutions disheartening, declaring she couldn't support something she believed to be contrary to Edgewater Residents best interests.
City Attorney Wolfe responded to Councilwoman Gillis' question, explaining that going it alone would expose the City to the full cost of litigation and increased risk of retaliation, whereas joining a coalition of many cities and counties would allow cost-sharing and reduce those risks.
Councilman Rainbird expressed frustration over the situation, noting Edgewater's moratorium was groundbreaking in City history. He asserted that the term "moratorium" hadn't been in Florida State Law until Edgewater's implementation. He argued that SB 180 isn't constitutional, showing dedication to protecting residents, and stated his willingness to face removal from the Council while maintaining pride in his stance. He highlighted that all legislators behind SB 180 face re-election, hoping they would reconsider their positions.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, confirmed that when asked, the National Home Builders Association had sent an email notice the day SB 180 passed, and that staff had published the City's declaration on the City's website to begin the pre-suit timeline provided under the statute.
Mayor Depew was uncomfortable with repealing the moratorium but acknowledged the legal reality. He stated he would prefer each Councilmember meet individually with City Attorney Wolfe before the second reading to get more information on the number of cities in the coalition, the potential financial exposure from a legal challenge, timeline for permit processing if the moratorium is repealed, and the impact of staff capacity. He proposed having a special meeting before the next routine Council meeting to further address the meeting.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, responded to a question from Councilwoman Gillis about the status of the comprehensive plan update, confirming that the work on the comprehensive plan is ongoing but progressing slowly due to workload. He stated that with 45 projects currently under review and only two (2) planning staff members, progress is not as fast as Council would prefer. He clarified that any changes to the comprehensive plan would not take effect for approximately three (3) years.
City Attorney Wolfe recommended moving forward with the first reading as presented and have further discussion, including the proposed individual meetings with Councilmembers and the special meeting, before the second reading.
title: 1st Reading - Ordinance No. 2025-O-08: Request to repeal the City-wide Moratorium and the Florida Shores Building Permit Moratorium in response to the passage of Senate Bill 180.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Councilman Rainbird to approve the request to appeal the Planning and Zoning Boards decision regarding the issuance of a conditional use permit and variance for the property at 1103 S. Ridgewood Avenue. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe provided the background: All Florida Plumbing, located at 1103 S Ridgewood Avenue, applied for a variance to allow outdoor storage to exceed the height of the privacy fence and to allow a yellow predominant building color, as well as a conditional use permit for outdoor storage, distribution, wholesale, warehousing, and storage within the B-3 Highway Commercial zoning district.
The Planning and Zoning Board unanimously approved both the variance and the conditional use permit. The adjacent owners, the Fox family, have filed an appeal, which under the City's Land Development Code, comes before the Council.
Mayor Depew confirmed Council consensus to grant equal time to both parties.
Jessica Gow, Cobb Cole Law Firm, representation for All Florida Plumbing and owner, Clayton Beasley. She provided a timeline:
All Florida Plumbing opened in Edgewater in 1993; outdoor storage was added in 1995 on the northern stage area; the building was originally painted yellow in 2009 to match the company's branding; the City adopted the Ridgewood Corridor design standards regarding paint standards in 2012; the City issued a certificate of occupancy for a building expansion in 2019; a permit was issued for a chlorine tank relocation in 2021; and a masonry wall was permitted in 2023, replacing a prior chain-link fence with slats. She argued the storage use predates applicable Ordinances, making it legally non-conforming, and noted the Land Development Code does not provide regulations specifically on outdoor storage for wholesale uses. She stated that aerial photographs from 1999, 2004, and 2018 confirm the storage footprint has been consistent.
She further argued that the building color, Benjamin Moore "delightful yellow", does not fall within the LDC's prohibition on neon or fluorescent paint, as neither of those are objective terms that would apply to the color. She noted that other bright-colored buildings exist in the Ridgewood Corridor. The Planning and Zoning Board's conditions included moving the front most storage rack further into the site, installing a stop sign, and notifying vendors of peak traffic times, all of which the property owner agreed to. She requested that the Council uphold the Planning and Zoning Board's determination.
Clayton Beasley, 1103 S Ridgewood Avenue, owner of All Florida Plumbing, addressed the Council. He mentioned upgrading the property since 1993 and was frustrated that the businesses appearance is being questioned. He pointed out the consistent color usage like the Holly Hill location, in place for 55 years without complaint. At a November 2024 meeting, he was advised by the Supervisor Miron and Chief Lariscy to seek a variance to satisfy neighbors. He was frustrated after being assured by Mr. Solstice that he didn't have to attend the June 2, 2025 meeting as it was being tabled, it ultimately proceeded without him. He had watched the meeting remotely and was troubled by the comments made about his business, particularly the chlorine tank which he said is supported on concrete with a containment system, secured by stainless steel cables and is rated to 130 miles per hour. It has survived multiple hurricanes and is not supported on wooden two-by-fours as had been stated previously.
Mr. Beasley maintained that he had complied with everything asked of him by the Planning and Zoning Board. He had also invited his Council representative to visit the property and tell him directly what needed to be fixed so that the matter could be resolved and he could continue doing business.
He reported that a recent traffic study revealed only three (3) vendor trucks used the nearby street and it was unrelated to the business. He seeks clear direction from Council to be able to continue operations undisturbed.
Councilman Rainbird interjected with a question regarding the chlorine tank's support structure, acknowledging that he had observed it during a prior inspection and apologized for having described it inaccurately. He mentioned heated phone calls he had witnessed between the two parties.
Councilman Rainbird noted that the Planning and Zoning Board had instructed the property to move storage so that it would not be visible above the fence, and asked whether the racks had been moved. Ms. Gow clarified that the requirement, as reflected in the Planning and Zoning video, was to move the product, specifically yellow plumbing piping, on the top rack further into the site, which had been done. The rack themselves were not required to be removed.
Mayor Depew asked Mr. Solstice for clarification on the Planning and Zoning Board's requirements. Mr. Solstice confirmed that the suggestion was to move the racks so they would not be visible from the street, install a stop sign, and provide a vendor list. Mayor Depew remarked that his understanding was that the rack itself had to be moved, not just the supplies.
Councilwoman Dolbow asked Mr. Beasley how much notice he had received about the meeting he did not attend. Mr. Beasley responded that he received notice between 11am and noon on the day of the meeting. Councilwoman Dolbow and Interim City Manager Mahoney agreed that it was unacceptable and unlawful.
Mayor Depew clarified that the Council wasn't criticizing Mr. Beasley's business, noting he had only heard positive feedback. He asked Mr. Solstice about the landscaping requirements when the property expanded in 2017, Mr. Solstice confirmed that a stormwater site plan was approved then, and to his knowledge, no landscape buffer was mandated by staff. He highlighted that the enhanced landscaping regulations Mayor Depew mentioned were adopted in 2024 for future applications and were not applicable during the businesses 2017 expansion. Mayor Depew suggested that staff should have properly guided the owner through expansion processes, identifying this as a past staff-level issue rather than the applicants fault.
Jennifer Fox, 115 E Turgot Avenue, applicant, initially intended to protest against the equal presentation time, referencing City policy that grants the appellant the floor and limits others to a three-minute comment period. However, acknowledging the Councils decision to allow equal time based on City Attorney Wolfe's advice.
Ms. Fox argued that storage and displays should be screened from view when adjacent to a residential street. She disputed Mr. Beasley's claim that $25,000 in storage racks constituted a hardship, countering that the Ridgewood Corridor standards forbid garish colors, citing the bright yellow building as an example. She asserted that combining 108 E Turgot allowed an unjust expansion of outdoor storage and cited misrepresentation in the building's use for impact fees. Moreover, she accused All Florida Plumbing of using the residential property as a commercial parking area under false lease claims, presenting evidence of trucks parked on the swale with no residency on-site.
She also argued that the two-story building permitted in 2017 was permitted as a warehouse, yet the business had operated as retail with outdoor storage, not as a warehouse,and that this represented a change in use without proper approval.
She asserted that the residents on E Turgot Avenue were not notified in 2017 when the variance for the building expansion was sought or when the building permit was issued, and that the outdoor storage racks above the fence line did not appear until after the two-story building was constructed.
Regarding the June 2, Planning and Zoning meeting, Mr. Fox stated that she and her husband were out of town and had been under the understanding that the appeal would be reheard at the August 4 meeting, not at a June meeting.
Ms. Fox highlighted persistent parking and Code Enforcement issues such as frequent deliveries parking on the swale and employees using the residential property at 108 E Turgot for parking during business hours, despite the property having no utilities or occupants. Ms. Fox stated that Code Enforcement had been misinformed about the property being leased to bypass parking codes. She asked that Council maintain and enforce the codes put in place.
Susan Paolillo, 122 E Turgot Avenue, discussed observing trucks unloading in front of a no-parking sign; damaging sidewalks; and contributing to the swales between homes filling back in. She also commented on the property at 108 E Turgot being in disrepair.
Marshall Heininger, 116 E Turgot Avenue, wasn't overly concerned about the color of the building and that his main concern was the conditional use for wholesale warehousing. He felt the truck traffic the business generated was incompatible with the residential street. For him, residential use on Ridgewood was acceptable but wholesale warehousing brought truck traffic that the site could not accommodate.
Councilman Rainbird asked if the property was zoned industrial. Mr. Solstice explained that it is classified as B-3 Highway Commercial with a commercial future land use designation. The term "industrial uses" mentioned by the Planning and Zoning Board pertained to the nature of the activities, warehousing and storage, which are permitted conditionally within the B-3 zoning, rather than implying the zoning was industrial.
Councilwoman Dolbow stated that in reviewing the totality of the evidence, she found that the storage blueprint from 1995 to the present was essentially the same, that the business had been there for over 30 years, had invested in Edgewater, had complied with what had been asked by the Planning and Zoning Board, and that the truck traffic reported there (three delivery trucks a month) were not excessive. She felt the Board's decision should be upheld.
Mayor Depew reiterated that responsibility lay, in part, with the City staff over the years for not guiding the property owner through proper processes. He expressed a desire to ensure that going forward, businesses expanding in the City receive clear guidance around required variances and landscaping obligations.
Councilwoman Gillis echoed concerns about equal Code Enforcement across the City, noting that other residents and business owners had been required to immediately correct violations while this situation had persisted for years. She felt requiring the property to come into compliance wouldn't put them out of business.
Interim City Manager Mahoney noted that the Council's options included overturning the Planning and Zoning Board's decision, which would then allow Code Enforcement to open cases regarding the building color and the outdoor storage use, with a third-party attorney separately reviewing whether the warehouse designation was consistent with the current use.
City Attorney Wolfe clarified the mechanics of the vote: a vote to approve the appeal would overturn the Planning and Zoning Board's decision to grant the variance and conditional use permit, siding with the Fox family and neighboring appellants. A vote against the appeal would uphold the Planning and Zoning Boards approval.
title: AP-2500: Request to appeal the Planning and Zoning Board’s decision regarding the issuance of a conditional use permit and variance for the property at 1103 S Ridgewood Avenue.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird to approve the request for Major Site Plan Approval for a proposed business park development, consisting of two 16,320 SF buildings, on a 3.05-acre property located at 2360 South Ridgewood Avenue. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Interim City Manager Mahoney provided the staff report. The Planning and Zoning Board recommended City Council approve the major site plan for the business park given unanimous support. Key conditions included installing a fence for privacy and lift station access, minor trip generation not triggering a traffic analysis, compliance with stormwater and design standards, and enhanced rear landscape buffers with Majestic Oaks. The developer will also extend the sidewalk to US 1, at their expense.
Steve Circle, engineer for the project, addressed the Council. He noted that the BPUD process with City staff had gone smoothly, with the project's stormwater facility set to manage 100% of onsite stormwater per current code. The property did not flood during hurricane Helene and Milton. He sought Councils approval to proceed.
Mayor Depew confirmed the 100% on-site stormwater retention requirement in the PUD agreement, which Mr. Circle affirmed. Interim City Manager Mahoney detailed the enhanced landscape buffer, consisting of 19 canopy trees, 56 understory trees, and 371 shrubs, with a 6-foot fence alongside the drive aisle in a 20-foot buffer.
Linda Mojer, 319 Leaning Oak Drive, a resident of Majestic Oaks, had been unaware of this development. She asked whether residents of Majestic Oaks should have received public notice prior to the meeting.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, explained that the City sends notice to property owners within 500 feet of the subject property. This surpasses the State law minimum, which only required notices to adjacent property owners. If Ms. Mojer's property was beyond 500 feet, she wouldn't have received a postcard. The property had been publicly noticed three (3) times during the PUD agreement process and again for the Planning and Zoning Board hearing, with a sign posted onsite. Mr. Solstice explained that each mailing involves preparing 60-80 envelopes, and further expanding the notice area would raises costs and staff workload. He acknowledged the fairness of Ms. Mojer's inquiry and offered to provide public notice records to the Council if requested.
Ms. Mojer acknowledged receiving notice for a previous development on the south side of the community, which gave them ample time to respond. She assured the Council she would notify her neighbors about this new development. Additionally, she remarked that she had believed the moratorium would block new development approvals during this time.
Mayor Depew clarified that this project was not within the moratorium area, which Mr. Solstice confirmed with a nod.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed concern that the approval of a business park felt somewhat inconsistent with the Council's simultaneous effort to resist the State's rollback of the moratorium. She had concerns regarding the stormwater impacts on the Majestic Oaks neighborhood given recent rainfall events.
Councilwoman Dolbow noted that the moratorium as structured had excluded the US 1 corridor and properties east of it, and that concerns surrounding the moratorium were primarily focused on redevelopment within flood-prone areas and the Florida Shores subdivision, not necessarily new commercial development elsewhere.
Mayor Depew asked how many other business parks existed on US 1 in Edgewater. Mr. Solstice responded that there were effectively none, this would be the first true business park to be built in Edgewater, which is part of why Council had approved the BPUD when it was first brought forward.
Mr. Solstice highlighted that the substantial buffers were the thickest and densest ever written by staff, a measure approved by the Council in December 2024 due to concerns about adjacent residential areas. He confirmed the project's compliance with the Land Development Code, comprehensive plan policies, and reiterated staff's recommendation for approval.
title: SP-2415: Request for Major Site Plan approval for a proposed business park development, consisting of two 16,320 SF buildings, on a 3.05-acre property located at 2360 South Ridgewood Avenue.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Councilman Rainbird to approve discussing the City Attorney's contract to send it out for request for proposals. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe informed the Council that after researching the tax exemption provisions for the Live Local Act, he confirmed the City could opt out of the 80-100% median income tax exemption. Other cities and the County had also done so. With Council consensus, he will prepare a Resolution for an upcoming meeting.
Councilwoman Gillis raised concerns about the City Attorney's contract, expressing discomfort with the legal guidance provided, especially related to SB 180 and its constraints on the Council's ability to challenge legislation rather than simply comply with it. She acknowledged previous dissatisfaction and opted not to terminate the contract, but to explore other options by seeking proposals. She recognized City Attorney Wolfe's strengths but wanted legal counsel that took a more offensive approach.
Mayor Depew and Councilman Rainbird expressed support for the RFP process, clarifying that they were not in support of immediate termination. Mayor Depew felt that the current ongoing budget cycle was a fitting time to explore proposals.
Councilwoman Dolbow stated that the City Attorney's job is to provide legal advice consistent with the law, not to tell the Council what it might want to hear, and that any attorney in that position would be bound to give the same guidance. Councilman Thomas stated that the Council had sworn to uphold the law and could not expect an attorney to recommend actions that break it.
City Attorney Wolfe stated that he was open to following the Council's direction, ensuring that it was legal and ethical. He advised that any challenge to SB 180 should be pursued in coalition with other cities and counties to both share expenses and minimize retaliation risks, rather than act independently.
Interim City Manager suggested that he could bring the RFP process details forward at the next meeting for a formal vote.
Ryan Solstice, 1937 Deep Lake Circle, pointed out that the RFP motion hadn't been publicly announced beforehand and lacked public input. City Attorney Wolfe confirmed that it was legal but not best practice. Mayor Depew agreed to address the concern by ensuring proper notice and its inclusion in the next agenda.
title: b. City Attorney

minutes_note:
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, noted that the City is currently without permanent leaders in several key positions, including the City Clerk and the City Manager, and questioned the status of positions like City Inspector. He expressed skepticism around the timing of the RFP for the City Attorney, suggesting it may have been pre-planned. Additionally, he was concerned that Mayor Depew had requested storm and hurricane prep work volunteers on Facebook but had not followed up. He further inquired about the purpose of Councilmembers' participation in ride-along's with the Edgewater Police Department.
Councilwoman Gillis explained her involvement in ride-alongs with various city departments is to grasp the operational needs and challenges firsthand, aiding her understanding of budget requirements.

minutes_note: Linda Mojer, 319 Leaning Oak Drive, addressed the Council regarding flood mitigation concerns and the proposed 1st Business Park development at 2360 South Ridgewood. Ms. Mosier stated that Majestic Oaks' opposition to the approved final site plan is focused on a single adjustment: that the commercial entrance to the business park should originate on Ridgewood/US-1, rather than routing truck traffic through Oak Branch Drive in the residential neighborhood. She argued that access from US-1 would eliminate the need to remove any of the 20 oak trees at the Majestic Oaks entrance, preserving their flood mitigation root systems and protecting the neighborhood canopy. She noted that while FDOT does not currently support a US-1 access point, she contended that resolving that issue is between 1st Business Park and FDOT, and that forcing truck traffic through the residential entrance does not conform with existing city ordinances restricting truck routes through residential areas. Ms. Mosier also cited safety concerns related to school children using Oak Branch to catch the bus, and noted that traffic through the Majestic Oaks entrance approximately doubled in 2023 with the completion of new housing in Phase 4. She concluded by asking Council to (1) enforce standing ordinances and (2) instruct staff to partner with 1st Business Park in lobbying FDOT for direct US-1 access.
