action_text: A motion was made by Councilman Thomas, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to approve Ordinance No. 2025-O-08. The motion failed by the following vote:
minutes_note:
The City Clerk read Ordinance No. 2025-O-08 into the record: An ordinance of the City of Edgewater repealing Ordinance No. 2024-O-62, Ordinance No. 2024-O-03, and Ordinance No. 2025-O-06, rescinding the temporary moratorium on annexations, rezonings, comprehensive plan amendments, site plans, preliminary plats, final plats, and certain building permits; providing for conflicting ordinances; providing for severability; and providing for an effective date.
The City Manager deferred to City Attorney Aaron Wolfe to provide the staff report. City Attorney Wolfe explained that Senate Bill 180 (SB 180), now signed into law, prohibits cities from proposing or adopting more restrictive or burdensome amendments to their comprehensive plans or land development regulations. Additionally, the law prohibits more restrictive or burdensome procedures concerning the review, approval, or issuance of site plans or development permits before October 1, 2027. The law is retroactive to August 1, 2024.
City Attorney Wolfe stated that SB 180 requires the city to prepare and post a notice of intent to repeal any adopted laws conflicting with its provisions, then proceed to repeal those laws. He noted that the day after SB 180 became law, the city received notice from the Volusia County Building Association requesting the moratoriums be repealed, with a follow-up request on July 1, 2025. The city subsequently posted its notice of intent to repeal on its website.
City Attorney Wolfe outlined three primary risks of non-compliance: (1) private enforcement actions under SB 180, which entitle prevailing plaintiffs to attorney's fees and costs against the city, with the potential for dozens or hundreds of lawsuits creating, in his words, a "cottage industry of attorneys suing Edgewater"; (2) ethics complaints filed against council members for failing to follow state law; and (3) the potential for the governor to suspend or remove council members for conduct that could be considered misfeasance or malfeasance. He stated that it was his recommendation that the City Council approve the ordinance and repeal the moratorium ordinances.
The public hearing was opened.
Linda Mosier, 319 Leaning Oak Drive, spoke on behalf of the Majestic Oaks HOA, representing 100 parcels. She described the 20-year-old oak tree canopy at the entrance to the Majestic Oaks community along Oak Branch Drive and noted concerns about a commercial development proposed at 2360 South Ridgewood, stating that the overhead plan renderings do not fully illustrate ground-level impacts. She expressed solidarity with the Council's position on the moratorium, stating, "The city's moratorium now sits between the state's overreach against home rule and unchecked development statewide. We feel you," and asked the Council to help Majestic Oaks advocate for its homeowners regarding the Oak Branch Drive entrance.
Greg Gember, Daytona Beach, addressed his remarks to Councilman Thomas as a newly seated member and urged the Council to vote no on repealing the moratorium. He argued that the Council need not comply with SB 180, contending that the city already has legal standing given that its moratorium was in process before SB 180 took effect, and that it could potentially be grandfathered in. He challenged the severity of the consequences outlined by City Attorney Wolfe, asserting that removal from office for this conduct would be the equivalent of a criminal act and that the federal constitution's prohibition on ex post facto laws would be protective. He called the meeting "the first test of your resolve" and urged the Council not to "quit at the first turn," stating: "Don't face a whole room full of people in two months and say that you quit on them at the first turn."
James McGinnis, 2607 Willow Oak Drive (participating by phone), spoke in opposition to repealing the moratorium. He recounted the substantial work undertaken to establish the moratorium and argued that the concept of SB 180 was sound but was altered by last-minute amendments that remove home rule authority from cities. He cited specific statutory provisions of SB 180 and argued that the bill threatens wetlands, sea turtle habitat, conservation lands, comprehensive growth plans, and impact fees. He urged the Council to vote no, to continue operating within existing laws, and to consider joining a group of municipal plaintiffs challenging SB 180. He referenced the U.S. Supreme Court opinion in Trump v. Casa, Inc. as relevant to standing in such challenges, and noted that Representative Fiona McFarlane had stated she would lobby for SB 180's repeal, and that the bill's original sponsor had expressed willingness to improve it.
Brian White, New Smyrna Beach, identified himself as a board member of 1000 Friends of Florida, a land use advocacy nonprofit, though he stated he was not speaking on behalf of that organization. He argued that the moratorium was enacted in good faith in response to real flooding and overdevelopment concerns, and that SB 180 represents "politics of fear and intimidation" designed to coerce municipalities into dereliction of their duty to protect residents. He stated that SB 180 is "an unconstitutional law" and that Florida's 1968 constitutional amendment granting municipalities home rule authority cannot be superseded. He urged the Council to keep the moratorium and to join the growing consortium of municipalities challenging SB 180, stating: "Take back your power for your citizens and keep it here in Edgewater."
Charles Kilborn, 5316 Diamondleaf Drive, offered a different legal perspective, arguing that SB 180 does not broadly apply to all new construction but rather applies predominantly to reconstruction efforts. He cited published legal opinion letters from law firms supporting this reading and referenced statutory language specifying that local governments may not assess impact fees on "reconstruction or replacement of a previously existing structure if the replacement structure is the same land use." He contended that much of the new construction in the city involves new land uses and is therefore not subject to SB 180's prohibitions. He urged the Council to step back, assess impact fees, seek outside legal counsel, and properly interpret the law before proceeding, stating: "I do not think 180 applies specifically to the city council in this circumstance."
Mike Ponietowski, Toboka Farms Village, described himself as a flooding victim twice over following Hurricanes Ian and Milton, stating that development of pastureland caused his home to flood on both occasions and that his neighbor's home had since been bulldozed. He challenged the Council to decide "who you stand with, Ron DeSantis and the developers, or the people who put you in those seats." He urged the Council to be brave, to codify the moratorium into the comprehensive plan and charter, and to consider policies such as raising houses rather than raising land grade. He warned that continued flooding would erode property values and ultimately the city's tax base, and called on the Council to vote no on repealing the moratorium.
Ted Noftel, Port Orange, framed the Council's choice as one between folding and "speaking truth to power." He acknowledged that the political cards were "stacked against" the Council given the positions of local representatives, the senator, and the governor, but encouraged the Council to stand firm. He suggested that if council members were suspended, they should allow it and run for office again, predicting they would win by larger margins. He urged the Council not to answer the anticipated lawsuits, instead forcing a judge to intervene, stating: "Your only option is to stand up to the power that developers have in this city, this county, and this state."
Jeff Brower, Volusia County Council Chair, expressed pride in the Council's prior vote to establish the moratorium and urged them to stand firm once again. He stated he had received a legal opinion suggesting the Council is on solid legal ground and has time to fight. He described SB 180 as "the most outrageous attack on local control" he had ever seen and warned that absent a challenge, local governments would have nothing left but "to go to ribbon cuttings." He outlined two non-exclusive paths forward: joining the coalition of lawsuits challenging SB 180, and working with the county on a legislative amendment process. He expressed support for both approaches and encouraged the Council to take a stand, noting that the legislators who voted for SB 180 are currently running for re-election. He cautioned, however, that government-to-government lawsuits are rarely short and the costs will rise through appeals, while also noting that he believes legislative pressure and public accountability are working. He concluded by urging the Council: "Stand your ground. I respect you for what you're doing. Don't back up on this moratorium."
Suzanne Shebert, Dream Green Volusia, spoke without a prepared statement, reflecting on her ten months of involvement with Edgewater residents concerning flooding issues. She named several residents she has worked alongside, Patrick Fisher and his wife Lynn, Gina and Tom Holt, Donna McDavid, Kim Penny, Robin Cassisi, Andrew Sherman, Ken Hooper, Claudia, and Mandy, and said these residents rely on the Council. She concluded: "I'm asking you to do the right thing tonight, so you can have peace, and so they can have peace."
Cindy Harris, unincorporated New Smyrna Beach, identified herself as a candidate for County Council representing District 3 and described how seeing Edgewater's flooding situation had motivated her to run for office. She praised the Council's advocacy work, including securing a state appropriation to armor the canals, and urged them not to back down: "You cannot stop now. You have got to continue this fight." She offered her personal assistance to the Council and the city in any way needed.
Mandy Bullard, 1417 Needle Palm, stated that she has attended nearly every meeting and again urged the Council to join the coalition challenging SB 180 and to keep the moratorium. She noted that Volusia County adopted the charter form of government first in the state and that the county is currently ranked the most at-risk in Florida for flooding and extreme property loss. She argued that council seats are "ineffective and powerless" without a fight, and that the Council is "effectively being removed by doing nothing." She stated: "We want people that fight for us. We'll fight for you."
Catherine Panteske, Growth Beaucia (address protected), stated she was present on behalf of her aunt, a resident of Edgewater, and urged the Council to join the coalition pursuing litigation against the state over SB 180. She argued that SB 180 directly infringes upon constitutionally protected home rule authority under Article 8, Section 2(b) of the Florida Constitution and the Home Rule Powers Act of 1973. She criticized the county's approach of seeking a legislative amendment as "not only weak but also delays critical progress." She characterized SB 180 as "a calculated attempt by the legislature, aided by our local delegation, to strip away local authority," and argued that litigation is "the only meaningful mechanism" to challenge it. She reminded the Council: "Your political future does not lie in Tallahassee. It lies right here with Edgewater residents." She spent her final seconds urging the Council not to fold, and to join the lawsuit.
Gina Holt, 1798 Hideaway Lane, concurred with all previous speakers and urged the Council to stand its ground. She noted that none of the legislators in Tallahassee voted for were known to her, and that Volusia County is well-documented as poorly drained in historical soil surveys. She characterized SB 180 as "the poorest written bill" she had encountered in 40 years of work adjacent to the legal field, and urged the Council to join the coalition and push for the bill to be amended: "Put the pressure back where it belongs for these people to fix what they screwed up."
Tim London, 2632 Woodland Drive, Edgewater, expressed full support for all comments made during the hearing and noted that the moratorium effort extends well beyond Edgewater, since cities and counties statewide were undertaking similar measures. He encouraged the Council to recognize that they have allies and to fight alongside them: "Do not repeal the ordinance."
The Mayor closed the public hearing.
Mayor Depew stated that it is not in his nature to stand down and do nothing, and indicated that he would recommend the Council pursue a multi-pronged approach: supporting the county's amendment process, continuing to advance the goals of the moratorium on an administrative level, and joining the statewide litigation coalition. He indicated that while he had personally wanted to wait until ten or more cities had joined the coalition, sufficient participation now existed to proceed, and that joining was not inherently adversarial toward legislators, but necessary to defend home rule. He asked City Attorney Wolfe for his opinion on joining the group lawsuit.
City Attorney Wolfe stated he recommends joining the group lawsuit challenging SB 180, citing strong constitutional grounds for overturning the statute and the possibility of a preliminary injunction stopping enforcement. He noted that as of the prior Thursday, the lead attorney on the litigation had three or four cities committed and expected ten by the time of the meeting and fifteen to twenty by filing.
Councilwoman Gillis stated she had not received a single phone call, email, or message asking her to remove the moratorium, and reaffirmed her commitment to the residents of Edgewater. She stated: "If I get removed, I'll walk through this town with my head held high. I work for you." She described losing sleep over the situation and expressed her commitment to the community, including her grandchildren, and the desire to protect the natural character of the city. She was emotional but resolute.
Councilwoman Dolbow (by phone) stated she was in consensus with her colleagues and wished to pursue both the amendment process and join the coalition.
Councilman Thomas expressed full consensus on both items and stated he stood with the Council.
Councilwoman Gillis stated she had already expressed consensus on joining the coalition multiple times.
The Mayor sought and received unanimous consensus from all five council members to: (1) support the county's amendment process, and (2) direct the City Attorney to prepare a resolution to join the litigation coalition for a vote at the next regular meeting.
Councilman Rainbird stated he felt bound by his oath of office to uphold state law, referencing his career as a state law enforcement officer from 1970 to 2001 and as a county deputy sheriff through 2005. He stated: "I am not going to be an outlaw now." He expressed his support for fighting SB 180 through proper legal channels and indicated he believed the law could be beaten, but that the fight should be conducted correctly through the coalition.
Councilwoman Dolbow (by phone) stated that as much as SB 180 negatively affects residents, she feels the Council is obligated to follow state law, and that is where she stands.
Mayor Depew returned the discussion to the moratorium ordinance itself. He raised a question about the sufficiency of the Volusia County Building Industry Association's notice letter as a valid safe harbor notice under SB 180, noting that the statute requires a complainant to set forth the specific facts and reasons explaining how the local government's action violates the statute prior to filing suit, and that upon receipt the local government has 14 days to respond. He stated that the letter, as read into the record by City Attorney Wolfe, merely stated that SB 180 had been signed and requested that permits be accepted, citing the statutory null-and-void language, without specifying how the moratorium had actually burdened any particular party.
City Attorney Wolfe read the letter into the record: "Good afternoon, Mr. Solstice. I'm reaching out to see when all permits will be accepted at the City of Edgewater. With the final approval from Governor DeSantis on SB 180, all moratoriums are to be declared null and void," followed by the statutory language. He opined that while he did not have the full email before him, the letter appeared to meet the "spirit of the statute" in placing the city on notice.
Mayor Depew and Councilwoman Gillis both questioned whether the letter genuinely met the statutory standard, noting that it did not explain how the moratorium specifically burdened anyone. Councilwoman Gillis characterized it as having been "thrown together" hastily. Mayor Depew further noted that Building Director testimony indicated business had been proceeding as usual since SB 180's passage, specifically referencing a public records request (FOIA Request No. 2025-776) confirming that two permits had been issued and none had been held since the bill was signed, and questioned how any party could demonstrate legal injury or standing if no one had been prevented from obtaining a permit. He stated: "We're voting an ordinance to repeal that we don't know how our residents are being affected by the ordinance."
Mayor Depew also asked for direction and confirmation that, regardless of the vote on the ordinance, staff would continue to advance every goal underlying the moratorium , including completing the comprehensive plan update, reviewing and updating relevant codes, and awaiting the stormwater master plan expected in December. The City Manager confirmed that those goals could and would continue.
Charles Kilborn returned to the podium during the Council discussion period to reinforce his earlier legal argument, citing a Holland & Knight opinion letter stating that SB 180 specifically prohibits moratoriums on reconstruction or redevelopment of hurricane-damaged property and "does not prevent all building moratoriums for new construction." He urged the Council to revisit the legal interpretation before proceeding.
Councilwoman Gillis and Mayor Depew also questioned whether, given that City Attorney Wolfe had opined that the moratoriums are already null and void ab initio under SB 180, repealing an ordinance that was already legally void served any practical purpose.
Councilman Rainbird made clear his view that despite his sympathy for residents, he felt bound by his oath to follow state law and moved to take action on the ordinance.
Mayor Depew stated on the record that he would recommend revisiting the matter if and when a valid, specific safe harbor notice is received from an affected party.
title: 1st Reading - Ordinance No. 2025-O-08: Request to repeal the City-wide Moratorium and the Florida Shores Building Permit Moratorium in response to the passage of Senate Bill 180.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Thomas, to approve Resolution No. 2025-R-25.1. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
The City Attorney read Resolution No. 2025-R-25 into the record: A Resolution of the City of Edgewater, Florida, designating the administrative authority to review, process, and administer plats and replats in accordance with Senate Bill 784; authorizing recording; repealing resolutions in conflict herewith; providing for severability and applicability; and establishing an effective date.
City Attorney Wolfe explained that Senate Bill 784 requires the city to appoint an administrative authority, defined as a city employee, to administratively approve final plats. The resolution designates Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, as that administrative authority.
The public hearing was opened.
Mandy Bullard, 1417 Needle Palm, returned to the podium and stated simply: "I'm just so proud of you all. That's it."
Charles Kilborn, 5316 Diamondleaf Drive, again addressed the Council, affirming Mayor Depew's earlier analysis of the safe harbor letter and citing the Holland & Knight opinion letter he had been reading during the meeting. He argued that the notice letter does not qualify as a valid safe harbor notice both for the reasons the Mayor articulated and because it does not explain how the moratorium made the city's action illegal, which, he argued, is a distinct statutory requirement. He reiterated his reading that SB 180 "does not prevent all building moratoriums for new construction" and urged the Council to properly interpret the law before acting.
The public hearing was closed.
Mayor Depew acknowledged this item as a distinct matter arising from Senate Bill 784 (not SB 180) and stated that the Council must comply with this bill. He expressed concern about the practical effect of removing Council oversight over final plat approvals, referencing the Balco Road subdivision as the only instance in his recollection where a final plat had been denied or reverted by the Council. He asked City Attorney Wolfe whether, under the new structure, staff could still keep the Council informed of final plat decisions and whether any avenue existed for Council input. City Attorney Wolfe confirmed that City Council would no longer have control over the approval or denial of final plats under this structure, though Mr. Solstice could keep the Council informed of decisions.
Mayor Depew noted he had been a "lonely no" on several major subdivisions over his tenure and had seen one final plat, the Balco Road project, denied by the Council and subsequently reverted. He stated this represented a meaningful loss of Council authority.
Councilwoman Gillis noted that the new administrative role adds significant responsibility to Mr. Solstice's existing workload.
Councilman Rainbird echoed this concern, stating: "He's got enough as it is."
Councilwoman Dolbow stated she was in favor of the resolution and, noting that something needed to be done to comply with state law, offered to make the motion.
Councilwoman Gillis noted that the Council's best avenue for protecting residents going forward is to ensure strong conditions are applied at the preliminary plat stage, before final plat review becomes solely administrative.
title: Resolution No. 2025-R-25: Request for approval of a resolution designating the administrative authority to review, process, and administer plats.

minutes_note:
Sean Maroney, Interim Deputy Director of Public Works, presented a slide show overview of the City's stormwater system, the properties recently acquired from the County, and the status of catch basin repairs.
Mr. Maroney described Florida Shores' stormwater system, noting its 1990's design where streets function as part of the drainage system. This approach was chosen to lower stormwater assessments by avoiding underground piping and align with residents preferences.
In regards to the County owned properties, Mr. Maroney highlighted that the transfer affected the area west of Willow Oak Drive, which includes the Silver Palm Canal and the 29 1/2 Street Canal. The Silver Palm Canal had been maintained by City crews for years, even though it was on private property. With the County's donation of about nine (9) acres, the City now formally owns the land they were already maintaining. The second aspect is a fifty-foot easement that extends roughly one (1) mile west into the hammock along the 29 1/2 street canal. This canal, likely untouched in fifty years and originally dug as an access road into the hammock, has since been cleared by City crews, improving drainage for the west side of Florida Shores.
Regarding the 29 1/2 Street Canal itself, Mr. Maroney described it as running straight west from a mid-block section between streets 29 and 30, accessed via a public right-of-way easement.
Mr. Maroney addressed the catch basin repairs, noting 40 of 100 catch basin boxes had been cut, likely in the early 2000's to help accelerate drainage. Though originally focused on water quality, these cuts helped with flooding. The State permit required their repair, leading to some localized water stacking. The City has since added relief pipes to the berms, ensuring water flows to the canals faster, minimizing the full stack height build up.
Mr. Maroney concluded by noting that the stormwater master plan remained the most significant tool available to the City, as piecemeal fixes, while helpful, do not address the system as a whole. He stated that the consultants running the master plan had been informed that the boxes were now restored.
Mayor Depew commended Mr. Maroney, Interim Public Works Director Jeff Lariscy, and the entire department for their work, particularly in response to an approximately eight-inch rainfall event around two (2) months prior, noting that all water had receded within about an hour and that the team had been prepared immediately.
At Mayor Depew's request, Mr. Maroney explained how residents may submit Public Works requests. He confirmed that all stormwater, streets, utilities, and similar concerns come directly to him for review.
title: Stormwater - 29 1/2 Street Canal and Basin Box Presentation

He noted that a postcard he received referenced only a case number and made no mention of Majestic Oaks, which caused him to discard it. minutes_note:
Resolution No. 2025-R-17 was read into the record by staff. Finance Director Bridgette Vaissiere presented the item, explaining that in compliance with Florida Statute 200.065, the Council is required to publicly announce the tentative operating millage rate and tentative budget. The staff-recommended millage rate is 6.33 mills per thousand dollars of taxable value, held flat from the prior year. This rate represents a 7 percent increase over the rollback rate of 5.9161 mills. The current taxable value for operating purposes is $2,222,709,693. Ms. Vaissiere noted that the increase above rollback covers rising operational and maintenance costs, a 6 percent employee wage increase, and the addition of new positions, including three police officers, a police sergeant, three firefighter/driver engineer EMTs, a full-time public information officer, an accountant, a Parks and Recreation team lead, and a Deputy City Clerk. action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to approve Resolution No. 2025-R-71 Authorizing Participation in the SB 180 Lawsuit. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
attachments: 2025-R-71  Authorizing Participation in Lawsuit Relating to SB180
minutes_note:
Resolution No. 2025-R-71 was read into the record by staff. Interim City Manager Mahoney recommended approval, noting that the Resolution authorizes the City to participate in a lawsuit seeking declaratory and injunctive relief from the provisions of SB 180, which imposes a blanket statewide prohibition on local home rule authority over land use and zoning regulations.
Patrick Fisher, 2100 Air Park Road addressed the Council in support of the resolution. He acknowledged that SB 180 may have been originally intended to help Floridians rebuild storm-damaged properties more quickly, but stated that in practice the law far exceeds that purpose by stripping local governments of their ability to manage growth, infrastructure, and public safety without providing any mechanism for local adjustment. He argued that joining the coalition of cities challenging the law is urgent, noting that a court victory may only apply to cities that actively participate, leaving those that stand aside to bear the full burden of SB 180's restrictions.
Brian White, New Smyrna Beach resident spoke in support of the Resolution. He had been traveling the County and State encouraging municipalities to join the effort against SB 180. He drew a connection to the City's successful stormwater management from the previous evening's rainfall, attributing it to the Council's home rule authority to make proactive local decisions. He stated that problematic language was inserted into SB 180 at the eleventh hour with a chilling impact on home rule statewide, and that this is not a partisan issue but a matter of local residents having a voice in decisions that affect their community. He commended the Council for its courage in previously upholding a development moratorium in the face of pressure from state-level politicians, and expressed strong support for joining the litigation.
A representative of Slow the Growth Volusia urged the Council to join the coalition of cities pursuing litigation against the state over SB 180. She argued that the legislation is a direct assault on local home rule authority, which she traced to its roots in the 1968 Florida Constitution and the Home Rule Powers Act of 1973. She was critical of the county's apparent strategy of simply seeking a legislative amendment, calling that approach "weak." She raised a legal concern based on the U.S. Supreme Court's June 2025 ruling in Trump v. Casa, noting that federal courts may now be required to limit injunctive relief to named plaintiffs only, which could mean that cities not joining the lawsuit would not benefit from any emergency injunction obtained by others. She urged the Council to recognize that their reelection is decided by the residents of Edgewater, who are asking them to fight for their community.
Councilwoman Dolbow expressed enthusiasm for the Resolution and the importance of defending home rule.
Councilwoman Gillis noted that the Council had initially faced concern about being among the first cities to act, but that many cities have since joined and that they are "stronger together."
Councilman Rainbird noted that SB 180's implications extend beyond land use to the city's charter review process and its ongoing land development code work, both of which are potentially constrained by the law's provisions.
Mayor Depew stated for the record that City Attorney Wolfe had advised this course of action as the best route forward, with a good chance of success. He expressed full support for home rule and noted the Council's continued willingness to work with state legislators while simultaneously pursuing litigation.
title: Resolution No. 2025-R-71 Authorize Participation SB 180 Lawsuit

First, in the matter involving an appeal of the denial of a final plat, the court has scheduled a hearing for September 22, at which both sides will present arguments on the submitted briefs. A final order is expected to follow.
Second, All Florida Plumbing and Electrical Supply Company has filed a petition under the Florida Land Use and Environmental Dispute Resolution Act, which is designed to provide an informal, expedited mediation process for private landowners in disputes with local governments. Invocation of the Act tolls the company's time for pursuing court action against the city's decision to deny a conditional use permit and variances. The parties have agreed to a mediation date of October 10, with Darren Elkind serving as special magistrate. City Attorney Wolfe explained that if mediation does not resolve the dispute, the matter proceeds to a hearing where the special magistrate gathers information, takes testimony and evidence, and ultimately makes an advisory recommendation to the City as to whether the City's action was unreasonable or unfairly burdened the property. If the recommendation is unfavorable to the City, the matter would return to the City Council for a vote on whether to accept it. The recommendation was not binding. City Attorney Wolfe stated he would keep the Council informed.

Regarding City Council meeting frequency, Mr. Mahoney sought consensus to return to a single monthly meeting in October, with the next scheduled meeting being October 6. The Council agreed.

action_text:
A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Thomas, to open discussion regarding Interim City Manager Mahoney’s title. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to open discussion regarding making Joe Mahoney the permanent City Manager. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Councilman Thomas shared a personal account of his hospitalization on September 7. Despite being in the hospital, he wished to vote on the SB 180 lawsuit and the millage rate at the September 8 meeting. Manager Mahoney personally came to the hospital, coordinated with hospital staff to allow Councilman Thomas to vote, and also secured a legal opinion from City Attorney Wolfe on whether Councilman Thomas could vote by gesture if unable to speak after a procedure. Councilman Thomas stated the episode demonstrated that Manager Mahoney thinks outside the box and genuinely cares about the City and its Council and recommended the Council consider making him permanent.
Councilwoman Dolbow offered her deepest condolences to Officer Jewell's family and to the Police Department for the loss of their "brother in blue," thanking all officers for their pledge to serve and protect.
Councilman Rainbird indicated he had a substantial report and requested to go last, which the Mayor accommodated.
Mayor Depew expressed deep sorrow for Officer Jewell's family and praised City Manager Mahoney and Acting Police Chief Geiger as the "glue" that held the City and community together during the tragedy, noting that Mr. Mahoney had kept him informed throughout. He echoed the sentiments of Councilman Thomas, then announced a memorial ride for the following Saturday, registration at Teddy Morris Harley Davidson in Ormond Beach beginning at 11:00 AM, with all proceeds going to the Jewell family. He also thanked the American Legion for a successful fundraising event
.
Councilwoman Gillis extended condolences to Officer Jewell's family and the Police Department. She expressed gratitude to surrounding law enforcement agencies and municipalities that had reached out, covered ground for Edgewater's officers during services, and offered assistance, including Senator Wright's and Representative Treymont's offices. Regarding City Manager Mahoney, she noted that she had seen more positive changes in the last three to four months than in the previous two to three years, crediting Mr. Mahoney with much of the progress.
Councilman Rainbird provided a detailed report, covering the following events:
• Attended a vigil for Charlie Kirk on September 16 in New Smyrna Beach, where State Representative Chase Treymont was present and expressed support for Edgewater's SB 180 stance.
• Attended the memorial for Officer Jewell in front of the Police Department.
• Attended the Police Department memorial service for Officer Jewell at Edgewater Alliance Church, noting the massive turnout from surrounding municipalities and describing the emotional impact of seeing motorcycles lined up beneath a large flag.
• Assisted in preparing the memorial ride at Godfather's Customs in Edgewater, with city staff jumping in to help.
Councilman Rainbird then stated that while watching news coverage of Officer Jewell's murder, he kept seeing the word "interim" attached to key city leadership roles. He stated he owed the community the best leadership he could find and that the evidence of the past few months was clear. He made a motion to remove the "interim" designation from Mr. Mahoney's title.
Mayor Depew confirmed with Mr. Mahoney that he would accept the role, to which Mr. Mahoney replied affirmatively and noted he was open to a probationary period to put everyone's mind at ease. Mayor Depew then read an extensive list of accomplishments under Mr. Mahoney's tenure, including stormwater infrastructure investments, the Duck Lake project, strategic CRA property acquisitions, hurricane preparedness improvements, certified stormwater inspector certifications, Public Works operational changes, facility enhancements, collective bargaining agreement ratifications for police and fire, and more. He also summarized Mr. Mahoney's professional qualifications, including over 20 years of public safety and executive leadership experience, advancing from police sergeant to chief of police, and holding a Bachelor of Applied Science in Supervision and Management.
Mayor Depew noted that a nationwide search had previously been conducted with no satisfactory candidates, and that Mr. Mahoney had already built strong relationships at the state level. He clarified that the vote that evening would not be the final vote, but rather a motion to proceed with contract negotiations, with the contract to be approved at the October 6 meeting so citizens are given another opportunity to comment at that time.
City Attorney Wolfe clarified that the City Charter requires the City Manager to reside within the City of Edgewater within six (6) months after the probationary period ends.
Councilwoman Dolbow expressed that she had been very impressed by Mr. Mahoney's leadership and team-building. She emphasized her desire to have a discussion and noted that the prior candidate search had not been fully completed, the process was postponed due to scheduling conflicts, reducing final candidates from three to two. She corrected the record, noting that the $10,000 in budgeted relocation/travel funds was intended to cover all remaining candidates, not a single individual. She expressed enthusiasm for Mr. Mahoney taking the role and acknowledged his open communication, proactive approach, and effectiveness in addressing residents' concerns.
Councilman Thomas reinforced his earlier hospital story, adding that Mr. Mahoney had arranged for a paramedic to confirm he was medically fit to vote after a procedure, further illustrating out-of-the-box problem solving.
Councilwoman Gillis noted that she had received an exceptional volume of positive feedback from residents who had long-standing unresolved issues that Mr. Mahoney resolved quickly. She also reported that City staff had reached out to her expressing happiness with recent positive changes under his leadership.
Councilman Rainbird emphasized that Mr. Mahoney's six years as Police Chief meant he knew every aspect of the City, and that hiring from within had already proven effective, with Acting Police Chief Geiger stepping up seamlessly. He concluded that the learning curve for an outside hire would be substantial.
The item was then opened for citizens' comments.
Linda Mojer, 319 Leaning Oak Drive, acknowledged Mr. Mahoney's helpfulness but urged the Council, in the interest of transparency and good public relations, to place the final appointment on the October 6 agenda rather than voting that evening, so the broader public could participate. Mayor Depew confirmed that the final contract vote would indeed occur at the October 6 meeting and that the evening's motion was only to direct staff to negotiate a contract.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, expressed strong support for Mr. Mahoney, recounting that he had previously advocated for the purchase of pumps at an emergency management meeting and was pleased that Mahoney had followed through. He recommended approval.
Corrie Sapp, 2630 Travelers Palm Drive, stated she had no objection to Mr. Mahoney serving as City Manager but raised a concern that the motion appeared orchestrated given the volume of prepared information presented, and asked whether the Sunshine Law had been violated.
City Attorney Wolfe then restated the motion for clarity.
Mayor Depew confirmed this would proceed to the October 6 meeting for the final contract vote, with the public invited to participate.

minutes_note:

Councilwoman Dolbow also commented that Donna McDavid had previously served on a committee and expressed that it would be beneficial to draw in newer residents for such appointments, to broaden perspectives. minutes_note:
Interim City Manager Mahoney reported that five (5) proposals had been received in response to the City's request for proposals for General Legal Counsel services. The firms submitting proposals were: Aaron Wolfe's firm, Sabatini Law Firm, Smith Gramble and Russell, Vega Law Firm, and Vose Law Firm. The Council was presented with options to interview candidates privately, publicly at a special meeting, publicly at a regular Council meeting, or to select a firm immediately.
Citizens' Comments:
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, urged the Council to hear a discussion and review the facts before any vote on replacing City Attorney Wolfe. He stated he believed Mr. Wolfe had saved the City tens of thousands, if not millions, of dollars, and that his experience as a litigation attorney was invaluable, particularly with the SB 180 fight pending. He recommended renewing Mr. Wolfe's contract until the new City Manager and permanent Police Chief were in place, arguing that a change in legal counsel at this juncture would undermine Mr. Mahoney.
Renee Sortman, Umbrella Tree Drive, strongly agreed with Mr. Martin's comments, expressing concern that recent changes had removed experienced staff in rapid succession. She stated her belief that the impetus for the change was a personal friendship between the Mayor and Anthony Sabatini, and emphatically stated that the City should stay with Mr. Wolfe given his experience and credibility, particularly with the Lennar litigation and other pending matters.
Council Discussion:
Mayor Depew stated that his position was not personal to any individual, but one of fiscal responsibility. He noted that legal costs were projected to increase by $100,000 in the coming year and that such a significant increase warranted a competitive process. He emphasized that any transition would not be abrupt and that ongoing litigation would be handled appropriately. He stated his preference was for private interviews with all firms.
Councilwoman Dolbow stated she had reviewed all five (5) proposals and desired more time and private one-on-one meetings with each firm. She noted that three of the five firms were significantly more expensive than Mr. Wolfe's firm, while only one was slightly lower. She cautioned that fiscal responsibility should also account for the moral responsibility of continuity, especially given increasing litigation. She observed that whoever was selected would be billing the same hourly rates for the work being generated by Council decisions.
City Attorney Wolfe clarified that under the existing contract, either party may terminate without cause on 30 days' notice. He noted that should the Council choose a new firm, he could continue handling ongoing litigation matters or the insurance company could reassign counsel, depending on the Council's preference.
Mayor Depew confirmed the evening's discussion was not about terminating the current contract, only about the interview process going forward.
The Council reached consensus to conduct private one-on-one interviews with all five firms. Mr. Mahoney indicated he would work to schedule interviews and complete the process before the November City Council meeting, or sooner if schedules permitted.
Councilwoman Gillis indicated she would also be comfortable with a second meeting in October if needed. Councilwoman Dolbow stated November was acceptable.
The consensus was to target completion of private interviews and bring the selection to the November City Council meeting.
title: Discussion and selection of Legal Counsel for the City of Edgewater

action_text: A motion was made by Mr. Andrejkovics, second by Mr. Duane, to send a favorable recommendation to City Council to approve this item as written.
minutes_note:
Mr. Solstice stated the staff report, City staff recommends approval.
Mr. Fisher recommended a motion of continuance of this recommendation of SD-2405, until the stormwater master plan is returned to the City. Decisions of this scale should demonstrate conformity and feasibility with the City's forth coming stormwater management strategy by Jones Edmund and Associates. Size and scope here is enormous, construction plans submitted state main and receiving waters as Turnbull Hammock headwaters. Specifically, to Turnbull Hammock Conservation Area, which is situated East of I-95 and West of US-1, so basically all of Florida Shores. I get it, a 100-year storm standards, D.E.P. ( Department of Environmental Protection), St. John's River Standards, cup to cup, i's dotted and t's crossed, but the fact of the matter is our past reliance on their effectiveness has left us in our current predicament and searching for solutions. This is going to get done, no doubt about it, but it must be done right, and I know it would be a disservice to cut the corner right here.
Mr. Andrejkovics asked Mr. Wolfe if this was appropriate at this point.
Mr. Wolfe stated that it is not the role of this board to table things for down the road. The role of this board is to send a recommendation of either favorable or unfavorable to higher boards.
Mr. Andrejkovics told Mr. Fisher to cease his comments and opened the floor for public comment.
Mr. Glen Storch explained the legal options for the board.
Shaun Stefan, 3450 Old Dawson Ranch Road, applicant. Explained that Deering Park Center is the Edgewater portion of this very large piece of land, it's 70,000 acres. Within it we have gone through great lengths to preserve a large portion of the property. Currently 46,000 acres is set aside for conservation. In order for that to happen we had to take into consideration, wildlife corridors, hydrology, ecosystem, we also want to connect with the corridors on the outer portions of the property. We have many parts of this project are in Edgewater. So starting with Deering Park Center, 185 acres will be in conservation, in Deering Park North approximately 3,700 acres will be in conservation easements, to the West we have Farmington Eastern Gateway 100 acres of that will be in conservation and will also include the Edgewater Wetland Park, and a Wildlife Wetland Corridor bike trail which will connect through the property and North to State Road 44. Tonight we are discussing Deering Park Center, Single Family portion, we have commenced construction on our welcome center and improving the end of Indian River Boulevard. Deering Park Center will have a wide range of homes, as well as, some commercial options. There will be 250 homes in this neighborhood, surrounded by preserves, lakes, and we went to great lengths to preserve a lot of the Oak trees. Landscaping improvements of current Indian River Boulevard will be done to create tree hammock effect. We are incorporating native landscaping throughout community, which will be less water usage, healthy soils and ecosystems, and less fertilization.
Mr. Storch stated that all plats must be cohesive with the Edgewater Comprehensive Plan, City zoning, and the Land Development Code. The applicant has done all of the appropriate permits, and have provided a stormwater report for a 100 year storm event, there will be 155 acres of stormwater lakes in this development. Planning for the 100 year storm event criteria, results in significant decrease in run-off from the natural grade. All entitlements, permits, stormwater permits by County and City have been granted for this project.
Agnes Whittier, 223 Flagler Avenue, recently read an article that mentioned FEMA's new standards, and asked if their lakes will be able to handle a 500 year flood or is the flooding going to come over I-95?
Mr. Andrejkovics closed public comments.
Mr. Storch, we are already reducing the natural amount of runoff, on top of that we have the 100 year standard and additional outstanding waters, that has been planned for in this development. at this point we meet or vastly exceeded the requirements we have been given.
Mr. Andrejkovics opened for board comments.
Mr. Hatcher questioned about the big and mature trees and wetland conservation overlay on State Road 442. Mr. Solstice explained that they cannot sneak in more than is planned for, they would have to come back for a complete re-plat.
Mr. Storch expressed that once, conservation easements are established they are permanent and will not be touched.
Mr. Hatcher questioned the elevation of roads compared to State Road 442. Can we put something in place that their artery roads are no higher that 442, that way all the houses are only twelve inches higher than 442? Mr. Warshaw stated that the City and the City's engineering standards dictate that there be a minimum separation of the roadway and what is analyzed as the mean season high ground water. We are putting that roadway at bear minimum separation from the ground water required by code.
Mr.Andrejokvics closed public comments and asked for a motion.
Mr. Storch approached and asked Mr. Fisher and Mr. McGinnis they legal reasoning that they voted no.
Mr. Fisher had no legal backing to his vote.
Mr. Andrejkovics confirmed with Mr. Wolfe the vote results.
Mr. Wolfe stated that it is a three to two vote, with recommendation to send the item to City Council.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilman Thomas, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to approve Resolution No. 2025-R-37 final year end of budget appropriation for fiscal year 2024-2025. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
attachments: 2025-R-37 Final Budget Adjustments - November FY25 with Exhibit A
FY25 FINAL Budget Amendment detail pending 10.20.2025 Additional Detail
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Resolution into the record.
Bridgette Vaissiere, Finance Director, explained that Florida Statutes require the City Council to adopt a final budget and all adjustments within 60 days following the end of the fiscal year, and that any budget amendment must be adopted in the same manner as the original budget unless otherwise specified in the Charter. She noted that the City Manager and Staff preformed a final year-end budget-to-actual review of revenues and expenditures for each fund.
Ms. Vaissiere advised the Council that four line items had been incorrect on a prior exhibit and were being corrected with the final exhibit amendment. The first correction addressed the fire impact fund, which had inadvertently been shown as the recreation impact fund, for an amount of $12,750 related to the uplift of donated equipment. The second correction moved an insurance true-up of $31,004 to the proper insurance fund line rather than the workers' compensation line.
She then detailed the years' final expenditures. The City wide amendment of $179,222 included $24,911 for transfers and a cost increase of $154,311. Of this, $119,400 covered State insurance premium, with Police and Fire pensions receiving $72,631 and $46,769 from the State insurance fund, noted in the general fund. An emergency generator repair due to a lightening strike at Fire Station 55 cost $24,911 with insurance reimbursement being sought. Furthermore, $10,000 was allocated to Senate Bill 180 litigation in Fiscal Year 2025, with more costs anticipated in Fiscal Year 2026.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Mayor Depew thanked all Staff involved with the budget amendment for their hard work.
Councilwoman Dolbow noted that the City is paying $10,000 for the SB180 litigation in fiscal year 2025 and asked if they would be paying more in 2026. Ms. Vaissiere confirmed that while the initial retainer fee was $10,000, Staff is anticipating some additional cost moving forward. That will be before them in fiscal year 2026. City Attorney Wolfe clarified for Councilman Rainbird that there may be an additional cost of $10,000 if there is an appeal of the ruling in the underlying litigation.
Councilwoman Dolbow received confirmation from City Manager Mahoney that Edgewater is the only City in the County still participating in the lawsuit.
Councilman Thomas expressed his frustration with the state mandated laws and how they left the municipalities to figure out how to pay for them.
Mayor Depew closed the public hearing.
title: Resolution No. 2025-R-37; Final Year End Budget appropriations for Fiscal Year 2024-2025.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilman Thomas, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to approve Other Business Item No. AR-2025-0457: Request for approval of Deering Park North/Deering Park Center Phase 1 Proportionate Share Agreement. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, presented a traffic agreement for Deering Park, requiring $819,605.25 from the developer for traffic impact costs identified by the Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA). This agreement, in line with sections of the Edgewater and Volusia Land Development Codes, ensures funding for necessary roadway improvements, while the City expects to generate about $479,386 from multimodal impact fees at the building permit stage.
Mayor Depew asked if they had already agreed to this and it was back before them due to a title issue; Mr. Solstice said no, what he may be referring to is the quit claim deed that was on the Consent Agenda.
Mayor Depew asked if the new City Engineer had reviewed this; Mr. Solstice said it had been reviewed by the City's third party engineers as well as Volusia County and FDOT. He also confirmed that there are no stormwater concerns as this was purely a traffic agreement with no stormwater components.
Councilwoman Gillis had concerns about moving forward as they had not been presented the stormwater master plan yet. Mayor Depew had also expressed those concerns and had been advised that Mr. Storch would be holding off until December with any kind of stormwater concerns.
Mr. Storch, representation for the applicant, confirmed that they had agreed to have the plats that deal with stormwater continued after the stormwater report is presented and explained what is before Council currently.
Mayor Depew clarified before the roll call that this is not approving anything regarding development; just traffic.
Councilman Rainbird felt it was positive that they were doing infrastructure before the building.
Mr. Storch assured Council that if they had any concerns regarding stormwater, they would come back before them.
Ernie Cox, with Deering Park, discussed the traffic impact analysis approved by the County, City and FDOT; the improvements to be made to State Road 442 and the I-95 interchange; and their commitment to writing an $819,000 check to help get those improvements done.
Councilman Thomas asked whether the agreement covered Williamson Road; Mr. Cox informed him that it was not part of this agreement.
Councilman Rainbird expressed enthusiasm for the infrastructure-first approach, contrasting it with years of experience hearing developers promise road and traffic improvements that never materialized. He also noted that the stormwater containment failures experienced during prior developments had negative impacts on residents. He felt this agreement was a much more responsible approach.
Mayor Depew confirmed with Mr. Cox that should any stormwater issues arise in connection with the stormwater master plan, the developer would return to Council. Mr. Cox confirmed this and expressed that Deering Park looked forward to listening to the stormwater master plan presentation.
title: AR-2025-0457:Request for approval of the Deering Park North/Deering Park Center Phase 1 Proportionate Share Agreement.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Thomas, to approve Other Business Item No. AR-2025-0458: Request for approval of a Wastewater Agreement between the City of Edgewater and Deering Park. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, explained the wastewater utility agreement between Edgewater and Deering Park. The agreement sets timelines for new residential development, ensuring upfront payment of wastewater utility impact fees, which allows the City to expand plant capacity ahead of development. Deering Park will handle improvements for Lift Station 40 and the force main on Indian River Boulevard, while the City will expand the wastewater treatment plant capacity. Staff recommends approval.
Patrick Fisher, 2100 Airpark Road, raised concerns about the agreement and emphasized the need for transparency and fairness for taxpayers and noted that the agreement was essential under the Deering Park North MUPUD Ordinance. He highlighted the potential fiscal risks, an apparent lack of clear requirements for City engineering inspections and FDEP certification, and the missing exhibits make it difficult for the public to understand. He requested that all exhibits and fiscal impact summaries be available before final approval.
Cindy Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, highlighted that Deering Parks development had been ongoing for nearly 30 years. She had concerns regarding prepaying impact fees, suggesting that if impact fees increase over time and a building freeze occurs, the City could lose substantial value. Additionally, she stated that the wastewater plant was not yet completed and asked the Council to consider these potential financial losses.
Mayor Depew expressed frustration that utilities from the west are being directed east instead of situating the Public Works expansion closer to developed areas. Although the PUD had been agreed upon before he was elected, he opposed the situation and felt that high utility bills party funded future expansion.
Councilman Rainbird commented that the City had made irreversible decisions in the past that might potentially not be worth it.
Mayor Depew asked for the exact amount of impact fees being paid under the agreement, City Manager Mahoney responded that the utility agreement had been negotiated for over a year and that Deering Park had agreed to construct the force main at 442, at an approximate cost of 8 million dollars.
Mr. Solstice explained that the prepayment amount for the first set of residential development was $5,524.920. The agreement allowed the City to update the impact fee audit, and when updated, the agreement could also be updated accordingly. He said that the prepayment was meant to avoid waiting three (3) to four (4) years while the City still had to build to capacity. He reiterated that the City had negotiated for Deering Park to build the force main for it's capacity from the site eastward to the main trunk line near Orange Street, and that the City's responsibility under the agreement remained the plant expansion.
title: AR-2025-0458: Request for approval of a Wastewater Agreement between the City of Edgewater and Deering Park.

action_text: This Other Business Item was recommend for approval.
minutes_note:
Mr. Solstice provided the staff report and stated recommendation.
Chairman Kennedy opened the public hearing.
Glen Storch stated the legal standards and Ordinances for approving a plat, and how they apply to all three projects. Mr. Storch explained that the plat hearing will be held after the stormwater study that is to be conducted on December 1st. They have met all City, County, and State requirements, and will have approximately 4,000 acres in conservation easements. They have designed and are constructing the extension of Indian River Boulevard and the first segment of Williamson, the traffic and drainage improvements of the State Road 442 interchange, constructing approximately 400 acres of interconnected lakes and stormwater systems, and have designed and are constructing the Welcome Center.
Ernie Cox and Shaun Steffen explained that they've planned this development with the idea of, conservation before development. The amount of conservation compliments the Volusia and State Forever Programs, as it consists of interconnected stormwater system and low impact development techniques, such as all of the lakes bordered with natural vegetation, containing fish, and attraction of wildlife. This development, inspired by the Babcock Ranch Development, will hold 20% greater stormwater than required, with 24% less water runoff after development. They will be planting over 7,000 trees and shrubs. The Welcome Center is under construction and expected to have a Certificate of Occupancy by summer of next year. To briefly describe the three development phase we have presented tonight for South of Indian River Boulevard:
- Phase 1A will be a 55+ community on 157acres consisting of 273 homes with 471 trees to be planted.
- Phase 1B will be a 55+ community on 76 acres consisting of 115 homes with 218 trees planted. This phase will consist of larger lake views.
- Townhome Phase will be two-story town homes on 93 acres consisting of 258 homes, it will have 1,087 trees to be planted and will be located near the Welcome Center.
Chairman Kennedy opened the public hearing.
Chairman Kennedy stated that if the development is anywhere close to Babcock Ranch it will be a tremendous asset to the city.
Mr. Fisher questioned who manages the flow of stormwater into the hammock. Mr. Cox explained the history of Turnbull Hammock and answered that, the management of this system is the Deering Park Stewardship District, which is a government entity by the Florida legislature.
Mr. Solstice added that city staff is allowed to access and maintain if needed.
Mr. Andrejkovics had seen a video about the Babcock Ranch project on Youtube and thought the information was educational.
Mr. Cox stated that one of the engineers on the Babcock Ranch team, now works on this one.
Mr. Hatcher inquired which direction the stormwater sheet flow went prior to I-95.
Mr. Cox stated that the planning and engineering staff have been working with the state for a water quality improvement grant within the Turnbull Hammock to test and see if they can implement control features. Before I-95 was constructed, some of the water flowed into the St. Johns and some flowed to the Turnbull Hammock. After I-95 water predominantly flowed West to East and then South. They are working to hold more water and not discharge when the water is high.
Mr. McGinnis questioned the piping, last time the drawings showed the piping as optional and this time they are labeled as proposed for stormwater flow. He also wanted to confirm what the plan is when the waters are high and where it will go once lakes have reached maximum.
Mr. Cox explained how the proposed plans are submitted, and clarified that any overflows at the highest point of the lakes will go West into the swamp.
Lana Fisher, 2100 Airpark Road, asked the Board to consider that they receive a recommendation from staff on how to vote.
Mary Forester, 1937 Edgewater Canal Road, had concerns about hearing contradictory information about how the water and flooding is going to be handled.
Mr. Storch stated, that St. Johns sent investigators down and they said that there is no basis for the complaints. The community that was accusing Deering Park of causing flooding, Deering Park had paid surveyors to show where that community's blockage was.
Mr. Solstice stated that one of the requirements implemented during the rainy season was that they had to hold the stormwater on site.
Susan Greaser, Pelican Lane, felt that if all native vegetation is put in place, that would naturally fix the flooding issue. They are trying to do it right, new and the first time.
Mr. Storch advised that the problem is lack of maintenance.
Judy Bordeaux, 2916 Oak Trail, said she had heard many developers say they are going to hold the water on their land and all overspill water would go into the swamps.
Mr. Hatcher mentioned that the Board has seen a lot of subdivisions come through, and none are like this one that work with natural Florida from day one.
Mr. Storch stated that they would like to think its the smart way to do it, for marketing too.
Chairman Kennedy closed the public hearing and asked for a motion.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to accept Lennar's settlement offer — that Lennar will not seek attorney's fees or costs against the City, the City will not appeal the court's ruling, and the final plat will be issued by Development Services Director Ryan Solstice. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Mayor Depew stated for the record that a executive session was held before the special meeting to discuss options. He affirmed the Council's commitment to residents' best interests, highlighting the main community concern: ensuring sufficient stormwater protection near the Edgewater Preserve on 35th Street.
City Attorney Wolfe presented the background and legal context of the matter. The City Council had previously denied the final plat application for Edgewater Preserve Phase 2. Lennar subsequently filed a petition for writ of certiorari to appeal that denial. The circuit court granted Lennar's petition, ruling against the City.
City Attorney Wolfe explained that the City's Land Development Code requires Council approval of a final plat that meets all land development regulations and complies with the approved preliminary plat. Under applicable case law, once an applicant demonstrates its application meets the City's criteria, the burden shifts to the City to demonstrate by competent substantial evidence that the application does not meet those standards.
The Court found that Lennar met its initial burden, pointing to the City staff's recommendation for approval, unanimous approval by the Planning and Zoning Board and approvals by a third-party engineer and third-party surveyor. The court then found that the City failed to meet its burden, determining that the citizens objectors who spoke at the hearing offered only unsworn opinions, speculation, and assumptions about flooding without any demonstrated technical expertise in stormwater management or the City's Land Development Code. The Court further noted that no witness testified to having observed flooding from the Phase 2 property after Lennar completed its stormwater retention ponds, and that none of the citizens comments were tied to the City's published criteria for final plat approval.
City Attorney Wolfe discussed the City's options moving forward, highlighting that the appeal is discretionary, allowing the appellate court to deny it without merit review. A second-tier proceeding is limited to whether procedural due process was offered and if the correct law was applied by the circuit court. A stay of the ruling is not automatic; if denied, the City must issue the final plat, making the appeal moot. Mr. Wolfe mentioned Lennar's motions for attorney's fees, potentially substantial and not likely covered by the City's insurance.
City Attorney Wolfe reported that Lennar had made a same-day settlement offer: if the City agrees to not appeal and directs Development Services Director Ryan Solstice to issue the final plat, Lennar will not seek attorney's fees or costs against the City.
City Attorney Wolfe also addressed questions raised regarding why photographs and videos were not entered into the record at the quasi-judicial hearing, explaining that a City Attorney's role in such proceedings is to serve as legal advisor and ensure proper procedure, not to act as an advocate for either side. He noted that the City Council, sitting in a quasi-judicial capacity, acts as a judge and must remain impartial, and it is therefore not appropriate for the City Attorney to advocate for one position or present evidence on behalf on the City.
City Manager Mahoney provided an overview of concessions Lennar had already made. Prior to the Phase 2 final plat denial, Lennar had agreed to reduce the development by 68 lots and create additional compensating stormwater storage ponds. Following the denial, Lennar agreed to eliminate Phase 5 of the development entirely and convert the land to additional compensating stormwater storage.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, clarified that Phase 3, 4, and 5 had originally been submitted together but that Phase 5 had since been pulled by Lennar. He confirmed that three (3) subsequent submissions have been made without Phase 5 included, that the road access and turn lane associated with Phase 5 have been removed from the plans, and that the engineering reflects the Phase 5 area as compensating storage. He noted that Phase 3 and 4 will come before Council for preliminary plat and construction plan approval in the upcoming year.
Mayor Depew stated his discomfort with appealing due to the current legal record and disappointment about the lack of evidence at the quasi-judicial hearing. He recognized Lennar's meaningful changes and noted fewer issues after storms, confirming that increased stormwater capacity, which was a primary resident concern, had been achieved. He also highlighted SB 784's reduction of Council's authority over future plat approvals.
Councilwoman Dolbow stated that she was satisfied with the outcome of the prior discussion and expressed her desire to move forward positively. She acknowledged the concessions made by Lennar both before and after the denial, and emphasized the importance of the Council understanding applicable law and asking the right questions before voting in future matters.
Councilwoman Gillis had been troubled to learn after the fact that no evidence had been submitted into the record at the quasi-judicial hearing. She expressed appreciation for the elimination of Phase 5, calling it a meaningful concession, and noted that converting the area to stormwater management was what the Council had sought from the beginning. She requested confirmation that the removal of Phase 5 was documented in writing and not merely verbal assurance.
Councilman Thomas stated that although the City lost the lawsuit, the Council's action achieved the intended outcome of securing meaningful stormwater improvements for the affected residents. He characterized the result as a win for the community.
Councilman Rainbird expressed frustration with the judge's ruling that the citizen testimony lacked expert credibility, questioning whether lay witnesses should be required to hold professional credentials to have their observations considered. He stated that he would make the same decision again if placed in the same position, and was encouraged that Lennar removed an entire phase of the development. He acknowledged, however, a sense of limitation in what the Council can accomplish given evolving State legislation.
The Council reached a unanimous consensus that Phase 5 should be used solely for stormwater purposes and not returned for residential development, and directed that this position be communicated to Lennar.
Regarding accountability for future flooding issues, City Attorney Wolfe confirmed that a maintenance bond on the subdivision would be available as a remedy for any failures, and that it is typically held for two (2) years, with the possibility of litigation if failures occur after the bond period.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Mary Forrester, 1937 Edgewater Canal Road, expressed concern about the City's land development code lacking explicit guidelines on water runoff and building heights. Additionally, she highlighted traffic safety issues at the Air Park Road and Park Avenue intersection due to past serious accidents and questioned the accuracy of the information shared at a recent Planning and Zoning Board meeting regarding that intersection.
Joe Ryan, 2309 Lime Tree Drive, stated that he had only just learned that no evidence had been submitted at the quasi-judicial hearing and found it concerning. He expressed support for not appealing, acknowledging that it would be a waste of money, but urged the Council to ensure there are mechanisms to hold Lennar accountable if flooding occurs as a result of the development.
Following public comment, Council returned to discussion. Councilwoman Dolbow asked whether the motion to accept the settlement could be conditioned on the permanent removal of Phase 5. City Attorney Wolfe advised that Phase 5 was not part of the settlement offer and that he had only learned of it that afternoon, and therefore it could not be formally included in the motion. The Council instead expressed unanimous consensus that Phase 5 should not be brought forward for residential development.

action_text: A motion was made by Mayor DePew, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to table item 9h - Resolution No. 2025-R-39 Request to support the widening of Old Mission Road to the next Council meeting which is the date as followed of January 5th, Monday at 6pm. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Resolution into the record.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, provided a staff report and recommendation.
Mayor Depew asked for Citizens comments and received none.
Mayor Depew and Council expressed a desire for more details about the stormwater implications of the widening, particularly given the area's flooding issues. Councilman Rainbird and Thomas discussed the dangerous conditions on the road, including the deep retention ponds and hazardous curves. Councilwoman Gillis questioned the potential impact on private property and how the widening would be accomplished.
City Manager Mahoney advised that there are no current designs for the widening but felt those concerns would be taken into account. This is just giving support for the widening that may take place in the future.
Mr. Solstice advised that the County had already purchased some of the right of way on Old Mission and said that any design the County does, they will typically send it to City staff for review. The City will extend the offer to run the design through the stormwater master plan model.
The Council agreed that they supported the concept but wanted more information about the specific plans and to ensure the city would be part of the planning process; City Attorney Wolfe confirmed that he would rewrite the Resolution and have it heard at the following meeting.
Mayor Depew passed the gavel to make the motion; Mr. Solstice asked that they mention the intent of the rewrite is for public health, safety and stormwater support. Council agreed.
title: Resolution 2025-R-39: Request to support the widening of Old Mission Road.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Thomas, to approve SD-2401 Request for Preliminary Plat and Construction Plan Approving for Deering Park Center Active Adult Single Family Phase 1a located south of Indian River Boulevard within the Deering Park center. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, provided a staff report and recommendation.
The applicant team, represented by Glenn Storch, Ernie Cox, and Shaun Steffens, gave a comprehensive presentation covering multiple aspects of the overall Deering Park development. They described the 4,000 acres already placed in conservation, the construction of Indian River Boulevard, drainage improvements, stormwater systems, welcome center, wetland park, and Sun Trail bicycle trail.
Mr. Cox detailed several funding sources they had secured, including $7.1 million from DEP for the wetland park, $1.5 million for water quality improvements, $1.4 million for widening SR 442, and $1 million from FDOT for the Sun Trail expansion. He announced plans to submit an application in January for a K-8 charter school focused on STEM education.
The team addressed stormwater management, explaining their system would decrease runoff from the property by 24% after development and that their de-watering operations during construction kept all water on-site, not allowing it to impact surrounding areas.
Mayor Depew opened for Council Comments.
Councilwoman Dolbow felt excitement for the first phase of the project and discussed the positive tax values to the City.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed concern about voting on the plats immediately after receiving the stormwater master plan, suggesting they table the decision until January to allow more time for review. Councilwoman Dolbow pointed out that Deering Park had been included in the stormwater master plan and that it decreased the flow of water, exceeding expectations.
Mayor Depew respected that Mr. Storch had waited to present on Deering Park until after the stormwater master plan was completed and acknowledged Councilwoman Gillis' concern but noted the land would be developed regardless and that the developers were working cooperatively with the City. He advised all the positives that this development would bring to the community.
Councilwoman Dolbow felt that the developers had been very transparent and had shown what they were capable of. She asked City Manager Mahoney how he felt about tabling the items; Mr. Mahoney advised that he would prefer a vote and asked Mr. Wolfe about the legal repercussions of tabling.
City Attorney Wolfe clarified that the Land Development Code didn't speak to tabling, and once the applicant met their burden of showing compliance with requirements, the burden shifted to the city to demonstrate non-compliance.
Councilman Rainbird praised the developers for their transparency and listening to suggestions but noted he had submitted questions from residents that had only been answered that morning. Mr. Cox said they were happy to answer any questions but the questions asked did not pertain to the criteria set forth in the PUD and in the code related to the preliminary plats. The developers assured Council they would address any issues that arose and emphasized their commitment to being good partners with the city.
Mayor Depew asked if there was a motion to table and a second, upon receiving none, he went back to Council comments.
Councilman Thomas stated that he had been involved with this project since 2005 and the developers had always compromised and tried to work with him whenever he had any issues.
Further discussion ensued over the statute regarding approval, the de-watering process and how the development would handle water during a major rain event. Mayor Depew received confirmation that they would be consistently monitoring the stormwater runoff.
Mayor Depew asked for citizens comments.
Jim Cameron, Jim Cameron Consulting, discussed his history with the Chamber and gave his support for the project, asking Council to do the same.
Agnes Whitter, 223 Flagler Avenue, inquired over the plans for construction, the sewer lines and the financial burden to Edgewater. City Manager Mahoney clarified that there are no current financial obligations to the City.
Tim London, 2632 Woodland Drive, expressed concern over who was liable if something goes wrong, Mayor Depew advised that the City has bonds in place.
Linda Mojer, 319 Leaning Oak Drive, felt that there was no harm in tabling the items and voting in January.
Wayne McCloskey, 509 Wildwood Drive, had toured the project property and was impressed by what he had seen. He felt the developers had addressed every concern.
Mr. Storch cited Florida Statute 177.071 which requires approval, approval with conditions, or denial with specific citations of requirements not met.
Mayor Depew felt as though all the concerns had been met.
