minutes_note:
Mayor Depew introduced the item and noted that the public would be permitted to ask up to two (2) questions each, with comments limited to eight (8) minutes. The presentation was delivered by Jared (Senior Project Manager, Jones Edmunds), Brett Cunningham (Jones Edmunds), and Chris Fagers (Meade and Hunt).
Project Overview and Data Collection: Jared outlined the primary tasks of the Stormwater Master Plan: data collection, stormwater model development, flood protection level of service analysis, identification of problem areas, improvement alternative analysis, and a capital improvement plan. Over 1,100 field locations were visited to collect data on stormwater features, including invert elevations, pipe sizes, materials, maintenance condition, and photographs.
Model Development and Verification: A highly detailed stormwater model was developed extending beyond City limits, from the Indian River Lagoon to SR 44. The model was verified against observed flooding from Hurricane Ian (25-50 year return period), the September 14, 2024 rainfall event (20-50 year), and Hurricane Milton (20-25 year). Five design storm events were modeled: mean annual (2-year), 10-year, 25-year, 100-year and 500-year.
Flood Protection Level of Surface: Analysis identified structure, residential yard, and roadway flooding for each design storm event. In a 100-year event, approximately 610 buildings are projected to flood above finished floor elevation, 990 road segments would experience greater than six (6) inches of flooding, and significant percentages of residential yards would be inundated. Twenty-five problem areas were identified Citywide and prioritized as Tier 1, 2, or 3.
Identified Problem Areas: Tier 1 and 2 problem areas include six (6) key flooding zones: Florida Shores South (374 buildings, 403 acre-feet flood in 100-year events), Florida Shores North (56 buildings, 132 acre-feet flood in 100-year events), Florida Shores West (6 buildings, 73-acre feet), Edgewater Acres (impacted by off-site flow, undersized culverts), the G2/G11 Canal, and Pelican West. These areas face flooding due to severe weather, outdated stormwater systems (1950's & 60's), inadequate pond space (only 36 acres in South Shores vs 195-260 needed), limited ditch/culvert capacity, topographic low spots, and more impervious surfaces reducing natural water storage.
Alternative Evaluation and Capital Improvement Plan: Chris Fagers presented the phased capital improvement plan developed from analysis of over 110 alternatives. Twenty-five improvements were recommended across four (4) phases.
Phase 1 (no property acquisition required): Projects include pump stations (50 CFS each) on three (3) ponds south of SR 442, directing water via pipelines to the river; culvert upgrades on Volco Road (two 36-inch RCP's); continuation of the G2/G11 Canal project, which includes increasing culvert sizes, adding four ponds, and two pump stations at Pine Bluff and Pearl Street (grant-funded); a 50 CFS pump installation at Duck Pond north of SR 442; enhancements to the 18th Street Canal (expanded to 30-feet, large box culverts, tide gate at Riverside Drive); a pump at the wastewater reuse pond for Edgewater Acres; improved drainage in Edgewater Acres; a cross-connection channel from 27th Street ponds to Silver Palm Ditch; and removal of undersized culverts on Silver Palm Ditch. Phase 1 aims to mitigate flooding for 172 buildings in 100-year events and about 67% in 25-year occurrences. Projected cost: $83 million to $121 million (excluding the G2/G11 project).
Phase 2 (requires property acquisition): Projects include a 2-acre pond near Canal Road/Mockingbird in the G2/G11 basin; culvert upsizing under Park Avenue and removing old railroad bed culverts; expanding an existing pond near Massey Air Park to 40 acres connecting to Pine Tree Drive; a 30-acre pond in Florida Shores South; a 10-acre pond west connecting to Mango Tree Ditch; a 25th Street canal connecting to Silver Palm Ditch; and a new pond and outfall to the river near Pelican West. This phase projects to remove 449 buildings from the 100-year floodplain at an estimated cost of $43 million to $56 million.
Phase 3(supplements Phases 1 and 2): Projects include expansion of the G2/G11 pond to 17 acres; a 20-acre Mango Pond in North Florida Shores; box culvert improvements under Indian River Boulevard; potential modifications to Phase 1 pump stations; a 23rd Street cross-connection to Silver Palm Ditch; and a connection from Florida Shores to the Pelican West outfall system. Phase 3 is projected to remove 485 buildings from the 100-year floodplain. Estimated cost: $20 million to $28 million.
Phase 4(ultimate resiliency/sea level rise scenario, looking to 2100): projects include a 100-acre pond in Florida Shores South (within an approximately 450-acre search area) and pump stations on the Massey and Mango ponds. This phase is modeled with future sea level rise scenarios and is projected to remove 496 buildings form the 100-year floodplain. Estimated cost: $70 million to $100 million.
Total estimated capital cost: $216 million to $305 million (not including property acquisition costs).
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, proposed similar solutions, including pond pumps and canal improvements. He credited City Manager Mahoney for the Duck Pond pump and advocated for prompt, cost-effective measures given the impending hurricane season. He noted concerns about Volco Road culverts and the 18th Street Canal outfall.
Ernie Cox, Deering Park, asked whether the presentation had addressed stormwater conditions west of Interstate 95 and requested clarification on whether that area had been studied.
Jared (Jones Edmunds) responded that west of I-95 was not a priority due to little development and no flooding being observed. Deering Park's proposed development was modeled at the City's request. It allocates 400-acres (21%) for stormwater management across its 2,000-acre site. The modeling indicates Deering Park would cut peak flow rates into Little Cow Creek and Turnbull Hammock by up to 50% in 25-year and 100-year events, thanks to significant flow attenuation from the planned stormwater ponds.
A representative of Deering Park (identified as a property owner/developer) confirmed that the development exceeds the required 15% stormwater pond area at 21%, and that discharge routes include Little Cow Creek to the Indian River Lagoon and Crane Swamp to the St. Johns River as secondary and tertiary outlets. He expressed confidence that the development would not increase flooding in Edgewater.
A citizen inquired if the 20-21% stormwater storage at Deering Park would reduce water flow under I-95 to Edgewater and if future development was modeled. Jared confirmed the ponds do reduce flow. The citizen also expressed inflation concerns and asked about the model verification and the 18th Street Canal dredging permit status, highlighting the need for surrounding areas to manage their stormwater.
City Manager Mahoney responded that permit applications were submitted in September, design work is complete, letters have been sent to the Army Corps of Engineers, FDEP, and St. Johns Water Management District, and that a contact at the Army Corps has responded and escalated the project for potential expedited permitting.
Mayor Depew expressed strong support for the plan, noting its importance for Federal and State funding. He referenced past discussions with Congressman Corey Mills about whether the City had updated its stormwater master plan, which is a prerequisite for federal funding. Daytona Beach and Port Orange secured funding partly due to completed stormwater master plans. Mayor Depew highlighted low-cost projects, such as the Volco Road culvert and the nearly completed G2/G11 canal project. He stressed updating the plan to prevent increased costs and suggested a quarterly update starting January to ensure consistent progress.
Councilwoman Gillis noted, in layman's terms, that the stormwater model can be used to evaluate all future development proposals for their stormwater impacts, referencing both the Deering Park modeling and the Live Local project in front of Edgewater Landing as examples of the model's practical utility.
Councilman Thomas expressed reservations about the property acquisition in later phases, disapproving of such measures. He questioned if Phase 1 completion might negate the need for Phase 2. A Jones Edmunds representative clarified that Phase 1 tackles the 25-year storm, but Phase 2, especially a 30-acre pond in Florida Shores, is essential to meet the 100-year storm requirement. He added that limited open space leaves this acquisition as vital for adequate flood protection. Councilman Thomas noted the presentations' clear mention of "increasing impervious area" and "loss of surface storage" as key flooding factors, affirming previously contested concerns.
Councilwoman Dolbow noted that Florida Shores is not under a FEMA 100-year flood zone designation, hence repetitive loss provisions do not apply. The 50% damage threshold for mandatory elevation is only for structures in the FEMA 100-year flood zone, as seen in other municipalities post-Hurricane Milton.
Councilman Rainbird commended the presentation's thoroughness and raised concerns about funding the $450 million cost. He emphasized the urgency of action before the next hurricane season and praised City staff's ongoing maintenance. He advocated for two (2) immediate projects: enhancing the 18th Street corridor for a Florida Shores outfall to the Indian River and acquiring land in southwest Florida Shores for a retention area linked to Turnbull Hammock, mentioning existing discharge permission. He backed the Mayor's quarterly update plan and supported advancing near-term improvements.
City Manager Mahoney confirmed that staff would digest the plan and provide an update at the January Council meeting, with quarterly updates to follow. He noted that staff had already begun some low-cost improvements, including removal of Silver Palm Canal crossovers to increase flow.
title: Presentation by Jones Edmunds regarding the stormwater master plan

title: Regular Meeting - December 10, 2025

minutes_note:
Mr. Conroy suggested adding citizen comments to future agendas to allow the public to provide input. The committee agreed this would be beneficial.
Mr. Fisher raised the issue of obtaining input from other entities within the City, including Council and staff. He suggested that City Manager Mahoney could query department heads for input. Mr. Fisher noted that staff might be reluctant to speak directly in meetings, so an anonymous feedback mechanism might be beneficial. The committee agreed that soliciting input from staff would be valuable.
The committee discussed planning for public input beyond the already scheduled January 17, 2026 meeting specifically for residents. Ms. Bullard suggested considering a meeting prior to the City Council Meeting. City Manager Mahoney advised of a possible agenda item to solicit information from citizens.
Mr. Fisher also expressed that the committee should consider all suggestions, even those potentially restricted by Senate Bill 180, since the bill has an end date and the committee only convenes every five years. He noted it would be helpful to at least document ideas for future consideration.
The committee then began a section-by-section review of the charter:
Section 1.01 General Powers: The committee discussed the 35-foot height restriction east of U.S 1
Section 1.02 Construction: No changes were noted or discussed
Section 2.01 Corporate Limits: The committee briefly reviewed the description of the corporate limits.
Section 3.01 Composition: No changes were noted or discussed
Section 3.02 Districts: The committee discussed the makeup of council districts and the potential future need for redistricting, particularly as new developments like Deering Park grow. Ms. Mojer asked when redistricting was last done and questioned the adequacy of using the decennial census for redistricting timing.
Section 3.03 Qualifications: No changes were noted or discussed
Section 3.04 Elections and Terms: The committee discussed the canvassing board and asked for clarification on who serves on the canvassing board.
Section 3.05 Compensation: The committee had an extensive discussion regarding compensation for the mayor and council members. Chairman Conroy shared his personal experience that the current compensation is insufficient given the time commitment and expenses involved in representing the City at various meetings and organizations. He suggested giving council members the option to take monetary compensation in lieu of health care benefits if they don't need the City's insurance. The committee also discussed the need for comparative data on compensation from similar-sized cities. Additionally, the committee discussed council being entitled to per diem when traveling or attending events.
Section 3.06: No changes were noted or discussed
Section 3.07 General Powers and Duties; Municipal Government Training: The committee suggested shortening the two-year time frame for completing required training, recommending either 6 months or one year instead. Mr. Conroy suggested consulting with current council members about their experiences with the training timeline.
Section 3.08 Prohibitions: The committee raised concerns about potential loopholes regarding elected officials taking jobs with other cities after leaving office. The committee requested City Attorney Wolfe research this issue. The committee also mentioned consulting with the Finance Director regarding the percentages for the net taxable value of debt as well as maintaining a percentage of all operating funds.
Meeting went into Recess at 4:57 PM
Meeting Reconvened at 5:05 PM
Section 3.09 Vacancies: The committee discussed adding specific reference to Florida Statute 112 in the City Charter to ensure clarity.
Section 3.10: No changes were noted or discussed
Section 3.11: Procedure - Rules and Journal: The committee discussed the citizens' comments portion of Council meetings. Mr. Conroy expressed support for maintaining both the beginning and end comment periods, and some members discussed whether three minutes was sufficient time for speakers. Ms. McDavid suggested allowing citizens to request additional time if needed.
Section 3.11 Procedure - Voting: City Attorney Wolfe noted that Edgewater's requirement for three votes to pass an Ordinance or Resolution is somewhat unusual. Ms. McDavid inquired about making certain topics require a super majority vote, particularly for significant zoning changes or environmental impacts. Attorney Wolf agreed to research the legality of such a provision.
Section 3.12 Ordnances and Resolutions: No changes were noted or discussed
Section 3.13 Initiative and Referendum: No changes were noted or discussed
The committee continued through Sections 4.01-4.06 regarding the City Manager, City Attorney, and City Clerk. The committee suggested adding requirements for annual performance evaluations for these positions, and requiring all Council members to participate in these evaluations.
Concerns were raised about the vulnerability of having all three Charter Officers (City Manager, City Attorney, and City Clerk) under direct council supervision, noting that a council could potentially remove all three simultaneously, severely disrupting city operations. Suggestions were made to potentially move the City Clerk position under the city manager's supervision to provide more stability and employment protections.
At this point, the committee agreed to stop at Section 4.07 and continue the review at the next meeting.
title: CHARTER REVIEW

He estimated that the permitting process would be complete by June of that Year and that State appropriation funds would be utilized, in coordination with the City's Grant Administrator, to help fund the project.
Public Works Software Management System: City Manager Mahoney reported that a new software management system was coming online for Public Works to address administrative work flow deficiencies identified. He thanked Interim Director Jeff Lariscy for identifying and implementing the software, noting it was expected to streamline operations and track maintenance more efficiently.
Dedicated Stormwater Inspection Position: City Manager Mahoney announced the creation of a dedicated Stormwater Inspection Position that would work closely with the City Engineer. The position would participate in the review process for stormwater site plans, conduct both scheduled and unannounced on site inspections, and create an inspection schedule covering approximately 1,222 stormwater pipes and 200 stormwater features such as culverts, swales, and basins through the City.
Public Facing Project Dashboard: City Manager Mahoney announced that City staff was developing a public facing dashboard to be hosted on the City's website. The dashboard would allow the public to click on a location or project and obtain a summary, the type of funding utilized, and an expected completion date.
Team Member of the Month Program: City Manager Mahoney announced a new employee appreciation and recognition program called "Team Member of the Month." Each department may bring forward a candidate each month. The employee's accomplishments are reviewed at the director's staff meeting, and a selection is made. The award includes a $50 gift card donated by the Edgewater Police Volunteer Association and a certificate.
City Manager Mahoney announced Rusty Boyer as Team Member of the Month for November 2025. Mr. Boyer, an equipment operator and spray technician, has over 26 years of service with the City of Edgewater, displaying professionalism, reliability, and a strong work ethic. During the stormwater event on October 10,2025, Boyer took on extra responsibilities within the stormwater division, handling over 300 TracEZ requests. He managed the prioritization, tracking, and documentation of complaints, improving efficiency and reducing the backlog to under 80 in less than three months. Mr. Boyer's leadership and initiative ensured continuous operations and embody the City's core values of responsiveness, teamwork, accountability, and excellence. His recognition was unanimously supported by directors and the City Manager for his outstanding contributions.
Following the presentation, Councilman Thomas shared a personal observation about Mr. Boyer. He recounted that during the storms of the prior year, he had personally witnessed Mr. Boyer and a fellow City worker assist a nurse who worked the night shift and was unable to get her car out of her driveway because of a fallen tree.
Mayor Depew agreed with the sentiment and commended Public Works broadly.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve Resolution No. 2026-R-02. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Resolution into the record.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, explained that the request to vacate a portion of Hibiscus Drive and the southeastern right of way of 31st Street for building construction within the B 2 Neighborhood Business Commercial zoning. Platted in 1956, the vacation would return the right of way to adjacent owners, with 0.48 acres added to the applicant’s land and 0.06 acres to 3103 India Palm Drive. The owner at India Palm Drive had no objections, and no opposing public input was received. The proposal aligns with the Comprehensive Plan by supporting infill development and redevelopment, ensuring no access issues for nearby businesses, and with no utilities running under the street, a dead end sign would be installed. Staff recommended approval.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Rob Merrill, Cobb Cole Law Firm, came forward on behalf of the applicant, noting a Planning Board recommendation of approval and a staff recommendation of approval. He stated that several individuals in the room were present in support of the application and offered to answer any questions.
Cindy Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, asked whether the property bordered the side of Indian River Elementary School and raised questions about potential future land use, specifically whether the right of way might be used as an access or egress for the elementary school and whether the flooding in the area had been thoroughly researched.
Mayor Depew responded that the matter was addressed in the Stormwater Master Plan and noted that the railroad tracks in the vicinity was a limiting factor.
Councilman Thomas requested further clarification on the map, asking which properties bordered
the area.
Councilwoman Dolbow inquired about the location of the dead end sign, questioning if it would be near the storage units or further down. Mr. Solstice clarified the parcel south of the storage unit wasn't included in the vacation, and that three parcels on Hibiscus and India Palm were part, extending to 31st Street on the south. He stated that the property owner south of 31st would be allowed to fence that section, as it would turn into private property. Councilwoman Dolbow also wondered if the parcel above the subject was owned by the applicant. Mr. Solstice confirmed that it was not and mentioned that while staff advised including the full street, it wasn't necessary as access would remain available.
Mr. Solstice further noted that the vacation would save the City from the cost of paving the road, that there were no utilities running underneath, and that it did not restrict access to properties to the north.
Mayor Depew noted that there was no public opposition and that the neighbors in the area were in favor.
title: Resolution 2026-R-02: Request to vacate a portion of Hibiscus Drive and the Southeastern right-of-way of Thirty First Street.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve Resolution No. 2026-R-03. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Attorney Wolfe read the Resolution into the record.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, explained that the Water Quality Infrastructure Grant provides businesses the means to upgrade their sanitary sewer systems. The grant involves $150,000 from the City of Edgewater and $600,000 from the county, totaling $750,000. Mr. Solstice stated that Incertec, a metal finishing company, is relocating its headquarters from Titusville to Edgewater and remodeling the former Factory Direct building. Incertec plans to create roughly 150 jobs with an average salary of $54,000 over three years, projecting around $60 million in economic impact. Staff recommended approval.
Mayor Depew discussed the importance of large industrial employers like Incertec to the City's tax base, citing companies such as Boston Whaler, Everglades Boats, and Dodger Manufacturing as key contributors through personal property taxes in addition to ad valorem taxes. He asked if the City could recover the $150,000 investment within the first year via these revenues. Mr. Solstice affirmed that the tax income from the planned 50,000 square foot expansion, combined with new jobs, would likely cover the investment.
Councilman Rainbird said that the personal property tax is a significant benefit.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Avenue, asked for clarification on whether the equipment tax was the same as property tax. He also inquired if the grant for Incertec was available to other businesses.
City Manager Mahoney explained that the grant is available to any business meeting the criteria and highlighted that Incertec's collaboration addresses their wastewater issues, bringing significant economic benefits to Edgewater.
Mr. Solstice elaborated on the technical nature of the grant, explaining that Incertec's metal plating process results in metals in the wastewater stream, and the grant supports the installation of a treatment system to bring the discharge down to residential standards, ensuring no environmental issues and compliance with the City's pretreatment program.
Councilwoman Dolbow was excited that Incertec had chosen to call Edgewater home, noting that they were relocating from Titusville and expanding, bringing more jobs to the local Southeast Volusia area.
Mayor Depew added that the company was expanding on a concrete slab already in place from the former Factory Direct facility, meaning no additional impervious surface would be added. He also felt the grant was the County helping to subsidize better treatment of wastewater before it is discharged.
Councilwoman Gillis concurred with that perspective, noting the environmental benefit of the pretreatment approach.
title: Resolution 2026-R-03: Request to pledge support for the Water Quality Infrastructure Grant from Volusia County to support the expansion of a new business, Incertec.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve Resolution No. 2026-R-04. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:

Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, reminded the Council that the CDBG G 2 and G 11 canal improvement project involves sections owned by the County, lacking City easements. The Stormwater Use Agreement would allow the City to implement grant identified improvements, maintain them, and manage the canal proactively, granting legal access to previously restricted areas. This is crucial for addressing stormwater matters effectively within the City's jurisdiction. Staff recommended approval.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Avenue, suggested showing a map for clarity on the specific canals involved. He shared concerns about the stagnant condition of a canal near Ridgewood that drains to Old Mission Road, leading to mosquito issues. City Manager Mahoney clarified that the G2 and G11 canals were included in the agreement, encouraged Mr. DeVoe to provide his contact info for more detailed answers, and highlighted the upcoming public dashboard for viewing comprehensive project information and maps.
Cynthia Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, expressed concern that the City maintaining the County's portion of the canals would increase the City's workload and potentially raise the stormwater fees. She questioned the extent of the canals in County jurisdiction, whether additional City staff would be required, and if the City charged the County for maintenance. She referenced a past situation where the City undertook State maintenance near I 95 and questioned if fees had subsequently been issued for the State.
Mayor Depew thanked her for the comment and invited City Manager Mahoney to address them during Council comments.
Councilwoman Gillis' understanding was that this agreement would allow the City to access areas they are currently not allowed to touch. She had received calls from residents about County ditches in their backyard in Edgewater and felt frustration at not being able to help them.
Councilman Thomas stated that he viewed the canals as receiving Edgewater's water, and that he was glad to have a place for the water to drain. He gave his support.
Councilman Rainbird asked who had the authority to declare an emergency in relation to the expanded capabilities of the agreement. Mayor Depew indicated that it would be Council.
title: Resolution 2026-R-04: Request to approve a Stormwater Use Agreement with Volusia County for the G-2 and G-11 canals and associated improvements.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Thomas, to renew City Attorney Wolfe's contract for another three years. The motion failed by the following vote:
attachments: Aaron Wolfe - Proposal for Legal Services
Sabatini Law Firm Proposal for Legal Services
Vose Law Firm - Proposal for Legal Services
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney noted that four (4) respondents had originally been available for interviews by City Council following the Request for Proposals process for general legal counsel. He advised that the Vose law firm had rescinded their proposal earlier that day, leaving three (3) remaining law firms for Council's consideration: Doran, Foxman, Sims, Wolfe & Yoon, the Sabatini Law Firm, and the Vega firm.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Chuck Martin, 205 Cherrywood Lane, brought up Council formerly unsuccessfully attempting to terminate City Attorney Wolfe. He expressed concern for transparency, claiming he was informed following that meeting, Mayor Depew went to Beachside Tavern with an attorney. He said that Councilwoman Gillis was also present and wondered if City Attorney Wolfe's termination was discussed. Mayor Depew acknowledged the comment, mentioning the conversation was tied to Florida League of Cities and a board matter. He invited implicated Councilmembers to respond during their comments.
James Rogerson, 2850 Lin Gina Terrace, spoke in strong support of City Attorney Wolfe. He noted Mr. Wolfe's 36 years in the community, 14 years with Edgewater, and handling of over 40 state and federal lawsuits. He pointed out that Mr. Wolfe's firm represents the City of New Smyrna Beach, Town of Ponce Inlet, and several school boards. He also emphasized Mr. Wolfe's history of proven counsel. He felt hiring the Sabatini Law firm was the wrong thing to do.
Mandi Bullard, 1417 Needle Palm Drive, had no accusations but did have a specific concern regarding the Lennar lawsuit. She noted that during the quasi judicial hearing, City Attorney Wolfe did not submit any evidence into the record. She found it surprising that nothing was entered as evidence, especially since many residents testified about flooding issues. She questioned why there
was an absence of evidence submitted in that proceeding.
Tim London, 2632 Woodland Drive, spoke in favor of selecting a new law firm as he felt this could be an opportunity for Edgewater to initiate a fresh start focused on enhancing trust and integrity. He preferred the Sabatini Law Firm.
Renee Sortman, Edgewater, raised specific concerns about the Sabatini Law Firm, noting its termination by Treasure Island for unprofessional behavior and citing claims of tardiness and poor legal advice. She also mentioned Mr. Sabatini's controversies, including a Walton County Sheriff's critiques and noted his frequent absences when in the Florida House. She praised City Attorney Wolfe for his integrity and expressed worry about the City's approach.
Jim Fox, 207 Francis Drive, thanked the Council for personnel changes that have taken place at the City. He felt City Attorney Wolfe did not follow the rule of law or the City Charter, and stated that he had provided Councilmembers with a document outlining the alleged Charter violations. Mayor Depew repeatedly asked Mr. Fox to address the Council rather than members of the public in attendance and warned him that further warnings would result in his removal.
Laura London, 2632 Woodland Drive, criticized the City Attorney, citing ineffective counsel and poor judgment, and urged the Council to replace him as she felt his actions favored developers over citizens and were a betrayal of public trust.
Christine Armstrong, 2303 Lime Tree Drive, Edgewater, spoke in favor of Mr. Sabatini, highlighting his military service and strong ethics. She dismissed critical publications as biased and endorsed him for City Attorney, believing he would prioritize Edgewater's residents over big business. Additionally, she commended Mayor Depew's dedication to the community.
Cynthia Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, spoke in defense of City Attorney Wolfe, suggesting the outcome of the Lennar hearing was due to procedural limitations and emphasized the need for appeals in legal challenges. She noted Mr. Wolfe's long service and excellent work. She felt skeptical of Mr. Sabatini, the location of his office and proposed re bidding the contract if they did not continue retaining Mr. Wolfe.
Corrie Sapp, 2630 Travelers Palm, defended Mr. Wolfe regarding the Lennar case, noting that while Mr. Wolfe was prepared, there were no engineering reports or evidence provided to support the flooding complaints. She felt he shouldn't be blamed for lack of documentation.
Donna McDavid, 1201 Bond Street, stated that regardless of the direction Council goes, two members of Council should recuse themselves from the vote, claiming they had admitted to her directly that they had violated the Sunshine Law.
GiGi Bennington, 121 Virginia Street, stated she had served on City Council for over 17 years and City Attorney Wolfe had been attorney for most of that time. She firmly defended him and asserted that his role was to protect the Council's actions, not the people, and she praised his resilience. She criticized the decision to replace him and claimed personal awareness of Sunshine Law violations, stating she would be willing to attest if needed.
Unidentified, 3422 Victory Palm Drive, expressed frustration with the Council more broadly, voiced anger over high utility bills and what he felt was a lack of accountability. He wondered whether the City could afford to take on additional responsibilities such as county ditches while utility costs remained so burdensome for residents. Mayor Depew thanked him for his comments and noted that additional time for citizen comments would be available following the agenda item.
Mayor Depew asked for Council comments.
Councilman Rainbird stated that he had not voted to repeal the moratorium and that was the only time he had violated his oath. He invited anyone with further documentation of improper conduct to come forward. He stated that he works for the citizens of Edgewater and that everything he has done on the dais reflects that. Addressing the fiscal concerns raised by members of the public about utility costs, he acknowledged the difficulty of lowering bills when so many things require funding, but reaffirmed his commitment to the residents he represents.
Councilwoman Dolbow was concerned about the firms $425 per hour billing as it seemed fiscally irresponsible. She compared the two remaining candidates: Doran, Foxman, Sims, Wolfe & Yoon, where Mr. Wolfe offers 36 years of experience, 14 serving Edgewater, and holds the highest AV rating, emphasizing their 157 combined years and representation of 18 government entities. For Sabatini Firm, she noted it's six years old, founded by Mr. Sabatini, a former Lake County Commissioner and Florida House Representative. She had concerns over his recent firing from Treasure Island for absenteeism and poor advice and mentioned worries about the firm's case in Walton County, including Mr. Rollins recently joining the Florida Bar.
In terms of the Lennar case, she said that Mr. Wolfe was defending an undocumented decision.
Mayor Depew admitted that he had hoped to retain the Vose Law Firm, describing their representative as having grown up in Volusia County and having significant municipal experience with over 40 municipal government clients. He assured that his stance wasn't a personal reflection on Mr. Wolfe, recognizing his long service. Depew identified three concerns: advice provided by Mr. Wolfe in a December meeting contradicted by an Ordinance, lack of legal guidance when voting "present," and the unfulfilled promise of Mr. Wolfe attending pre meeting briefings. He commended Mr. Wolfe's stance against SB 180. Addressing Sabatini Law Firm, Mayor Depew shared insights from his conversation with Treasure Island's Mayor, praising Mr. Rollins and asserting the firm’s readiness to appoint a dedicated paralegal and attorney for Edgewater. He also favored Mr. Wolfe handling ongoing litigation during any potential transition.
Councilman Thomas acknowledged the value of having reliable legal counsel. He felt Mr. Wolfe was the most intelligent person he had ever met and had protected him from adverse consequences multiple times. All the firms he interviewed had stated that they would fight for the City of Edgewater, he just hated to throw Mr. Wolfe's experience out the door.
Councilwoman Gillis felt dissatisfaction with certain aspects of the attorney's performance and had previously stated her concerns. She respected Mr. Wolfe's capabilities but desired a more proactive approach. Addressing the Lennar litigation, she criticized the lack of initiative, stating that no evidence was presented and showing that the City wasn't engaging adequately. She made it clear that the decision was solely focused on what was best for the City's future, rather than her personal feelings. She spoke against personal attacks.
Gavin Rollins, Sabatini Law Firm, addressed several concerns brought to light. He clarified the situation with Treasure Island, mentioning some disagreements among Councilmembers but noted that the firm continued its representation for several months and facilitated a successful transition to Vose Law Firm. He spoke on his experience, having served twice as a Councilmember and County Commissioner. He stated that their firm's approach is proactive, aiming to identify and tackle issues before they arise.
City Attorney Wolfe stated that he was prepared to act on direction from the Council but needed their
guidance to initiate any action. Regarding the Lennar litigation and the evidence issue, he questioned the presence of evidence: the hearing focused on whether the final plat for Edgewater Preserve Phase II adhered to the Edgewater Land Development regulations. He pointed out the lack of evidence showing that the plat was inconsistent with these regulations. He mentioned that during construction, the retention pond had breached and released water; however, the judge concluded that there was no evidence of flooding after the construction of the pond was completed. This breech wasn't considered evidence of the plat's inconsistency with the regulations. He was open to address any additional questions they have.
Councilman Rainbird highlighted that Lennar acknowledged its mistake by reducing the number of homes and canceling phase 5, demonstrating an admission of an error. He felt frustration with the overall situation, emphasizing that the Council should not require directions for the attorney on every matter. It was mentioned that the City Attorney's role at the Lennar hearing wasn't understood to be that of a neutral arbitrator. This brought up the idea that the city might have needed separate legal representation for the case. Also, it was noted that because no case was actually initiated by the city, there wasn't anything to appeal.
Following the extended discussion, Mayor Depew addressed one final point, clarifying that he had asked Mr. Wolfe not whether evidence had been submitted, but whether he had evidence ready to submit. He stated that Mr. Wolfe had indicated he had not. He also expressed appreciation for the work Mr. Wolfe had done in opposing SB 180 and acknowledged that as a proactive measure for which residents had been grateful.
Councilman Thomas asked Mr. Wolfe how many meetings he had missed during his 14 years of service, Mr. Wolfe replied that he did not believe he had missed any. Councilman Thomas expressed appreciation for the consistent guidance and legal action Mr. Wolfe had provided over the years.
Following the failed vote, Mayor Depew asked about a motion for another law firm. Councilwoman Dolbow had concerns over the remaining options, feeling Vega's hourly rate was fiscally irresponsible and that Sabatini's 7 year experience compared to Mr. Wolfe's, plus their plan to use a paralegal was troublesome.
Mayor Depew clarified that Sabatini proposed hiring a paralegal alongside a dedicated attorney for Edgewater, not substituting attorneys. Mr. Rollins confirmed that three (3) barred attorneys and a paralegal would be dedicated and available 24/7 with no travel billing.
City Manager Mahoney advised that if a decision were to be made that evening, it should be on a month to month basis, and that Council would need to determine whether Mr. Wolfe's firm would continue to handle existing litigation regardless of the general counsel decision.
Mayor Depew proposed a compromise: engage the Sabatini Law Firm on a month to month basis, schedule a special meeting in six (6) months to evaluate the relationship and determine whether to formally re-bid the contract, and allow Mr. Wolfe's firm to continue with all current litigation. He noted that this would provide a 30 day transition period as provided for in the contract.
City Attorney Wolfe noted that he would cease accepting new business from the City and not attend further meetings, including the Charter Review meeting the following day. He planned to continue with the two RPO hearings scheduled for Wednesday morning and the All Florida Plumbing final hearing on the 15th as these fall under current litigation. Additionally, he mentioned two ongoing liability cases he would continue managing for the City.
Mr. Rollins confirmed that he would attend the 4pm Charter Review Meeting the following day and indicated that both he and Mr. Wolfe could work collaboratively through the 30 day period.
title: Selection of General Legal Counsel (City Attorney)

action_text: A motion was made by Mr. McGinnis, seconded by Mr. Hatcher, to approve CPA-2411. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Mr. Solstice provided the staff report and City's recommendation.
Mr. Waltz reviewed the proposed land use amendment and development plan, highlighting reduced residential density, increased buffers, storm water and drainage improvements, and preservation of existing vegetation and trees. He stated that the proposal is consistent with the City’s Land Development Code.
Chair Kennedy opened the public hearing.
Mr. Fisher questioned the stormwater capacity, emergency overflow, and phasing of the project. The applicant’s engineer stated that stormwater would be retained on-site, with the pond designed for a 100-year storm event and overflow directed to the canal. It was clarified that the project would consist of two phases, with the stormwater system constructed during the first phase.
Mr. Hatcher questioned the size of the pond, relocation of a historic tree, construction methods, and the amount of fill required. The applicant’s representatives addressed the proposed tree relocation and stated that fill would be obtained from the western portion of the site.
Mr. McGinnis questioned the presence of protected wildlife species. The applicant’s representative stated that all applicable wildlife regulations and permitting requirements would be addressed during the appropriate stage of development review.
Janet Shira, 148 William Street, expressed concerns regarding lot configurations, buffers, wildlife corridors, tree preservation, and protection of adjacent properties. The City Attorney provided clarification regarding the matters applicable to the item under consideration.
Kathy Roland, 119 Ash Street, expressed appreciation for changes made to the proposal and raised concerns regarding potential impacts to the neighboring subdivision, canal, and wildlife.
Allan Tanguay, 4332 Sailfish Circle, requested additional information regarding the proposed boat ramp and expressed concerns regarding manatee activity in the canal and potential safety measures.
Chair Kennedy closed the public hearing.
title: 1st Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-O-01: Request for a small scale comprehensive plan amendment from Volusia County Urban Medium Intensity to City of Edgewater Low Density Residential for the property located at 4401 S Ridgewood Avenue.

action_text: A motion was made by Hatcher, second by McGinnis, to adopt Ordinance No. 2026-O-02. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
The City Attorney, Gavin Rollins, performed a quasi judicial swearing of all spectators.
Chair Kennedy opened the public hearing.
Ms. Shira, confirmed that she stated that she was speaking as an expert witness and provided an overview of her professional background, including approximately 20 years of planning experience and prior A.I.C.P. (American Institute of Certified Planners) certification. She expressed concern regarding the proposed lot sizes and configurations, stating that the Development Agreement and Comprehensive Plan should ensure that the approved lot configurations remain consistent. She emphasized the importance of the proposed buffer to the quality of life of adjacent residents and requested consideration of a permanent wildlife corridor within the buffer. She also expressed concerns regarding tree preservation, stating that the Tamarac plan preserved historic and specimen trees, while the current proposal would result in the clearing of a significant portion of the property.
Mr. Waltz recognized that Ms. Shira's testimony has been added to the record and that this is being recorded.
Mr. Waltz stated that they were willing to revise the language regarding confirmation of the proposed buffers and boundaries. He explained that construction plans and final engineering have not yet been completed; therefore, the final tree count could not be confirmed. He agreed to cap the maximum number of residential units at 137 and clarified that language regarding swimming pools and spas was not intended to circumvent setback requirements.
Mr. Waltz further stated that the stormwater outfall would be designed to higher standards and would continue to drain to the existing drainage location. Regarding the proposed boat ramp, he stated that an existing environmental permit is in place and that the number of proposed slips and docks has been reduced. He confirmed that the development would comply with all applicable manatee regulations.
Mr. Andrejkovics asked whether the proposed changes needed to be addressed at this time. Mr. Solstice stated that he would need to cross-reference the applicable documents.
Carol Golas, 123 Cedar Street, asked whether an environmental study had been conducted regarding dredging of the canal and potential impacts to wildlife. The Mr. Waltz stated that an Environmental Resource Permit had been obtained.
Mr. Hatcher asked whether the project would return to the Board following preliminary plat approval. City Attorney confirmed that the current request was for preliminary approval and explained that minor revisions could be made prior to final review. Mr. Waltz stated that the Board could approve the request with conditions.
Mr. McGinnis suggested tabling the item until the proposed changes were incorporated into the applicable documents. Mr. Rollins advised that the Board could temporarily table the item and noted that the proposed changes and representations were on the record and that the Board would have an opportunity to review the final version before development commenced.
Janet Shira expressed concern regarding the minimum 15% tree preservation requirement and its inclusion in the Development Agreement. Mr. Waltz stated that the development would be required to comply with the Development Agreement and applicable City Code requirements.
Mr. Hatcher asked whether one month would provide sufficient time to make the necessary revisions. Mr. Waltz responded affirmatively. Mr. Solstice stated that either proceeding with conditions or allowing time for revisions would be appropriate.
Mr. Hatcher stated that development is expected but emphasized the importance of improving the development process and maintaining transparency.
Chair Kennedy closed the public hearing.
title: 1st Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-O-02: Request for a rezoning from Volusia County MH-1, Mobile Home Park to City of Edgewater Residential Planned Unit Development (RPUD) for the property at 4401 S Ridgewood Avenue.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve All-Florida Plumbing & Electrical Supply Co. Settlement Agreement. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney provided a staff report and recommendation.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Councilman Rainbird inquired whether the settlement represented a clean slate for all parties involved. City Manager Mahoney stated that while it would not prevent future complaints all matters are currently settled.
Councilman Rainbird felt that All Florida Plumbing was making generous offers and they are responding to complaints from residents accordingly; Councilman Thomas agreed that it was a good compromise for everyone and praised All Florida Plumbing for being a positive small business in the City.
Mayor Depew said that it shouldn't have gotten to the point that it did and discussed the previous issues relating to Planning & Zoning and the business. He expressed remaining concerns regarding All Florida Plumbing and the impact it could have on other businesses in the City.
City Attorney Rollins explained that All Florida Plumbing had previously requested a variance, which was denied. He stated that entering into the settlement would effectively grant a variance; however, such action would not set a precedent, as future requests must be considered by the Planning & Zoning Board on a case-by-case basis.
City Manager Mahoney advised that Staff is looking to clarify details via Ordinance or the Land Development Code to create parameters for on street parking as it may be needed throughout the City in certain locations.
Mayor Depew reiterated his concerns regarding large trucks going down the residential streets; City Manager Mahoney stated that the Ordinance does allow trucks to deviate from their truck route. He had spoken to All Florida Plumbing, they have tried to change deliver times but no one can guarantee that it's never going to happen.
City Attorney Rollins assured that it is a well written contract with protections for the City.
Councilwoman Dolbow felt that All Florida Plumbing had done everything they were supposed to do and that they had put the business through the gamut because of a feud. She hopes that in the future, they don't target businesses or people over a couple complaints and that a lesson had been learned. action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Thomas, to approve Ordinance No. 2026-O-01. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, presented the request for a small scale comprehensive plan amendment to change the future land use designation of the property at 4401 South Ridgewood Avenue from Volusia County Urban Medium Intensity — which allows 4 to 8 dwelling units per acre — to City of Edgewater Low Density Residential, which allows a maximum of 4 dwelling units per acre. Staff found the request consistent with adjacent land uses and recommended approval, characterizing it as a net reduction in residential density.
Mark Wofford, Attorney with Cobb Cole representing the applicant, explained that the property has been annexed for over a decade but the land use classification had never been updated. The change would reduce maximum density from 335 to 167 dwelling units. He further noted that the county classification required a minimum density of 4 units per acre, whereas the proposed city classification would allow anywhere from 0 to 4, providing more flexibility.
City Attorney Rollins noted Councilmembers should disclose any ex parte communications regarding this quasi-judicial matter.
Councilmembers disclosed receiving numerous emails and calls from residents, with Mayor Depew noting at least 25 emails and 1-2 calls, while Councilwoman Gillis spoke with residents at town halls. Councilwoman Dolbow disclosed a meeting with Mr. Watson and Associates. Councilman Rainbird had no additional disclosures beyond what was noted in his council report. City Attorney Rollins explained the difference between the comprehensive plan amendment (broader planning goals) and zoning (more specific), noting they could approve the comp plan and deny zoning as separate votes.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Renee Richards, 136 Jones Fish Camp Road, requested Council not move forward with the project, citing tax payer concerns, infrastructure impacts and environmental preservation needs. She felt the property was one of the last pristine coastal parcels in the area and requested the Council either table the matter or place a moratorium on new developments. Mayor Depew and City Manager Mahoney clarified that a moratorium was no longer permissible under SB 180.
Kim Long, 3312 Mango Tree Drive, questioned the zoning change from mobile home to residential, noting mobile home zoning would preserve 35% of 42 acres (15 acres of upland forest) and house fewer people with less concrete and fewer cars compared to single-family homes. She stated that while she was initially supportive of residential development on the property, learning about the amount of proposed impervious surface changed her view. She asked Council not to change the zoning.
Cheryl Davis, 356 Riverfront Way, asked whether the city could obtain money from builders for new school construction needs.
Paul Romanoski, 1872 Umbrella Tree Drive, admitted he was not opposed to development but was unfamiliar with the project details and had concerns about impervious surfaces and freshwater intrusion into the lagoon. He emphasized the importance of proper water handling near the river. He stated that his information had come largely from a brief conversation with Kim Long. Mayor Depew noted that his concerns were better directed to the PUD item next on the agenda.
Ken Cartisano, 3312 Mango Tree Drive, reiterated concerns about the projects' readiness based on Planning and Zoning board presentations with numerous errors. He felt the project was not ready to be approved by the board, let alone the Council, and cautioned members to be very careful with proceeding.
Councilman Rainbird asked if the rezoning approval could still allow the property to be developed as a trailer park. City Attorney Rollins explained that they do have existing zoning and a development order that could allow mobile home construction to begin relatively quickly (within six (6) months).
Councilwoman Dolbow felt it made sense to bring the property into conformity with the City's comprehensive plan and the surrounding US 1 corridor, noting that this was effectively a housekeeping matter. Councilwoman Gillis echoed this, clarifying explicitly for the public and viewers that voting on this item did not constitute approval of the proposed development, the development itself would be the subject of the next vote. She confirmed with City Attorney Rollins that the Council could approve the comp plan amendment and still deny the zoning.
Mayor Depew clarified that this was to bring the property into conformity with the City's comprehensive plan requirements, not an annexation because the property already had been annexed previously.
Councilwoman Gillis inquired over the possibility of denying the comprehensive plan amendment; City Attorney Rollins stated that denying would allow them to move forward under existing entitlements, but they already have significant vested rights within their development order.
Councilman Rainbird asked if the property was available for purchase if someone found funding. Mr. Wofford said their client was under contract to purchase the property but was unsure of the specific contract terms.
City Manager Mahoney confirmed that the City would provide utilities as it was already annexed.
title: 1st Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-O-01: Request for a small scale comprehensive plan amendment from Volusia County Urban Medium Intensity to City of Edgewater Low Density Residential for the property located at 4401 S Ridgewood Avenue.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Councilman Rainbird, to deny the first reading of Ordinance No. 2026-O-02, request for rezoning from Volusia County MH-1 Mobile Home Park to City of Edgewater Residential Planned Unit Development for the property at 4401 South Ridgewood Avenue on the grounds of lack of support from surrounding residents, lack of neighbor consensus, density concerns, and impacts on surrounding properties and water quality. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, provided a staff report and recommendation. Staff noted improvements in the Haven Sound proposal including 100-year storm water requirements versus 25-year requirements for Tamarack 3, enhanced water quality standards, native vegetation requirements, and better environmental protections.
Mark Wofford, Cobb Cole, presented an extensive comparison between the two projects, highlighting reduced density (165 to 137 units), required garages (none required for Tamarack vs. minimum 2-car garages for Haven Sound), improved storm water management (1 million gallons vs. 1.4 million gallons storage), and enhanced buffer areas particularly on the southern boundary (30 feet vs. 40 feet). The presentation included detailed engineering drawings and environmental impact assessments.
Mr. Wofford addressed Taylor Morrison construction issues raised by residents, stating the company was aware of concerns and would ensure all comments were reviewed by staff. He noted statutory rights for third-party inspectors but added development agreement language committing to city inspectors when staffing allowed.
With respect to gopher tortoises, Mr. Wofford confirmed that a current study had not yet been submitted as such studies are only valid for 90 days. He assured that all tortoises would need to be relocated before construction under either the existing or the proposed plan.
City Attorney Rollins administered an oath to those wishing to provide expert or factual testimony, and residents present raised their right hands.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Janet Shira, 148 Williams Street, testified as an expert witness on behalf of herself and the following directly abutting property owners: Amy Matt (139 William Street), Michael and Jennifer Vasquez (145 William Street), Harry Fowler (4490 Myrtle Street), Steve Wilson (4485 Myrtle Street), and Ben and Pam Davis (151 William Street). Ms. Shira stated that the Planning and Zoning Boards favorable recommendation was contingent upon addressing all objections, an aspect she felt was overlooked in staffs recommendation. She did not object to the comp plan amendment in isolation but opposed the RPUD rezoning on two primary grounds: the amount of impervious surface requested, and the failure to preserve adequate upland area in its natural state.
Ms. Shira cited the Indian River Lagoon overlay, which mandates at least 35 percent of open space landscaped with existing native vegetation. She argued that this requirement limited the Tamarack project to four(4) units per acre, undermining the developer's claims of a significant reduction in density from the County's 8-unit maximum.
On impervious surface, Ms. Shira noted Tamarack 3's approved plan had 12 acres of impervious surface, under 30% of the 42 acres. In contract, Havensound planned for 14.5 acres of impervious surface just for the lots, excluding roads and parking. This would push the total impervious coverage to over 46%.
On tree preservation and open space, Ms. Shira highlighted that Tamarack 3 preserved 526 trees (30 percent) across 14.7 acres without needing a plan amendment. She criticized Haven Sound for saying they lacked tree data despite having submitted construction drawings the previous year. Ms. Shira urged the Council to either deny both applications or require detailed tree preservation data.
Kim Long, 3312 Mango Tree Drive, opposed the zoning change, citing a lack of green space in the Taylor Morrison plan and comparing the density with the existing wildlife. She noted significant wildlife presence on the property, including large gopher tortoises, numerous burrows, and various bird types. Ms. Long mentioned that a mature oak retains up to 100 gallons of rainwater per day.
Jim McGinnis, 2607 Willow Oak Drive, addressed tree preservation requirements under building codes, emphasizing the need to protect wildlife and preserve the property. He also expressed concern about clear-cutting practices.
Dwight Cunningham, 3044 Travelers Palm Drive, had concerns about wildlife habitat destruction and clear-cutting impacts. He spoke out against too much building, saying the city's job is to look out for the people living here currently, not to boost profits for developers.
Cora Steincamp, 339 Riverfront Way, urged against approving another Taylor Morrison project until they completed their current development. She detailed construction issues, inadequate reserves ($27,000 for 138 units), and management problems including a resident receiving 76 violations.
Jim Lovgren, 182 James Fish Camp Road, discussed HOA problems in his Taylor Morrison development that require state investigation, ongoing flooding issues that have affected neighboring properties. He criticized scare tactics used at Planning and Zoning meetings and felt Council should vote no.
Cheryl Davis, 356 Riverfront Way, suggested tabling the item until all requested information had been provided.
Renee Richards, 136 Jones Fish Camp Road, again urged consideration of taxpayers over development.
Mr. Wofford responded to the testimony provided by Ms. Shira and read the full text of the Indian River overly open space provision, emphasizing that it allows open space to consist of existing vegetation or planted native species, something he believes Ms. Shira omitted. He estimated that approximately 441 trees would be preserved (25%) versus Tamarack's 526 (30%), mainly due to a larger pond. He challenged Ms. Shira's impervious surface figures, revealing that an analysis with Havensound at 0.48 and Tamarack at 0.49, both accounting for all paved areas. He agreed to ensure the 35% open space would exclude the ponds wet areas. The increased per-lot impervious coverage was deliberate to avoid future variance requests from homeowners. He briefly addressed HOA concerns, indicating that Taylor Morrison was aware of the issues discussed.
Ms. Shira was given brief rebuttal time, during which she referenced the approved Tamarack site plan and stated its total impervious surface was documented at 12 acres, equating to a 0.30 ratio — not 0.49 as presented by the applicant. She also cautioned that newly planted native species, often described as "sticks," do not substitute for preserving the mature trees already on the property.
Mayor Depew stated that he was not afraid of the mobile home park scenario and believed that the original Tamarack plan was the stronger of the two (2). He emphasized that mobile homes offer lower density, less concrete usage, and no garages. He highlighted that Tamarack's approval seems unutilized, hinting at possible economic challenges for the applicant, thereby favoring the original project.
Councilwoman Dolbow identified significant pros of Havensound, such as it's 100-year storm standard, native vegetation requirement, and improved internal drainage, finding it favorable for protecting the Indian River Lagoon. She did however have concerns over missing playgrounds, parking, and Taylor Morrison's past management issues. Despite that, she favored Havensound for the benefit of the lagoon.
Councilman Rainbird admitted that he did not like either plan. He had concerns about street widths and parking based on his own experience observing his sons neighborhood in Woodbridge Lakes. He felt that he couldn't find a way to favor either project and called for better designs from both.
Councilwoman Gillis felt that if they cared about the lagoon, they would not be attempting to develop it in the first place. She felt pressured by past scare tactics to approve projects and favored the Tamarack plan due to extensive community discussions. She had seen minimal support for Havensound contrasted with significant opposition. She suggested that conservation groups look into acquiring the land, with the estimated cost being around $6 million.
Councilman Thomas echoed Councilman Rainbird's concern about density and tight lots, expressing a strong dislike for 50-foot lots. He acknowledged the stormwater improvements but stated he wanted more green space, bigger lots, and a plan worth going home to. He suggested sending the project back to the drawing board.
City Attorney Rollins noted for the record that the Council should focus on land use compatibility, traffic impacts, stormwater, and surrounding neighborhood concerns, not on the applicants identity or prior business practices, as legally permissible grounds for a quasi-judicial denial.
Further discussion ensued with Council and Mr. Wofford. Several Councilmembers explored the possibility of continuance, with specific requests including: larger lots; more green space; a designated playground; overflow parking; preservation of additional historic trees; and clearer data on the number and location of preserved trees. Mr. Wofford indicated willingness to address playground inclusion, parking specification, lot configuration, and additional details on tree preservation. He did however acknowledge that the density reduction of 20-30% was not feasible.
City Attorney Rollins advised that a continuance to a date certain was permissible, but an indefinite continuance would function as a denial, and the Council would need to specify a date if choosing to continue.
Mid-vote, Councilwoman Dolbow clarified that the only reason she was saying no was that she would have preferred to see the applicant return with reduced density and revised criteria.
Councilman Rainbird initially stated no before clarifying that he meant yes to the motion to deny. Interim City Clerk Toupin confirmed each members vote for the record.
Meeting went into Recess
Meeting Reconvened

action_text: A motion was made by Councilman Rainbird, second by Councilman Thomas, to approve Ordinance No. 2026-O-03. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney highlighted that a Charter amendment in November 2020 set Mayoral and Council salaries at $9,005.12 and $7,631, respectively. Due to the City's growth and increased responsibilities, staff reviewed compensation, ranking Edgewater 12th of 15 in Volusia County. They recommended increasing the Mayor's salary to $20,000 and council members' to $18,000, starting December 7, 2026, coinciding with the next Council terms. Amendments are permitted by Section 3.05 of the Charter and can be adjusted or discontinued.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Sandra Snodgrass, 980 Canal View Boulevard, Port Orange, spoke in favor of the Ordinance as she had seen Council stand up for the citizens.
Jim Lovgren, 182 Jones Fish Camp Road, spoke in favor of the Ordinance, stating that regardless of how Councilmembers voted on any particular item, they were drastically underpaid. He noted the extensive personal time they devoted to community outreach, charity involvement, and public service
Donna McDavid, 1201 Bond Street, spoke in opposition of the request, arguing that a pay raise should be a result of consistently fulfilling responsibilities, not precede it. She cited concerns such as Councilwoman Gillis not participating in an investigation she initiated that had cost the taxpayers $13,000, perceived disengagement by members during meetings, and Mayor Depew's incomplete Charter Officer evaluations. She emphasized that raises should come after proven excellence and consistent commitment as outlined in the Charter.
Christine Herbert, Palm Coast, spoke in support of the Ordinance, she had witnessed Council genuinely caring about their residents and personally believed they should receive the raise.
Janet Shira, 148 Williams Street, spoke in support of the increase, noting how much time Councilmembers must invest across all the City matters.
Councilman Rainbird asked where the specific dollar figure originated. City Manager Mahoney explained that he had constructed a spreadsheet comparing compensation across all 15 Volusia County municipalities. The proposed increase would bring the City to 6th place (5th place when accounting for full benefits).
Councilwoman Dolbow expressed discomfort with more than doubling Council pay, noting Edgewater's health insurance costs $9,000 per member annually. She acknowledged the need for employee raises and stated a preference for a smaller Council increase given the ongoing compensation study.
Councilman Thomas noted that he had been on Council previously and could never vote himself a raise. He however did acknowledge that in order to attract qualified candidates to public office, some level of compensation was necessary. He described the demands of the role as extending at all hours in any situation, and stated he planned to vote yes.
Mayor Depew discussed what both Daytona Beach's Mayor and New Smyrna Beach's Mayor make and that he had previously opted out of the City's health insurance. He did express his view that the proposed salaries represented an appropriate gap given Edgewater's population position relative to those Cities.
Councilman Rainbird reiterated that he had not requested this specific dollar amount and asked where it had originated. He compared what the lowest paid City employee made compared to what the Council does and felt that the role was not truly part-time, citing the personal vacation days he had to use to interview Charter officers, attend events, and how he had to respond to constituent calls at all hours. He had his own reservations for the raise but gave his support as he felt it would attract future candidates and lift all compensation levels across the City.
City Manager Mahoney added context by noting that the total annual impact on the City's approximately $80 million operating budget would be roughly $50,000. He also advised that a compensation study for City employees was underway and expected back by mid-to-late April.
Councilwoman Dolbow asked if the proposed figures aligned with population comparisons and noted that DeLand, which has roughly double Edgewater's population, is at $20,000 with no health insurance coverage. She questioned if doubling the salary was appropriate. City Manager Mahoney acknowledged that there is no perfect formula and reiterated that the recommendation could be adjusted in any direction.
City Attorney Rollins clarified that per the Charter, the increase would not take effect until the next Council is seated following the November election, meaning the current Councilmembers may not personally benefit from the increase in their present terms.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-O-03: Increasing the Annual Salary for the Mayor and City Council Members

attachments: WRFL - Potable Reuse Response Letter - City of Edgewater
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney introduced Bob Polizzi, Water Plant Manager for the City of Edgewater.
Mr. Polizzi provided background information on potable reuse. In 2020, Florida's Legislature tasked the Department of Environmental Protection (FDEP) with establishing rules for it, and by 2025, reclaimed water was allowed as a public water supply source. Potable reuse requires a special advanced treatment water facility between wastewater and public drinking systems. Mr. Polizzi indicated Edgewater's water comes solely from 14 groundwater wells, with the Consumptive Use Permit (CUP) allowing withdrawals beyond current needs, and four more wells permitted for future use. He stated that there are no plans or intentions to implement the practice as potable reuse isn't necessary. The 2027 CUP renewal will require considering this as a water supply option by Florida law but there are no specific deadlines for adoption.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Sandra Snodgrass, 980 Canal View Boulevard, Port Orange, speaking on behalf of Let Volusia Vote, urged municipalities to sign a petition for Charter review amendment changes to protect the aquifer and drinking supply. She stated that Florida's aquifer is at great jeopardy due to overdevelopment, saltwater intrusion, and excessive pumping. She implored the Council to be at the forefront of municipalities in the area in taking a formal stance against the practice.
Mayor Depew felt that the City should take formal steps to ensure that neither his generation nor future generations would be forced to consume reused water.
Councilman Thomas understood that the State requires acknowledgment of potable reuse as part of the permitting process, though it's confirmed that the City is not moving in that direction. City Manager Mahoney affirmed that the City has absolutely no plans to pursue potable reuse and that he would support bringing formal options to Council.
Councilman Rainbird pointed out that Edgewater is well-positioned to sidestep this issue thanks to the Deering Park well fields, four active well fields, and two reserve wells. He questioned whether Edgewater could stop nearby municipalities from injecting treated water into a shared aquifer. City Attorney Rollins responded that it would probably not be legally feasible without a nuisance argument, making it difficult to prevent such actions by other cities.
Councilwoman Dolbow expressed interest in seeing both a draft Ordinance and a Charter amendment brought before Council, acknowledging that while this is not an imminent concern, decisions made today would matter for future generations. She did point out that even a Charter amendment could potentially be preempted by future State law, as has occurred in other land use contexts.
Councilwoman Gillis agreed, she knows they are not planning this now, but it would not sit right with her in 20 years if they could have prevented something from happening in the future and did not take action.
City Attorney Rollins summarized Council's three (3) options: a Resolution as a strong, non-binding statement; an Ordinance to formally prohibit using reused water for drinking, requiring two (2) readings; or a Charter amendment to be voted on. He warned that State permitting for wastewater expansion does involve a reuse plan, meaning a Charter amendment or Ordinance could, in uncertain terms, impact future permits.
City Manager Mahoney stressed that this could bring risks to the $19 million SRF grant application.
By consensus, the Council directed City Attorney Rollins and staff to return at the next Council meeting with both a draft Ordinance and draft Charter amendment language, along with a legal analysis of how each option could potentially impact permitting for water facility expansion, so the Council may make a fully informed decision.
title: Discussion Request by City Council regarding Blackwater/Potable Reuse

action_text: A motion was made by Ms. Bullard, second by Ms. Mojer, to recommend approval to add sec 1.01. (K) Community Engagement and Public Information. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Mr. Conroy read Section 1.01k.
Ms. Mojer expressed satisfaction with the final language as she felt it captured her intended goals. Ms. Bullard asked about incorporating HOA networks specifically to ensure information delivery. Ms. Mojer explained that community engagement served as an umbrella concept that would include using HOA networks and other community contacts without necessarily specifying HOAs explicitly.
Mr. Fisher inquired about funding amounts and resources; City Manager Mahoney estimated that current legal advertisements cost about $30,000 annually but cautioned against specifying budget percentages in the charter due to variable operating budgets.
Mr. Conroy noted that despite fulfilling legal notification obligations and providing substantial online information, some residents still feel uninformed. He felt residents needed to be more attentive to the City website but did question how communication could be enhanced. Ms. Mojer felt that more could be done in regards to public relations from the City.
Mr. Fisher noted that currently the City notifies residents in a 500-foot radius and suggested that maybe that be expanded. City Manager Mahoney mentioned hiring a new Public Information Officer to improve messaging and noted that while the city currently goes beyond legal requirements by notifying property owners within 500 feet (compared to the legally required adjacent property notification), enhanced communication would benefit community relationships.
Ms. Bullard stressed that communicators should ensure clarity and understanding, instead of just fulfilling formal requirements, suggesting improvements are needed if people feel uninformed. Chairman Conroy agreed but noted that there will always be residents who claim ignorance despite efforts, underscoring citizens' duty to stay informed via city websites and resources.
title: CHARTER REVIEW

action_text: A motion was made by Ms.Bullard, second by Ms. Mojer, to recommend for approval to put forbidding flock cameras in the Charter. The motion failed by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Chairman Conroy confirmed the committee passed acting city manager communication and Section 3.13 (initiative and referendum). Mr. Fisher noted the initiative and referendum section passed, but reducing petition signatures from 10% to 5% failed (2-2 vote). The committee's approved charter amendments include the preamble, population-based district creation, five-year redistricting, appointed city clerk, landscape requirements, sale of city park property, annexation provisions, acting city manager requirements, and initiative and referendum procedures.
Mr. Conroy re-opened citizens comments.
Kim Long, 3312 Mango Tree Drive, discussed her issues regarding flock cameras and the harmful implications involved.
City Manager Mahoney confirmed that the flock cameras were included in the approved budget and had been publicly discussed during budget season. He felt that they were a helpful tool for law enforcement in their efforts to solve crimes.
Ms. McDavid noted that she had been at the budget meeting where flock cameras were discussed and said that was why public engagement and actually showing up to all the meetings was so important.
Mr. Conroy asked City Attorney Sabatini if he had anything to add; Mr. Sabatini said he felt they were working well as an organization.
Ms. Bullard reiterated her stance on flock cameras and felt it should go out to the voters as there was a lack of trust between residents and the City/Law Enforcement. City Manager Mahoney reported the estimated total cost of the cameras and tag readers a year and added that they are also in the City parks to make sure they are safe.
City Attorney Sabatini confirmed that the committee was satisfied with the language in their final recommendations document, noting that items marked as "failed" would not be included in the final charter amendment package. He explained that these notations served as record-keeping for the committee's decisions.
Mr. Sabatini indicated that with general consent from the committee, the recommendations would be formalized and transferred to the City Council for their review and ultimate decision on which items to place before voters. The committee provided consensus approval for the document's language.
