action_text: A motion was made by Ms. Bullard, second by Ms. Mojer, to recommend Section 1.01 I, Sale of City Property, to require voter approval. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney advised the Committee that Bridgette Vaissiere, Finance Director, was present to answer questions Ms. Bullard had at the last meeting.
Ms. Vaissiere inquired if the Charter Review Board planned to amend finance-related charter sections: 3.08F (reserves), 3.08D (borrowing limits), and 4.08 (financial procedures). She reported an operating reserve of $4,614,371.77, which would cover two months' expenses.
Ms. Bullard questioned the 15 percent reserve mandate, having found no similar requirements in nearby cities' charters, and queried the separation of reserve accounts including a 10 percent bond covenant. Ms. Vaissiere clarified that the bond covenant is part of the 15 percent reserve, consisting of pooled investments for various contingencies, and needs replenishment within five years after use. City Manager Mahoney highlighted the role of the reserves in disaster scenarios such as hurricanes affecting tax and utility revenues. Ms. Vaissiere also explained that bonds require maintaining certain amounts, potentially up to $1.2 million. For reserve revenue sources, she detailed contributions from general fund, water sewer, storm water, and refuse funds.
Ms. Vaissiere recommended attending June budget workshops for a deeper dive into budget details.
Ms. Bullard emphasized her desire to have protecting the parks and provisions regarding flock cameras into the charter. Further discourse ensued regarding the pros and cons of flock cameras.
Mr. Conroy directed the attention to the charter amendment documents provided by City Attorney Ross and reviewed previously voted items.
Mr. Conroy read section 1.01 paragraph I, regarding the sale of City park property; Ms. Bullard strongly supported the provision and noted that residents had requested it throughout multiple Councils with no action. Ms. Mojer agreed.
title: CHARTER REVIEW

action_text: A motion was made by Mayor DePew, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to open the period looking for a City Clerk for a period of two weeks. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney provided a staff report and asked Council for direction.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Cassandra Kilgore, applicant, thanked Council for their consideration and reiterated her interest in serving the community as the City Clerk. She also informed Council that she now had her Certified Municipal City Clerk designation.
Mayor Depew assured Ms. Kilgore that he meant no disrespect but he would like to open for applicants for seven (7) days. City Manager Mahoney suggested having it open for applicants for a two-week period to give staff time to advertise and get the job application out there.
Councilman Rainbird felt they already had quite a few people apply with plenty of time and if they did it again, they would go even longer without a City Clerk while Ms. Toupin served as Interim.
Councilman Thomas received confirmation that Interim Clerk Toupin was getting paid a Clerk's salary while doing the job.
Councilwoman Dolbow was okay with opening for applications for two (2) weeks; Councilwoman Gillis said she was comfortable appointing Ms. Kilgore but would also be on board with the two (2) weeks if that is what Council wants. She does want Ms. Kilgore to be included among the new applicants.
City Manager Mahoney asked if they would like staff to interview first, followed by Council; Mayor Depew confirmed that it would be the top five (5).
Councilwoman Gillis asked if it would be possible to have it addressed at the April 6th Council meeting so they could have a new Clerk. It was determined that staff needed more time.
City Manager Mahoney stated that depending on Council's schedules, they should have it completed and brought before Council by the May meeting.
title: Consideration of Appointment of City Clerk

attachments: WRFL - Potable Reuse Response Letter - City of Edgewater
minutes_note:
Jeff Lariscy, Interim Public Works Director, presented the staff report, explaining that the City serves 11,000 utility customers and currently uses 92% of reclaimed water for irrigation, with the remainder unfortunately being discharged into the Indian River. He noted that the planned wetland park in Deering Park would eliminate routine discharge into the river. However, the department must plan for future flexibility and maintain eligibility for grant funding. Staff recommended an ordinance rather than charter amendment to maintain future Council control.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Jeff Brower, De Leon Springs, strongly advocated for a permanent charter amendment ban rather than an Ordinance that could be changed by future politicians.
Greg Gimbert, gave his support for the charter amendment approach to protect residents from neighboring communities' decisions to inject treated wastewater into the aquifer.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed concerns for future water quality and supported a ban on both potable reuse and aquifer injections.
Mayor Depew supported letting residents vote on the issue.
Councilman Rainbird raised concerns about potential impacts on grant funding and water rates, noting that the City has adequate water supply through Deering Park.
Councilwoman Dolbow wanted more cost analysis and education before making permanent restrictions.
City Attorney Sabatini clarified that charter amendments can be modified outside the 5-year cycle through a special referendum. They don't have to wait for the next Charter Review Committee, they can change it during the next election cycle.

minutes_note:
Police Chief Geiger discussed recent feral hog activity, especially in the Florida Shores area. He explained the history of feral hogs in the U.S. and noted that it is not a problem unique to Edgewater but that the City had previously engaged trappers to address the issue.
He advised homeowners and businesses to remove outdoor food sources like insects in freshly mowed yards and acorns, and to keep trash near the house instead of the curb. He emphasized reporting hog activity, either via damage or rooting, to the City. Contact options include his email (cgeiger@cityofedgewater.org), the Animal Control Officer's email (dodell@cityofedgewater.org), and the non-emergency line. The City received a report of hog activity in the airport corridor over the weekend; FWC's trapper was notified and scheduled to visit on Thursday.
Chief Geiger explained that the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission handles wildlife management until issues arise in residential areas, then the City takes over coordination with trappers. The trapping can take from one day to a month. For hunting questions, Chief Geiger noted that Florida permits hunting on private property, but advised consulting an attorney. It's a misdemeanor to relocate feral hogs; hence, they must be humanely dispatched, with the meat often donated to shelters and churches.
Mayor Depew inquired about the reporting process and the City's use of contracted services for trapping feral hogs. Chief Geiger explained that residents can flag down a police officer, email the department, or call the non-emergency number, and an animal control officer along with a police lieutenant will evaluate the situation prior to engaging a trapper. He encouraged residents to consult with a private attorney for legal advice regarding shooting the hogs on their own property but noted he wouldn't discourage someone for protecting their property.
title: Feral Hogs - Understanding the Challenge

minutes_note:
Chief Geiger presented the Emergency Volunteer Program, initiated following Council consensus post-hurricane season. He highlighted disorganized volunteer efforts during Hurricanes Ian and Nicole, with tasks being duplicated. The new program, inspired by police and fire structures, will be managed by the Police Department to bring needed organization to volunteer efforts.
The program will be announced soon. Applicants must be 18+, able to travel, and willing to serve, with a 15-day application period. Accepted volunteers will attend an orientation at City Hall about expectations and storm procedures, receiving uniforms and safety vests.
Volunteers will be activated during a state of emergency, assisting with sandbag stations, water distribution, and phone lines, allowing staff to focus on essential duties. They will pause 24 hours before storms to be with families and will resume once safe, handling tasks like shelter support, road safety, and food distribution. Chief Geiger encouraged residents to contact police@cityofedgewater.org to get involved.
Mayor Depew expressed strong support for the initiative, noting he had previously discussed it at the Council level due to past events. He thanked staff for following through.
title: City of Edgewater Volunteer Disaster Response Program Implementation

JoAnn Anderson, President of the New Smyrna Beach Garden Club, stated that the organization is active in New Smyrna Beach, Port Orange, and Edgewater. She introduced the Butterfly Garden Certification Committee and highlighted Edgewater joining a nationwide effort to protect monarch butterfly populations in 2024 by planting milkweed and nectar plants, identifying it as the most recent amongst 22 Monarch Cities in Florida.
Garden Club member Dave detailed the monarch population's decline from over one billion in 1997 to 78 million in 2017, citing milkweed loss due to herbicides, urban development, climate change, and Mexican deforestation. The Club has worked with the City since 2023, participating in events, helping with a butterfly garden at the Environmental Services office, and a certified garden at Hawks Park using 100% native milkweed, receiving thanks from the staff for conservation efforts.
Ms. Anderson presented Mayor Depew with a custom poplar wood milkweed planter created by Garden Club members, expressing gratitude for the City's support.
title: Butterfly Gardening Certification Committee with the New Smyrna Beach Garden Club - Presentation of Monarch Butterfly Boxes to the City.

City Manager Mahoney introduced the item, noting that Chief Engineer Matt Creel could not be present; a brief video was shown in which Mr. Creel provided an overview of the Stormwater Master Plan.
City Manager Mahoney then described the plan as the City's largest stormwater infrastructure initiative. He emphasized its strategic importance for securing grants and government appropriations. Although called a "plan," it's more of a long-term engineering assessment evaluating future flooding risks and potential solutions. Not all proposed projects will be executed, nor have any been pre-approved.
City Manager Mahoney addressed community concerns by affirming that there are no plans for involuntary home acquisitions. He clarified that Phase 1, expected to last 10 years, does not include home acquisitions. Although Phase 2 mentions possible property acquisitions like easements or rights-of-way, these projects aren't mandatory and will depend on future Council decisions.
Phase 1 involves a $152,000,000 investment across nine (9) projects. The City has completed one project, with another under construction and two (2) in design. City Manager Mahoney noted the Volco Road improvement project is developer-funded and a federal request has been submitted for the Reuse Pond Pump Station design. Completion of Phase 1 is expected to significantly reduce flooding, especially during short rainstorms that are common in the rainy season.
Mayor Depew felt this was a huge missing piece of the puzzle and that it would help when seeking future funding opportunities. He thanked City Manager Mahoney and all staff involved in producing the study.
Councilman Rainbird asked if the City had received clearance to clear the sandbar in the 18th Street Canal; City Manager Mahoney confirmed that they had and advised that it would be addressed in his report.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve the second reading of Ordinance no. 2026-O-04: Potable Reuse Charter Amendment but to be clear that it includes the underground well injection Charter. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
attachments: WRFL - Potable Reuse Response Letter - City of Edgewater
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney confirmed this was the second reading with staff recommending approval.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Jeff Brower, De Leon Springs, expressed support for the Ordinance and noted that the measure had failed at the County level. He felt this was the most important issue in Volusia County and urged for another unanimous vote for approval.
Greg Gimbert, Daytona Beach, noted significant changes since the first reading, including that two gubernatorial candidates had both publicly stated this type of water injection would not occur on their watch, which he attributed partly to the actions taken by Edgewater. He thanked the Council for their heroic actions that were already paying off.
Mayor Depew closed the public hearing and opened Council comments.
Councilman Thomas applauded Edgewater's progress in water quality, highlighting that the city has only 84 remaining septic tanks and has commenced a wetland water recharge project to stop 840,000 gallons of diffused water from entering the lagoon daily. He contrasted this with Deltona's complete reliance on septic systems and Titusville's need to buy water from Farmton due to saltwater intrusion, using these examples to underscore the importance of protecting water sources.
Councilwoman Gillis indicated that she was prepared to make a motion.
Councilman Rainbird shared concerns, acknowledging the ecological and public health risks of water supply injection but opposed irreversible Charter amendments due to potential issues like higher utility rates, funding loss, and compliance challenges. He suggested a more flexible moratorium while trusting in the Council's capability to decide wisely. Councilman Thomas emphasized a "step by step" approach, with Mayor Depew agreeing that such topics should be put to a public vote while understanding these concerns.
Councilwoman Dolbow echoed many of the same concerns from the previous meeting, adding that she would like to have additional speakers present both the pros and cons of the measure in upcoming months before the November ballot, so that voters go to the polls fully informed. She stressed the importance of transparency and said she has been reaching out to individuals in various positions to gather more information. Councilman Thomas noted there is still much to be discussed regarding future water supply alternatives such as desalination.

action_text: A motion was made by Mayor DePew, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to hire Ms. Sarah Jacobsen for $93,000 a year as City Clerk. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney advised the Council that they had the opportunity to interview three candidates for the City Clerk position on April 21, 2026. He stated his belief that all three candidates — Celine Kidwell, Cassandra Killgore, and Sarah Jacobsen — were qualified for the position. He requested that the Council select an individual and make a motion to authorize him to negotiate an employment agreement with the selected candidate.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Cassandra Killgore, 819 S Cedar Avenue, Orange City, addressed the Council and thanked them for their continued consideration throughout the process. She reiterated her desire to provide the stability that the Clerk's office needs and that she would be honored to serve the City of Edgewater.
Councilman Rainbird thanked Interim City Clerk Toupin and HR Director Julie Christine for their work in coordinating the interview process.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed appreciation for Monique Toupin's ongoing contributions.
Mayor Depew felt all three (3) candidates were wonderful and straightforward in their interviews. He did indicate a preference for Sarah Jacobsen but felt they couldn't go wrong no matter who they chose.
Councilman Rainbird reflected on the qualities of each candidate. He noted that Cassandra Killgore's career had been spent entirely in Florida, giving her familiarity with Florida law, county law, and local law — a quality he described as a standout compared to candidates from other states. He also appreciated her consistent attendance at Council meetings. He shared that Ms. Jacobsen had a very positive presence but he did prefer Cassandra based on her Florida-based experience.
Councilwoman Gillis stated that her top two (2) candidates were Sarah Jacobsen and Cassandra Killgore, noting that both interviewed strongly.
Councilwoman Dolbow praised all the candidates as fully qualified and thanked Ms. Killgore for returning for a second interview. She expressed that longevity in the role was a primary consideration, identifying her top two (2) choices as Sarah Jacobsen and Celine Kidwell. Regarding Celine Kidwell, she noted Kidwell's seven-plus years in city clerk roles, including being a Deputy Clerk. Cassandra Killgore brought nearly three years of experience as a deputy city clerk and experience with the Fifth District Court of Appeals in Daytona Beach. Sarah Jacobsen has notable city clerk experience and a robust additional background. Her primary concern was each candidate's ability to work with the Council's varied personalities.
Councilman Thomas praised Celine Kidwell, highlighting her Florida background, residency in Pinellas County, and hurricane and FEMA experience. He recalled her sharing her toughest clerk's office experience—managing FEMA funding post-hurricane—and thought this would greatly benefit the City Manager in State dealings. While acknowledging all candidates as highly qualified, Thomas found Kidwell's specific FEMA experience particularly impactful.
City Manager Mahoney was asked by Councilman Rainbird to rank the candidates he interviewed for the City Clerk position. He confirmed all three candidates were experienced and capable but expressed a preference for Sarah Jacobsen. He highlighted her confidence and ability to manage multiple roles, suggesting she could bring additional responsibilities to the clerk's office.
Councilman Thomas expressed concern about Jacobsen's salary expectations, as she desired the top of the pay scale. City Manager Mahoney clarified that the advertised maximum was about $100,000, while the previous City Clerk earned $93,000. He mentioned an ongoing compensation study that might indicate the pay level is below market rate.
Mayor Depew suggested hiring Sarah Jacobsen for $93,000 annually, allowing renegotiation if needed. Ms. Jacobsen had mentioned a 30-day notice period, aiming to start around mid-June 2026.
Councilman Rainbird inquired about a residency requirement for the new City Clerk. City Manager Mahoney confirmed the requirement via Charter but mentioned a possible exemption could be negotiated in the employment contract, to be reviewed by the Council at the next meeting.
title: City Clerk Interview Discussion and Selection

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve AR-2026-0118: Request to remove a historical species Tree, Live Oak with a DBH of 56 inches for the property at 200 W Park Avenue for $61,000 and some change. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, discussed the request to remove a historic tree — a live oak with a 56-inch DBH — at 200 West Park Avenue for new warehouse construction. Per Article 5, Section 21-55 of the Land Development Code, removal of such trees requires City Council approval. The applicant must replace it with 22 new trees or provide a monetary payment instead. Mr. Solstice mentioned staff preferred the monetary option to support city landscaping projects, citing a fee resolution amounting to $61,575.66 at $25 per square inch, allowing the council discretion to adjust this fee.
Mayor Depew noted for the record that he had met with the applicant's attorney, Joey Posey, prior to the meeting.
Joey Posey, 420 S Nova Road, attorney for the applicant, provided a presentation on behalf of the property owner. He explained the property covers about 1.25 acres with three buildable parcels, the northernmost containing a historic tree that makes it largely unbuildable. The land is zoned as heavy industrial, allowing by right activities including heavy manufacturing, boat building, general manufacturing, and services like truck freight and towing.
He explained the property covers about 1.25 acres with three buildable parcels, the northernmost containing a historic tree that makes it largely unbuildable. The land is zoned as heavy industrial, allowing by right activities including heavy manufacturing, boat building, general manufacturing, and services like truck freight and towing.
Mr. Posey explained that the property owner runs a family business from Pompano, established in 1948. The business employs about 70 people and has built over 100 high-end custom luxury vessels, including Jimmy Buffett's last boat. They're fully booked until 2033. The Edgewater location was chosen due to its skilled maritime workforce and proximity to a marine manufacturing hub.
Mr. Posey outlined plans for a new facility employing 15 workers with wages ranging from $40,000 to $50,000 annually. These wages are considered high for boat builders, owing to the detailed work on boats priced between $16,000,000 to $17,000,000 each. He illustrated how the proposed building design fits into the aesthetic goals for Park Avenue's corridor. Current property value assessments generate about $3,600 in annual tax revenue for the city; however, post-construction evaluations, including $3,000,000 in new builds and $750,000 in land buys, would yield nearly $25,000 yearly in tax revenue, excluding equipment or impact fees.
Mr. Posey summarized the case for approval, citing infill redevelopment on a heavy industrial parcel, above-average wages, low infrastructure impact, ad valorem revenue growth, and the legacy character of the business. He noted that the Kelly Group, serving as contractor, and the project's landscape architect were also present to address any site-specific questions.
Mayor Depew opened and closed the public hearing.
Councilwoman Dolbow expressed strong support for the project and emphasizing the benefit of bringing another custom boat manufacturer to Edgewater. She noted that the tax benefits were particularly significant given that the equipment tax alone with exceed the real estate tax contribution.
Mayor Depew reluctantly supported cutting the historic tree, citing the arborist's report indicating it would die regardless of the development. He emphasized that the $61,000 payment could help plant new trees elsewhere. He also pointed out that under SB-180, the owner could bypass council approval with an affordable housing application.
Councilman Rainbird concurred, noting the ever-present risk of SB-180 and stated his support for the project. After a personal visit to the tree, he observed its poor condition, with substantial Spanish moss and precariously low branches.
Councilwoman Gillis remarked that after inspecting the tree, she was initially worried about its condition but was relieved it wasn't the oak in the right-of-way. Local homeowners and businesses support the project due to anticipated stormwater improvements, which influenced her decision. She also noted that she had spoken with the project engineers and asked whether there was any alternative configuration that could preserve the tree. She relayed that the engineers had walked her through multiple scenarios and concluded there was no workable solution that would both preserve the tree and meet the city's stormwater standards.
Councilman Thomas, though hesitant about removing a tree, supported the business venture due to Edgewater's reputation as a boat-building hub with companies like Boston Whaler and Edgewater Boats.
The Council reached agreement that the payment in lieu of tree replacement, in the amount of $61,575.66, was preferable to the 22-tree replacement requirement.
title: AR-2026-0118: Request to remove a historical specimen tree, live oak, with a DBH of 56 inches for the property at 200 West Park Avenue.

minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney noted discussions with Councilmembers about introducing a backyard chicken Ordinance. He mentioned a 2024 workshop where a draft Ordinance was discussed but never proceeded. Councilman Rainbird felt that rooster shouldn't be permitted as they can be loud at unpredictable times. Councilwoman Dolbow agreed, noting that hatchlings cannot be reliably sexed until they begin to mature, leaving residents uncertain about what to do if a rooster presents itself.
Mayor Depew recalled the 2024 workshop, noting the County Ordinance served as a model. He expressed comfort with advancing that framework for further discussion, while acknowledging that changes could be incorporated into any Ordinance draft prior to final approval.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed preference for advancing the County Ordinance over the 2024 workshop's modified version, as she found it better suited and more well-written for the area. City Manager Mahoney confirmed that he required Council consensus to proceed with drafting and bringing the item back.
The Council gave consensus to direct staff to proceed with preparing a backyard chicken Ordinance modeled on the County Ordinance for future consideration.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilwoman Gillis, to approve Ordinance No. 2026-O-12: Permitting the ownership and housing of chickens in residential areas. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Police Chief Geiger presented the proposed ordinance to amend Section 5.8, lifting the chicken prohibition in favor of a permitted ownership regime and introducing a new section about keeping backyard hens. Noting that about 94% of major U.S. cities have residential chicken policies affecting 6-11 million households, he emphasized that well-structured ordinances tend to elicit minimal complaints.
Chief Geiger outlined the key provisions involving hen limits; setbacks; permit requirement; primary concerns and revocation. He also referenced Palm Coast's 2025 pilot program, which was originally designed for 50 permitted residents with four (4) hens each. It was so successful it became permanent.
Councilman Rainbird raised concerns about waste management near the river due to the chicken manure's nitrogen content. He suggested receiving neighbor permission before issuing permits. Chief Geiger acknowledged these concerns, noted current challenges, and assured that Code Enforcement and permit revocation would address any violations.
Mayor Depew felt the Ordinance was thorough and well-written, covering education and waste management effectively.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Kim Long, 3312 Mango Tree Drive, admitted that most residents thought chickens were legal already and stated that the farms on Volco sell composted chicken manure and do not smell or have fly issues because they are managed correctly in a hot compost pile.
Cindy Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, expressed concerns about the Ordinance including the lack of minimum lot size requirement; the fact that chicks are not sexed at purchase which inevitably leads to roosters; chickens attracting coyotes and raccoons; the noise from hens; renters being able to obtain permission without landlord approval; and the absence of a shelter for displaced chickens.
Chief Geiger clarified that the Ordinance places no restrictions on what the owner can do with their chickens, including eating them. The only prohibition is on using them for commercial enterprise.
Mandi Bullard, 1417 Needle Palm Drive, stated her support for the Ordinance as her children wanted them. She felt that as long as everyone cares for their chickens accordingly, there shouldn't be issues. She also mentioned wanting to present a homeschool unit on chickens her family was doing.
Councilwoman Dolbow asked for clarification on whether renters need landlord approval and whether coop placement would be inspected to avoid low-lying flood areas. Chief Geiger confirmed that the City would not be involved in the tenant-landlord relationship but there would be coop inspections that would ensure the enclosure is predator-proof, meets size requirements, and incorporates appropriate stewardship measures.
Chief Geiger assured that he would present a full staff plan at the second reading.
Councilwoman Gillis noted that setback requirements would effectively exclude some smaller lots from being able to pull a permit regardless of the desire to participate.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-O-12: Permitting the ownership and housing of chickens in residential areas

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve SA-2606: Request for a waiver of all fees in association with the Wilkie Wonka Day Event. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney presented the item on behalf of applicant Robert Wilkie and explained that Mr. Wilkie had applied for a special activity permit to host Wilkie Wonka Day at Hawks Park on December 13, 2026. The event would feature a Christmas giveaway, Santa, food trucks, and music. Mr. Wilkie was requesting a waiver of the special activities permit application fee ($25), the park reservation fee ($250), and approximately $2,400 in police overtime and community officer overtime (20 hours and 10 hours respectively). Mr. Wilkie is present.
Robert Wilkie, 209 San Remo Circle, thanked the Council for hearing the item and explained that he was getting an earlier start on planning the event this year. He informed them that the format of the event was changing; rather than distributing gift signs at Christmas parades, all approximately $20,000 in gifts would now be given away at this event. The event would draw residents from New Smyrna Beach, Oak Hill, Samsula, and Edgewater. Any profits would benefit from the nonprofit strongforyou.org. He reported that last years event had over 2,000 attendees and included local businesses, vendors, food trucks, entertainment, kids' areas, and local school participation. He expressed his desire to grow the event into a formal annual City partnership similar to Port Orange Family Fun days, and asked the Council to consider that possibility.
Councilman Rainbird pointed out how much the children loved the event.
Councilwoman Dolbow thanked Mr. Wilkie, his family, and his employees for their contributions to the community.
Mayor Depew echoed his fellow Councilmembers sentiment and called for a motion.
Following the vote, Mayor Depew rained a policy question with the City Manager and requested Council consensus to explore creating an Ordinance that would set a threshold up to which City administration could approve fee waivers without Council action, streamlining the process for community events. Mayor Depew felt that given the timing of budget season, it was the perfect time to discuss the parameters.
Councilwoman Gillis suggested the possibility of the City sponsoring something through Mr. Wilkie's nonprofit if he were to apply. Mayor Depew stated that the City Manager should meet with Mr. Wilkie to explore partnership options.
title: SA-2606: Request for a waiver of all fees in association with the Wilkie Wonka Day Event.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve AR-2026-0156: Request to approve the Jones Fish Camp Public-Private Partnership Roadway Agreement. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, provided background on the history of the project, noting that the City approved the River Oaks Condominium project in 2005. In 2006, voters placed a Charter amendment restricting residential height east of US 1 to 35-feet. In 2023, the original River Oaks Condominium PUD (entitled for 308 units at up to 190 feet in height) was replaced by the Edgewater River Oaks MUPUD, which substituted 196-unit two-story apartment style buildings with dry stack storage, a hotel, and a marina.
Mr. Solstice explained that the developer had met with Riverfront Estates residents to gain input on design features such as traffic safety, transportation options, and aesthetics, which influenced the current roadway design. He noted that the previously approved Edgewater River Oaks MUPUD and Yardly apartment site plan included a proportionate share agreement for Jones Fish Camp Road reconstruction at $3,776,311.29.
Under the public-private partnership agreement, the developer will hire a contractor to construct Jones Fish Camp Road, with City reimbursement. Interim repairs will be done at no cost to the City, and the road must be completed within five years. This condition was crucial to Councilman Thomas, who was absent. The City's cost is $1,888,155.82, with the developer covering the other half. Multimodal transportation impact fees were identified to fund the City's portion.
Mr. Solstice outlined the enhancements from community feedback: two (2) roundabouts (including one at Alice Street), 10-foot lane widths for traffic calming, a north-side bike path, underground utilities, landscaped medians and roundabouts maintained by the developer indefinitely, and a stormwater pond on the developer's property to manage roadway drainage. The design includes a turn lane and provision for a future signalized intersection, ensuring no right-of-way is taken from existing south-side residents.
Mark Watts, Cobb Cole Law Firm on behalf of the applicant, explained that the agreement structure through a brief slide show. He highlighted the Council's condition from the previous year requiring the developer to engage with residents for the road design beyond a standard reconstruction. The original plan involved a basic two-lane road, but an enhanced design was achieved within the same budget by using impact fee revenues from other developments in the area alongside City contributions.
Mr. Watts highlighted key issues with the current roadway, including its substandard width and depth, inadequate shoulders, obsolete stormwater design, increasing demand from local residents, and overhead utilities. The agreement features include developmental oversights like checkpoints at 60%, 90%, and final design stages, costs overseen by the developer, performance bonding, insurance, indemnity, and a warranty post-city acceptance. The City will officially accept the roadway upon final inspection, with enhancements like roundabout landscaping and stormwater infrastructure remaining the developers responsibility.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Jim Lovegren, 182 Jones Fish Camp Road, expressed concern over the single-access road for the Jones Fish Camp Road community, noting that 6,500 new trips would be added daily. He cited safety risks like hurricanes and emergencies at nearby facilities. He mentioned a petition from 29 residents opposing the project without a second access and suggested a potential secondary route via US 1 to Riverfront Way.
Vince Boskovich, 353 Riverfront Way, spoke in support of the project. He had recently purchased a home in the Riverfront Way community in part because of the planned marina development and road upgrade. He stated that the developers were being very reasonable by paying half the reconstruction costs, and that the result would be something the community could be proud of.
Ann Snyder, 180 Jones Fish Camp Road, raised concerns about the construction impact on residents at the latter end of Jones Fish Camp Road. The construction dust and debris will impact homes and air conditioning units. Initially, she was informed the development would be a small boutique hotel and marina. While road improvements are needed, the prolonged construction period will be challenging for residents and requires consideration of its impacts.
Renee Richards, 136 Jones Fish Camp Road, stated her opposition to the project itself, noting she did not believe the road would be as pleasant during construction as described. She also had doubt about the market for a high-end hotel in that location given it's proximity to Boston Whaler, she felt the community did not need the development.
Lisa Archer, 176 Jones Fish Camp Road, expressed her support for the marina and the development. She was excited about the economic growth, the dry stack boat storage, and the hotel. She plans on using the facility herself. She did note a specific concern that the sidewalk along Jones Fish Camp Road narrowed in an unusual way near the Dollar General Market and hoped the upgraded road would fix that.
Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Avenue, asked whether the Council had considered hosting a community meeting specifically with the residents in the communities involved.
Mayor Depew reiterated his previous 'no' vote on the Marina project based on concerns about the infrastructure. He sympathized with residents affected by the prior approvals for Riverfront Estates' single-access design. Despite those concerns, Mayor Depew emphasized the necessity of following existing frameworks for stormwater and infrastructure improvements funded by impact fees. He urged Taylor Morrison to maintain communication with the HOA and requested Mr. Lovgren's input on alternative route access.
Councilwoman Dolbow had been supportive of the development from the beginning and was excited about the investment it represented for Edgewater. She expressed appreciation that the agreement included a five-year completion timeline rather than an open-ended one. She acknowledged the residents valid frustration about construction impacts but felt confident that the developer would work to minimize those impacts and make periodic road repairs as needed during the construction period. She was also particularly pleased that the stormwater pond on the developers property would benefit the road and surrounding residents.
Councilman Rainbird confirmed that the overhead utilities would be underground as part of the project. He had empathy for residents based on his own experience of a having a new development built directly behind his home. He questioned whether or not there was a possibility of a secondary access, noting that the Planning and Zoning principle of two access points existed for a good reason. He also urged the developers' representatives to direct their contractors to be respectful of sound Ordinances during construction and to be mindful of residents. He stated that while he would have liked to vote no due to the single-access situation, the inevitability of the project meant the enhanced road was the best available outcome for the community.
Councilwoman Gillis inquired about the nature of the improvements for Jones Fish Camp Road, specifically questioning whether the Council had the option to decide on enhancing the road design versus maintaining a basic standard. Mr. Solstice stated that no matter what the Council decided regarding this specific agreement, Jones Fish Camp Road had to be improved. The enhanced designed addressed multiple community concerns and that even a hypothetical secondary access would eliminate the funding mechanism for the road construction.
title: AR-2026-0156: Request to approve the Jones Fish Camp Public-Private Partnership Roadway Agreement.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to appoint Cassandra as the new City Clerk. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney reported that the previously selected candidate for the City Clerk position had declined the City's offer. He advised the Council that of the two (2) other candidates previously interviewed, Celine Kidwell had accepted another position elsewhere, and Cassandra Kilgore still remained interested. He sought direction from the Council on whether to offer the position to Ms. Kilgore or to re-advertise for a new recruitment process.
Mayor Depew stated that his preference was to re-open the posting for one (1) work week to see what additional applicants may apply, emphasizing the importance of the position and his desire for due diligence. He noted that each time the position had been advertised, stronger applicants had come forward. He had no issues with Ms. Kilgore and thought she was qualified but did not want the Council to fall short by not re-advertising. He felt Councilman Thomas should also have a say in the decision given his absence.
Councilwoman Dolbow was torn regarding the decision but felt the City needed stability in the City Clerk's office. She preferred to move forward with Ms. Kilgore or at least have further conversations with her about the position.
Councilman Rainbird spoke strongly in favor of offering the position to Ms. Kilgore. He noted that she had appeared before Council four (4) times, had strong credentials including experience with the 7th Circuit Court of Appeals, and had continued to demonstrate interest in the position despite the drawn-out process. He expressed concern that re-advertising would cause them to lose her to another employer. He reminded his fellow Councilmembers that the City had previously made an offer to a candidate from Colorado who ultimately declined, noting full disclosure that the City had been prepared to increase that offer and cover relocation costs.
Councilwoman Gillis acknowledged Ms. Kilgore's qualifications and noted that she was a strong candidate. She did wonder if the decision should be tabled to include Councilman Thomas, particularly given that the Charter Amendment discussion and other significant items had also been table for his participation. She suggested that if a special meeting was being scheduled for June 15th, the City Clerk decision could be addressed there as well.
City Manager Mahoney asked for clarity on the Councils direction, noting that if the item were to be tabled to the next Council meeting on July 6th or a special meeting on June 15, there would not be sufficient time to advertise, conduct interviews and schedule Council interviews within that window. He urged the Council to make a decision presently.
The discussion proceeded with general agreement that the special meeting tentatively set for June 15 would allow Councilman Thomas to participate. However, Councilwoman Dolbow ultimately called for a motion to appoint Ms. Kilgore.
Following the vote, City Manager Mahoney sought clarification that the offer would be at the previously established salary range of $93,000 to $97,500. The Council confirmed this, and Mayor Depew noted that as Ms. Kilgore resided in Volusia County, there would be no relocation expenses included in that offer.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve the 1st reading of Ordinance No. 2026-O-08. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, said the applicant is seeking to amend the future land use for three parcels from Volusia County Commercial (B-4) and Urban Low Intensity (R-3) to City of Edgewater Commercial. This involves a unique self-storage facility selling spaces as condominiums. Staff agreed that it is compatible with adjacent uses along US 1 and is one of the least intensive commercial uses next to residential areas.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Avenue, received confirmation that the project was exclusively for boat and RV storage, similar to a garage for boats, with no business operations allowed within the units.
name inaudible, Edgewater Landings, expressed concern about the number of trees visible in site photographs, suggesting that a storage facility would likely result in a significant amount of concrete. She asked about the impact on drainage and how increased impervious surface could affect properties across US 1.
Mayor Depew asked how many trees the applicant would be required to replant and whether the site's drainage would be designed to a 100-year storm standard.
Mr. Solstice explained that the applicant must construct a 100-year storm water system, as the previous 25-year standard is now outdated. The topography naturally drains east to west, with little flooding impact expected to Edgewater Landing. All projects must be added to the City's hydraulic model to ensure no negative externalities. City code requires 15% of a site for tree preservation and a 25-foot rear landscape buffer with approximately 40 trees in total as well as a 6-foot fence, per recent Code standards.
Robin Meyer, Edgewater Landing, raised concerned that the 100-year flood calculation standard may be outdated given the increasing severity of storms due to climate change. He noted that a 3-inch rainstorm puts approximately 18,500 gallons of water on a typical residential lot and asked if FEMA had any involvement with calculations and approvals.
Mayor Depew confirmed that FEMA regulations apply and acknowledged the inadequacy of the 100-year standard, and stated that the Council upgraded from a 25-year to a 100-year storm standard. He added that the City was updating its codes, but SB 180 delayed this.
Mayor Depew stated that he had initially been opposed to the project but changed his position after meeting with several surrounding property owners who were comfortable with the proposal, given that staff had identified it was the lowest-impact use possible for that location. He noted that no concerns had been raised in response to the posted public notice.
Councilwoman Gillis asked who would maintain the property once the units have been sold. Mr. Solstice said the applicant must form a condominium association to handle upkeep with a small fee. Ms. Gillis also asked about the units being covered or uncovered; Mr. Solstice noted that it was not finalized in the concept plan yet.
Councilwoman Gillis noted that many Edgewater Landings residents had submitted questions and encouraged those with specific concerns to participate more fully during the next item, the rezoning application, which is where the project itself would be discussed in greater detail. Mr. Solstice agreed, noting that this item was a comprehensive plan amendment and that the Council retained the most legislative discretion at this stage in determining whether commercial land use is appropriate for that US 1 corridor.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-O-08: Request for small scale comprehensive plan amendment to the Future Land Use Map for Parcel ID’s 8412-02-08-0010, 8412-02-08-0040, and 8412-02-08-0090 from Volusia County Commercial and Urban Low Intensity to City of Edgewater Commercial.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve the 1st reading of Ordinance No. 2026-O-09. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, noted that the three subject parcels currently carry a split zoning in Volusia County Commercial (B-4) on the front and Urban Low Intensity (R-3) on the rear. The request was to bring the entirety of the properties into conformance with City of Edgewater B-3 Highway Commercial, consistent with the existing land use pattern for that portion of US 1 south of Roberts Road.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Councilman Rainbird had concerns that if the rezoning was approved and the applicant later withdrew, the commercially-zoned property could then be developed for any B-3 use by right. He appreciated the current proposal and Mr. Solstice confirmed that while the commercial zoning would remain, factors like transportation costs, limited utilities, and access issues would restrict the intensity for future commercial uses on the site.
Councilman Rainbird also had concerns from San Remo residents about a potential road connection into the subdivisions cul-de-sac. Mr. Solstice explained that when San Remo was platted, a common open area was deliberately created to prevent such road connections without the homeowners' associations consent. This design indicated that a road connection was not anticipated.
Councilman Thomas asked about the development impact on the residents immediately adjacent to the western boundary, noting that duplexes would be more compatible with the existing residential character of the street than a commercial use. He was hesitant about the change.
Councilwoman Gillis noted that several of the Edgewater Landings residents she had spoken with were worried about an increase in traffic if the site were developed residentially. They preferred the lower-traffic storage use.
Mr. Solstice highlighted key regulatory steps pending before development could proceed: a conditional use permit from the Planning and Zoning board for outdoor storage (not allowed by right in B-3), a possible road vacation by the Council for the platted right-of-way, and a complete site plan review. He stressed numerous additional steps, underlining this as a fundamental land use ruling.
Councilman Rainbird asked about the utility situation. Mr. Solstice noted that utility capacity in that area is limited, which would further constrain the intensity of any potential commercial development.
Councilman Thomas advocated for a larger buffer on the western side, a sentiment Councilman Rainbird supported. Mr. Solstice said that, while not mandatory at this point, the applicant's preliminary concept plan positions the water retention pond at the property's rear. This layout, along with necessary stormwater facilities, is expected to ensure a minimum of 100 feet or more of separation between any parking or structures and the rear property line.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve the 1st reading of Ordinance No. 2026-O-10. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Mr. Solstice noted that the application was denied by the Council a year ago, necessitating a one-year wait per the Land Development Code. The applicant had reapplied, and this time, staff recommended approval. The Planning and Zoning board also supported the application.
Mr. Solstice explained that the primary applicant owns a vacant lot among three (3) parcels and plans to build a duplex. The area along Edgewater Drive is mostly single-family homes to the west and a mix of triplex, duplex, and single-family homes to the east, all of which are currently commercially-zoned and nonconforming. The comprehensive plan amendment aims to align these residential uses with zoning requirements, support the development of a duplex on the vacant lot, and address the area cohesively to eliminate spot zoning. Staff emphasized that commercial zoning does not fit the surrounding residential character.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Name Inaudible, Edgewater Landing, asked about traffic concerns along US 1 near that area, specifically noting that the speed limit increases from 40-45 mph to 55 mph just before Edgewater Landing, creating dangerous conditions for resident trying to enter and exit their development. She noted ongoing accidents due to speed changes and inquired about City plans for adjusting the speed limit in that area.
Mayor Depew acknowledged her concern and clarified that the properties in question are on Edgewater Drive, which is a dead-end road, not directly on US 1. He stated that the US 1 speed limit is set by the Florida Department of Transportation (FDOT), not the City of Edgewater, but confirmed that City Manager Mahoney is working with them on possible solutions.
Joey Posey, 420 S Nova Road, attorney for the applicant, came forward to address traffic concerns, noting that rezoning reduces intensity from commercial, which is a positive shift for traffic. Existing commercial entitlement could generate more traffic than the proposed residential use, which aligns with two (2) of the three (3) lots' current uses. He highlighted the applicants transparency and efforts to ensure neighborhood compatibility. He invited further questions.
Mayor Depew stated that he had not supported this application the last time it came before Council but had revisited the site and reconsidered. He noted that while he generally favors keeping commercial designations, the site is surrounded by residential uses. He stated that while there are some commercial fronting the main roadway, there is a home that sits in the middle of the parcels, making commercial zoning essentially impractical.
Councilwoman Dolbow noted that the neighboring property owners also wish to rezone, making it a natural grouping instead of a spot amendment. She reiterated her support for the application both then and now.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve AR-2026-0194: Request of guidance regarding the designation of the well at Kennedy Boat Ramp as historical and to allow Daughters of the American Revolution. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, reported that a request had been made by Daughters of the American Revolution (DAR) to seek historic designation for the well at the Kennedy Park Boat Ramp. In order to achieve the designation, City staff and the DAR would need to complete the Florida Master Site File. Once all the necessary documents are approved and completed, the City could then apply for the National Register of Historic Places. City staff was seeking guidance from the Council on how to proceed.
Sandra Shope, representing the Jane Sheldon Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, explained the purpose of the organization and said that the chapter includes members from New Smyrna Beach, Edgewater and Oak Hill. They came before Council hoping to renovate Edgewater's flow well as their commemorative historic preservation project. The proposal, a collaboration with the City, was developed with the guidance of City staff, especially Mr. O'Keefe.
Jennifer Fox, Chapter Treasurer and Edgewater resident, provided a detailed history of the well, accompanied by photographs displayed for the Council. She explained that the well is an artesian type, a naturally flowing structure tapped in the 1870's. By the 1920's, the well still drew visitors for its reputed health benefits. In the 1950's , a structure was added to form a wishing well, although the artesian flow continued. After being abandoned, the City in the 1980's tasked Cedar Park Nursery to rebuild it, properly mortaring the coquina rock and filling the center as it was no longer a water source.
Ms. Fox highlighted the DAR's improvement plan for the well, which involves installing a fountain with electricity and water, reconstructing with a new support beam and decorative bucket, removing a palm tree for better accessibility, and including a bench and historical plaque. The goal is a September completion with a dedicated ceremony.
Mayor Depew thanked Ms. Fox and felt it would be a great thing for the community and expressed gratitude to the DAR chapter for their dedication.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Councilman Rainbird thought the project was fantastic.
Councilwoman Dolbow expressed her excitement about the project, thanking the DAR for investing in Edgewater and its history. She stated that she was looking forward to seeing the end result.
title: AR-2026-0194: Request for guidance regarding the designation of the well at Kennedy Boat Ramp as historic and to involve the Daughters of the American Revolution.

minutes_note: Mayor Depew called the special meeting to order at 4pm.
title: CALL TO ORDER & ROLL CALL

minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney stated that a review of the City Charter is mandated every five (5) years. Five residents: Gary Conroy, Linda Mojer, Patrick Fisher, Donna McDavid, and Mandi Bullard, were selected for the Charter Review Committee. Over twelve meetings, they reviewed the Charter in Detail and suggested 14 amendments. The Council may choose to modify, ignore, forward the amendments to the ballot, or address them through Ordinance. If moved to the ballot, each amendment would return for first and second Ordinance readings.
Charter Review Committee Chair Gary Conroy addressed the Council, emphasizing concerns about population growth due to the Deering Park development, potentially doubling the City's size in a decade. He proposed introducing a sixth Council District when the population reaches 37,000, based on consultations with the Supervisor of Elections and City Attorney.
Charter Review Committee member Patrick Fisher then presented a comprehensive overview of the proposed amendments, beginning with the preamble and proceeding through the remaining question.
Q1 - Preamble
Mr. Fisher explained that the committee's original concerns were distilled into a proposed preamble as a high-level statement of principles and intent. He recommended adding language clarifying that the preamble is intended as interpretive guidance and does not create enforceable rights or causes of action. City Attorney Sabatini confirmed the preamble is legally sound as presented.
Discussion arose regarding the "legal defense fund" provision under item A of the preamble. Councilman Rainbird questioned what the fund would consist of and where the money would come from. Councilwoman Dolbow similarly expressed concern that the language implied creating a new, separate account and that the City already retained legal counsel. Mr. Fisher clarified that the intent was simply to maintain the City's existing legal defense capability, not to open a new fund. Council reached consensus that the language was redundant given the existing retainer with City Attorney Sabatini's law firm.
Councilwoman Dolbow also sought clarification on item C regarding "performance and repayment provisions in public funding agreements," to which Mr. Fisher clarified was a clawback provision intended to allow the City to recover public funds from developers or projects that failed to deliver promised outcomes. Councilwoman Dolbow and Councilman Rainbird expressed support for the concept. The annual State of the City address provision was also noted favorably by Councilwoman Dolbow and Mayor Depew.
Council gave consensus to move forward with the ballot with the exception of item A (legal defense fund provision), which was removed by consensus.
Q2 - Expanding the Council to 6 members at 37,000 population.
Mayor Depew acknowledged the necessity of adding representation as the City grows, though he expressed uncertainty about the logistics. Councilwoman Dolbow expressed agreement that more representation would be needed. Councilman Thomas raised the question of tie votes, and City Attorney Sabatini confirmed the total body would remain an odd number (7) with the Mayor included. Councilman Rainbird inquired about the legal structure, the Attorney confirmed no legal issues existed.
Council gave consensus to move Q2 forward to the ballot.
Q3 - Redistricting Every 5 Years.
City Manager Mahoney noted that the City currently redistricts in alignment with the decennial census under Section 3.02 of the existing Charter. This proposal would reduce that interval to five (5) years. Concerns were raised regarding cost, as redistricting outside of census years would require hiring an independent data firm. City Attorney Sabatini noted a legal risk if data was of poor quality. Mayor Depew and Councilman Thomas opposed the measure due to cost and burden. Councilwoman Dolbow suggested maintaining a ten-year cycle aligned with the census and addressing any expansion needs through Ordinance. Councilwoman Gillis concurred.
Council rejected Q3 unanimously, it will not move forward to the ballot.
Q4 - Appointed City Clerk
This proposal would transfer appointment authority over the City Clerk from the City Council to the City Manager. Mayor Depew stated that he was totally against the change and believed the position should remain under Council. He noted a similar measure had failed in New Smyrna Beach. Councilman Thomas expressed concern about ballot length and voter confusion if all 14 items were sent forward.
Q5 - Native Plants (80% Requirement for New Construction)
The proposed amendment would require all new construction within the City limits to include landscaping consisting of not less than 80% native and/or Florida-friendly plants as defined by Ordinance.
Councilman Thomas suggested the same outcome could be achieved through Ordinance or the Land Development Code, avoiding the inflexibility of a Charter amendment. Councilman Rainbird agreed, expressing concern that a Charter provision would be difficult to reverse if found to be problematic. Mayor Depew noted community support but raised concerns about costs to homeowners after a CO and the City's already high landscape standards on the US-1 corridor.
Councilwoman Dolbow advocated for native plants while proposing a lower initial requirement than 80%. She stressed the need to account for the Land Development Code and SB 180 restrictions, as existing law (valid until October 2027) might lead to legal risks for Ordinances perceived as more burdensome. City Attorney Sabatini highlighted that under SB 180, even small added burdens could lead to successful legal challenges.
Mandi Bullard, 1417 Needle Palm Drive, Charter Review Committee, supported the amendment, highlighting that the University of Florida's list includes over 440 native and Florida-friendly plants. The amendment's 80% requirement applies solely to new builds and aims to leverage these plants' minimal irrigation needs. Local nurseries can supply adequate quantities. She also added that an untreated yard typically contains 50% native plants, emphasizing the importance of trees and shrubs for effective water absorption.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, confirmed that the City's current Land Development Code requires 25% native plants, that builders along US-1 are currently achieving 40-50%, and that Deering Parks PUD requires 80-100% native plantings on most lots.
Discussion turned to the possibility of adding an effective date tied to the expiration of SB 180 to reduce legal risk. City Attorney Sabatini confirmed this would significantly reduce legal exposure. Councilwoman Dolbow and Councilman Rainbird expressed concern than an intermediate date, since SB 180 can be extended by hurricane events, would make any fixed date meaningless.
Councilwoman Gillis stated that she would give consensus to forward it to the ballot. Mayor Depew expressed strong support, noting this was one of the most frequently raised concerns from residents. Councilman Thomas stated he was opposed to placing it on the Charter but would not block it from moving forward.
Council gave consensus to move Q5 forward to the ballot.
Q6 - Stem Walls
The proposed amendments would require all new construction within the City limits to be built using a stem wall foundation without raising the land, as defined by Ordinance.
Mayor Depew supported the idea but questioned its City-wide necessity, suggesting it better fits Florida Shores per the stormwater master plan. Councilman Rainbird noted that stem walls protect individual homes but fail to address water flow onto neighboring properties, suggesting a greater concern with fill-and-build practices. City Attorney Sabatini indicated that under SB 180, the requirement could face legal challenges as a burden, with the City unlikely to win such lawsuits.
Councilwoman Dolbow highlighted potential ADA compliance issues and pointed out that the Florida Shores Stormwater Master Plan already targets flooding issues. Councilman Thomas expressed concern about the cost impacts on homeowners. Mr. Solstice clarified the differences between open and closed stem walls, emphasizing that the standard for Florida Shores is a finish floor elevation off 12-14 issues above grade. With about 70 buildable lots left, out of 7,600, he noted stem walls don't aid stormwater storage or conveyance. He affirmed the Stormwater Master Plan as the right approach for resolving flooding in the area.
Ms. Bullard clarified that the requirement was originally intended for residential new construction only, excluding commercial. She noted that local builder Nick Schultz advocated for stem wall construction as the most suitable foundation for Florida's coastal and sandy areas.
Mayor Depew stated he remained in favor of stem walls but acknowledged the majority sentiment.
Council rejected Q6 as a Charter amendment but reached consensus to schedule a workshop to discuss potential fill-and-build limitations and a possible stem wall Ordinance for new residential development.
Q7 - Water Conservation Fixtures
The proposed amendments would require all new construction to install water conservation fixtures as defined by Ordinance.
Mayor Depew felt skeptical, noting enforcement challenges and the lack of jurisdiction over fixture replacements post-occupancy. Councilman Thomas and Councilman Rainbird shared similar concerns. Councilwoman Dolbow also questioned enforcement capacity.
Ms. Bullard addressed the Council in support, arguing that the measure would apply only to new builds where large production builders are bulk-purchasing fixtures, making compliance simple and inexpensive. She noted smart water-conserving fixtures are widely available and effective.
Councilwoman Thomas expressed support for the concept but preferred it be addressed through Ordinance. Councilman Rainbird agreed.
Council gave consensus to reject Q7 as a Charter amendment; unanimous consensus was instead provided to pursue it via Ordinance instead.
Q8 - Annexation/Limitation on Increase in Density or Intensity.
The proposed amendment would prevent newly annexed property from being given a land use density or intensity higher than what the County designation allowed at the time of annexation.
City Attorney Sabatini noted that the City has existing discretionary authority to maintain annexed property at current density levels. He warned that making this a fixed Charter rule could invite legal challenges under Burt Harris, SB 180, and other laws, potentially leading to successful challenges. Councilwoman Dolbow highlighted concerns about property owners bypassing annexation but still developing at County densities, which would continue to strain City services without providing tax revenue or impact fees.
Mayor Depew voiced concerns regarding effects on commercial and industrial growth. Mr. Solstice explained that removing "intensity" would restrict the amendment to residential density, leaving commercial and industrial unaffected. City Attorney Sabatini agreed this change minimizes legal risk.
Councilwoman Gillis stated that she would support letting voters decide.
Council reached consensus to move forward with the Charter amendment with the word "intensity" stricken, applying the restriction to residential density only.
Q9 - Sale of City Parks
The proposed amendment would require voter approval via referendum before any City-owned property designated as a park could be sold, transferred, or conveyed. City Attorney Sabatini noted this type of provision is very common in Florida municipal charters. Council was unanimously supportive.
Council gave consensus to move Q9 forward to the ballot.
Q10 - Sale of City Hall
The proposed amendment would require voter approval via referendum before the City Hall property could be sold, transferred, or conveyed.
Mayor Depew stated that the Council had never formally discussed selling the City Hall property and that he wished to clarify that for the record. He acknowledged significant community interest and noted his own support for keeping City Hall in its current location as a potential anchor for a future downtown corridor. Councilwoman Gillis stated that she wished to have the specific property address added to the amendment, as the loose term "City Hall" could follow a future relocated facility rather than protect the current property.
Councilwoman Dolbow was concerned that including this in the Charter might restrict the City from exploring public-private partnerships or developing a downtown strategy. She recognized the importance of community investment in the downtown area but argued that the Charter could limit the Council's ability to find creative solutions. Councilman Thomas opposed limiting future Councils from seizing transformative opportunities, acknowledging public sentiment about the property, while Councilman Rainbird preferred to maintain flexibility by keeping the property free from Charter constraints.
Councilwoman Gillis and Mayor Depew stated they believed the property's disposition should be placed in voters' hands. City Manager Mahoney suggested an alternative approach of requiring a supermajority or unanimous Council vote to sell or convey the property, which could be enacted via Ordinance.
Council did not reach consensus to forward Q10 to the ballot and instead reach consensus to direct staff to draft an Ordinance requiring a supermajority Council vote for any sale or conveyance of the City Hall property.
Q11 - Community Engagement and Public Information
The proposed amendment would require the City to adopt and maintain an Ordinance establishing a community engagement and public information program, with expenditures for such programs declared a valid municipal purpose.
Linda Mojer, Charter Review Committee member, explained that the intent was to create structured ways for residents to engage with City issues proactively, rather than relying on brief public comments at Council meetings. This forward looking approach aims to ensure residents are informed about major decisions in advance and maintain engagement standards for future administrations.
Mayor Depew and Councilwoman Dolbow supported the idea but found the language vague, suggesting it could be attached via Ordinance or Council consensus. Councilman Rainbird proposed a resident-only online engagement platform as a potential tool.
Council gave consensus to pursue Q11 as an Ordinance instead.
Q12 - Acting City Manager
The proposed amendment would require the City Manager to designate, in writing, a qualified City officer to serve as an Acting City Manager during any temporary absence or disability, and would allow the City Council to revoke such designation and appoint another officer.
Mayor Depew highlighted that Sunshine Law constraints prevent Councilmembers from coordinating a revocation outside of official meetings, rendering short-notice revocations impractical. He pointed out that currently, the City Manager already provides written notice when absent. Councilwoman Dolbow agreed, confirming that the City Manager is well-suited to choose an acting replacement.
Council unanimously agreed that Q12 will not move forward.
Q13 - Initiative and Referendum
The proposed amendment seeks to lower the number of qualified voters needed to start a referendum petition from five (5) to three (3). Mr. Fisher explained that this is merely a numerical change designed to make it simpler for fewer residents to launch a petition. Mayor Depew noted its merits but voiced concerns over Edgewater's historical usage and potential for abuse.
Council unanimously agreed that Q13 will not move forward.
Q14 - Data Centers
City Manager Mahoney confirmed the publication of this item amongst the proposed amendments. The amendment aims to ban or restrict data centers in the City. City Attorney Sabatini pointed out that a blanket Charter ban might face challenges under SB 180, although the risk is lower than for residential development amendments, as data centers are less common. A one-year moratorium via Ordinance is legally defensible and there are Counties that have enacted such measures. Councilman Rainbird doubted the City's capacity to attract a data center due to land and power grid limitations. Councilwoman Gillis wanted it moved to voter consideration. Mayor Depew supported progression post-SB 180 expiraTion and discussed potential for a moratorium.
Council gave consensus to move Q14 forward to the ballot.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Mandi Bullard, 1417 Needle Palm Drive, urged the Council to push forward all items that had been discussed and allow residents to vote.
Denise Dale, 908 Fernald Street, a longtime advocate for native plant requirements since 2006, highlighted that Volusia County enforces a 50% native plant rule for new developments and urged the Council to adopt a higher standard. Additionally, she mentioned data centers should be dismissed due to the City's water limitations.
Rebecca Crews, 2139 S Riverside Drive, appreciated the Council and Charter Review Committee's efforts, supported stem walls proceeding via Ordinance, not as a Charter amendment. She highlighted the Council's current discretion over annexation densities and questioned the need for Charter restrictions. She generally back the City Parks and data center proposals.
Corrie Sapp, 2630 Travelers Palm Drive, acknowledged the value of reviewing the Charter but questioned how the Council's salary had been amended without a Charter change, stating that while she believed a salary increase was warranted, she did not agree with the manner in which it was done.
Sandra Mounts, 107 Shangri La Circle, expressed concern over the City Hall property, noting it was donated to Edgewater residents, with an altered ownership by a prior Council in 2015. She urged the Council to hold a voter referendum on the issue, including the property's specific address.
Allison Root, Executive Officer of Volusia Building Industry Association, expressed gratitude for the Council's detailed discussion and suggested addressing native plants, stem walls, water fixtures, and annexation density via Ordinances rather than the Charter to retain flexibility. She offered her association's help in drafting these Ordinances.
Kelly Dotson, Executive Director, Volusia County Association for Responsible Development (VCARD), expressed concerns that several proposed amendments exceed the City Charter's intended scope, suggesting they be addressed through the Land Development Code. She advised reconsideration of the Park and City Hall sale provisions due to potential costs versus benefits.
Bliss Jamison, 635 Airpark Road, thanked the Council and advocated continued dialogue. She emphasized that many proposed amendments mirrored current Florida Laws or standard practices and advised against redundant efforts. She urged Council to weigh the economic impact of Charter and land use revisions on business and employment, while supporting the upcoming workshop.
Following the public hearing, Interim City Clerk Toupin read back the Council's consensus determination on all 14 questions. Council confirmed the summary as accurate.

minutes_note:
