At Councilwoman Dolbow's request, Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, came forward to speak about Accessory Dwelling Units (ADU's) as a potential affordable housing option for the City.
Councilwoman Dolbow brought the concept before Council to gauge consensus on further discussion. Mayor Depew expressed strong support. He felt a special meeting could address both ADUs and a broader review of the Land Development Code.
City Manager Mahoney suggested a workshop or special meeting for both topics; City Attorney Rollins clarified the distinction between a workshop and special meeting. City Manager Mahoney recommended scheduling a special meeting with staff to present the two topics and that a formal action would likely follow at a subsequent regular City Council meeting rather than at the special meeting itself.
Councilwoman Dolbow raised concerns about the Sabatini Law Firm, hired as the City Attorney six (6) months ago. She highlighted controversy surrounding the firm's selection and Mr. Sabatini's alleged dismissal from a prior role and worried about potential risks and liabilities for the City in continuing with the firm.
Councilwoman Dolbow highlighted a recent ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, where the Sabatini Law Firm submitted appellate briefs with multiple "hallucinated" AI-generated cases. At least eight (8) of these cases were cited in the opening brief, which the court deemed as possibly poor judgment or deceit of clients. She questioned the assurance that similar unverified AI-generated citations weren't being used in the City's legal affairs.
Councilwoman Dolbow also felt that Mayor Depew's personal representation by the Sabatini Law Firm, noting that while not illegal, created the appearance of bias. She then noted that Mayor Depew and Councilwoman Gillis had both accepted campaign contributions from the Sabatini Law Firm for $1,000 each. She felt that because Councilwoman Gillis and Mayor Depew had voted to approve the Sabatini Law Firm contract, it created the perception of impropriety. She said that while she did not believe those things were illegal, they did not reflect well on the Council and that the public deserved transparency and clarity.
Mayor Depew responded that the Sabatini Law Firm had not misrepresented the City on any matter that he was aware of, that the firms representative contacts him prior to every council meeting as he requested and that the personal matter in which he is represented by the firm is public record and entirely public record and unrelated to City business. While acknowledging that the AI issue was worthy of concern, he felt bringing up the discussion was a matter of political optics, not substance. He invited Councilwoman Dolbow to bring the matter formally to an agenda if she wished it to be discussed further.
Councilman Rainbird stated that he was not happy with anyone using AI tools due to the limitations and inaccuracies that it can produce. He noted that his decision to support the law firm was based on dissatisfaction with the previous firm and that they were actually his second choice after another firm withdrew at the last minute. He still had trust in the Sabatini Law Firm and asked that they be mindful not to use AI in the City's legal matters.
Councilman Thomas suggested that Council seek a consensus on whether to place a formal review of the City Attorney's contract on a future agenda. Mayor Depew asked for consensus and no consensus was reached.
Councilwoman Gillis stated that she found the discussion amounted to political theatrics and expressed strong disagreement with the accusations made, noting that she had her own reasons for supporting the Sabatini Law Firms selection. She felt she acted on what she believed to be right and is informed by conversations with many residents beyond those who appear at City Hall.
City Attorney Rollins addressed the AI concern, clarifying that a recent case involved AI-generated citations during COVID-era legal filings. Such incidents occurred nationwide, leading to court caution but not disbarment. Since then, the firm meticulously reviews case citations and complies with the current AI usage standards. Regarding representing Councilmembers privately, the attorney confirmed this is done within ethical norms and cases unrelated to City business. The firm has no disbarments or ethics violations in any jurisdiction.
Mayor Depew thanked Mr. Rollins and confirmed that to his knowledge, no one at the prior law firm had been briefly disbarred for a period of time. He reiterated that he has had no issues with the Sabatini Law Firm's representation of the city and expressed regret that the discussion had become so political.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to add the community engagement provision (designated Question 11) as described and presented to Ordinance No. 2026-O-18, the Proposed Charter Ballot Language Ordinance. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney explained that the Ordinance covers the proposed Charter amendments and ballot language previously discussed at a special meeting. He suggested reviewing each amendment individually, with Development Services Director Ryan Solstice and Economic Development Director John Scott available for questions.
Question 1 - Charter Preamble
Mayor Depew read the proposed Charter Preamble into the record. It defines the City's key purposes: safeguarding public health, safety, environment, and welfare; maintaining home rule authority; ensuring transparent and accountable governance; promoting responsible planning and fiscal management; and committing to protect Charter authority, assess major expenditures, include performance clauses in funding agreements, publish annual State of the City reports, and declare stormwater rights.
City Attorney Rollins clarified that the preamble is largely aspirational in nature and that its legal binding effect is limited, with actual home rule authority determined by State law. Council reached consensus to move question 1 forward.
Question 2 - Expanding the Council to 6 members at 37,000 population
This would require the City Council, by Ordinance, to increase its membership to six(6) upon the City's official population exceeding 37,000, creating two(2) additional voting districts with a Council member elected from each newly created district at the next regularly scheduled election.
Councilman Rainbird asked how the population threshold would be determined and how new districts would be drawn. City Attorney Rollins explained that independent governmental sources such as the University of Florida's Bureau of Economic and Business Research or the U.S. Census Bureau's inter-year population estimates could serve as the data source. Once that threshold was triggered, staff would create co-equal population districts' maps and offer several options to the Council.
Councilman Rainbird worried about possible gerrymandering but City Attorney Rollins assured that districts must be co-equal by population as mandated by law. The details of the redistricting process would be handled by staff following standard procedures.
Council reached consensus to advance Question 2 to the ballot.
Question 3 - Native Plants and Florida-Friendly Landscaping Requirement.
This would require all new construction within the City limits to provide landscaping consisting of not less than 80% native and/or Florida-friendly plants as defined by Ordinance, upon the expiration of SB 180.
City Attorney Rollins stated that while the 80% requirement would be binding in the Charter, the specific native plant list could be detailed in an Ordinance. He mentioned that UF's recognized Florida Friendly Plant list could be included.
City Manager Mahoney expressed concerns about including the provision in the Charter due to its rigidity. He stressed that while the City already encourages native plant use, a Charter requirement might lead to undesired effects. Specifically, he highlighted the impact on the City's reclaimed water system: should native, drought-tolerant plants become widespread, the reduced need for reclaimed water could result in the wetland park being unable to handle the excess, potentially leading to discharges into the Indian River Lagoon. Consequently, he suggested its inclusion in the Land Development Code (LDC) as an Ordinance for greater adaptability over time.
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, explained that currently the LDC requires 25% native plants, and that in practice, newer developments often achieve approximately 50% through buffering and preservation requirements. He agreed that moving from 25% to 80% would be a significant shift, and echoed staff concern about reclaimed water capacity.
Councilwoman Dolbow was initially hesitant about the 80% figure but, after further research and discussions with a community advocate, she understood the arguments made. She saw value in advancing the requirement but favored its inclusion in the LDC instead of the Charter for flexibility. She suggested linking the 80% standard specifically to areas lacking reclaimed water access. She supported progressing with the requirement as an Ordinance.
Councilman Thomas said he would vote to eliminate the language from the Charter and preferred it move forward as an LDC Ordinance. Councilman Rainbird agreed, noting a preference for 50% rather than 80% if it were going into the Charter, but that 80% in the LDC could be acceptable. Councilwoman Gillis stated that she would have preferred it go to the Charter but could support an Ordinance, recognizing that residents were seeking stronger protections for new builds.
Council reached consensus that question 3 would not advance as a Charter amendment but would be brought forward separately as a LDC Ordinance, with the specific percentage to be determined through that process.
Question 4 - Annexation: Limitation on Density Increase for Annexed Property.
This would prohibit assigning or approving a land use density greater than that permitted under the applicable County land use designation in effect immediately preceding annexation, in order to protect public health, safety, welfare, and existing development patterns.
City Manager Mahoney highlighted concerns that adding this provision to the Charter may deter voluntary annexation by landowners. This could lead to development under County control in the City's utility area, impacting City infrastructure and services without collecting ad valorem taxes or impact fees. Although the City must provide utilities per the Interlocal Service Boundary Agreement (ISBA), annexation the Council to manage developments on those parcels.
Mr. Solstice explained the benefits of annexation, highlighting financial support for roads, parks, and infrastructure through City taxes. Connecting to central sewer over septic systems benefits the environment, especially near the Indian River Lagoon. Annexation aligns with the City's ISBA, requiring the City to provide services even without annexation, thereby benefiting customers through economies of scale.
Councilwoman Gillis stated that this provision matched residents' desires to curb unchecked development on the City's outskirts, dismissing the argument that developers will build anyway as inadequate grounds to dismiss these protections. She backed putting the question to a ballot vote.
Councilwoman Dolbow expressed concern about the unintended consequence of discouraging annexation; if developers proceed under County jurisdiction, the Council loses all input, yet still bears the service burden without any revenue. She stated that this was a significant fiscal concern, particularly given the City's infrastructure needs.
City Attorney Rollins explained that the provision wouldn't conflict with SB 180 as it maintains existing County-level density, but it won't stop developments under the Live Local Act as the Act allows State preemption of local controls for commercial or industrial zoning. This means a developer could still annex and then use Live Local to boost density.
Mr. Solstice confirmed that the Charter amendments as drafted are generally not effective until SB 180 expires, and that an Ordinance accomplishing the same goal could be adopted at the same time the Charter provision would take effect.
Council did not reach consensus to move question 4 forward as a Charter amendment. The majority expressed support for revisiting it as an Ordinance.
Question 5 - Sale of City Parks
This would require approval by a majority vote of qualified electors of the City of Edgewater at a referendum before any real property designated as a public park could be sold, transferred, or otherwise conveyed.
City Manager Mahoney stated that he does not anticipate selling major parks. He mentioned the provision's potential impact on granting easements for small park land areas. He advised considering a strong Ordinance, requiring super majority or unanimous Council approval, as an alternative to a Charter amendment for protection. City Attorney Rollins supported this approach as legally feasible.
Councilwoman Gillis stated that she supported the amendments going to the ballot, noting that residents are seeking permanence and protection against future Councils reversing protections with a simple majority vote.
Mayor Depew agreed that public land should be subjected to the public vote and expressed support for advancing question 5 to the ballot.
There was also concern that the word "conveyed" in the language could prevent even long-term leases, such as space for a YMCA or a girls' club. City Attorney Rollins confirmed that a long-term lease could be considered a conveyance under that language.
John Scott, Economic Development Director, outlined public-private partnership models seen in other cities and emphasized that municipalities can use their properties to attract private investments without selling the land. These partnerships could significantly increase property tax revenue and enhance community amenities.
Council reached consensus (4-1) to move question 5 forward to the ballot.
Question 6 - Sale of City Hall
This would require approval by a majority vote of qualified electors before the real property currently owned by the City of Edgewater and designated as City Hall (Parcel ID No. 7452-01-00-0067) could be sold, transferred, or otherwise conveyed.
City Manager Mahoney voiced concerns about the vulnerability of City Hall's location for infrastructure and the need to redevelop Park Avenue. He felt that a Charter restriction may hinder decision-making, block partnerships, and limit funding for future City facilities. He proposed a strong Ordinance with unanimous or super majority Council approval to protect the property but remain flexible. Acknowledging the lifted deed restriction, he emphasized honoring its spirit by incorporating a community center of similar size into future redevelopment.
Councilwoman Gillis felt strongly that the property should go to the ballot, noting it was the original intent that the property remain in public hands and that a prior Council's removal of the deed restriction was wrong. She stated that talking about making money off the land sounded like selling it, which was the outcome residents feared and that without Charter protection, a future Council could change course easily.
Councilwoman Rainbird understood that the intent was to protect the property, but found the Charter amendment's rigidity problematic. He worried that a unanimous prohibition might block beneficial actions despite widespread resident support, due to the high cost of a special election. He favored exploring public-private partnership like those in Mount Dora, preserving City land while bringing in private investment. He recommended a unanimous vote requirement for an Ordinance instead of a super majority.
Councilwoman Dolbow stated that she was absolutely against selling the land but acknowledged the City would need private investments to realize any meaningful vision for the downtown area. She noted that the $100,000 spent on visioning sessions remained unimplemented, and pressed for the Council to finally act on that vision rather than allowing it to sit on a shelf. She supported public-private partnerships that keep the land in City ownership.
Councilman Thomas felt that placing the restriction in the Charter would handcuff future Councils and hinder future options. He would prefer to keep options open while ensuring any decision required strong consensus.
Mayor Depew noted that historical intent of the original deed and supported an Ordinance requiring unanimous Council approval. He felt the lack of a finalized downtown vision warranted caution in committing to any specific restriction.
Council failed to reach consensus to advance question 6 as a Charter amendment. Mayor Depew sought and obtained consensus for staff to draft a strong Ordinance, requiring super-majority Council approval, for the sale, barter, or trade of the City Hall parcel, to be address in a future meeting.
Question 7 - Prohibition of Data Centers
This would prohibit the approval, construction, expansion, or operation of any new data center within the City limits and would prohibit the City from issuing any development approvals, permits, or comprehensive plan amendments authorizing a data center. The definition of "Data Center" encompasses facilities for data storage, cloud computing, AI computing, cryptocurrency mining, collocation services, or digital processing. The provision may only be amended or repealed by voter referendum.
City Manager Mahoney made it clear the neither he nor staff supported a large data center in Edgewater. He highlighted that the definition of a data center may evolve with technology, and a rigid charter definition could lead to issues. He instead suggested implementing a temporary moratorium through an Ordinance while working on a lasting solution within the LDC.
Councilman Thomas received a brief explanation of data centers and why people are concerned with the construction of them.
Councilman Rainbird acknowledged that data centers do serve important national purposes but agreed that Edgewater does not have the room, water resources, or the grid capacity to host one.
Mayor Depew had concerns regarding the long term health effects of large electromagnetic field generators near residential areas, the impact on the aquifer, and the drain on water and power resources. He felt Edgewater was not an appropriate location for a data center.
Councilwoman Dolbow agreed, noting that residents had contacted her extensively about data centers as a top concern, and that the resources required were incompatible with the City's conservation goals. She does not want to see one near the City.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed support for the Charter amendment and additionally raised the idea of implementing a temporary moratorium to prevent any attempt to push a data center application through before the Charter amendment could be voted on or adopted.
Mayor Depew and Council affirmed consensus to support the Charter amendment. Council also reached consensus to direct staff to bring forward a temporary moratorium Ordinance on data centers.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Linda Mojer, 319 Leaning Oak Drive, asked the Council to reconsider a previously forgone Charter amendment regarding a provision for proactive community engagement. The proposed language urges the City to provide meaningful opportunities for residents to share issues and priorities while engaging early in policy development.
Councilwoman Dolbow had appreciation for the intent of the proposed language on community engagement but voiced concerns over the lack of specific direction or measurable requirements.
Councilman Rainbird agreed with the goal of more engagement, he questioned the definition, noting that current efforts via social media and public meeting are already in place and yet residents' participation remains low.
Mayor Depew suggested strengthening the language by specifically referencing the role of the Public Information Officer (PIO), as well as expanding the geographic notification radius for development proposals, and other concrete measures to enhance community engagement.
City Manager Mahoney offered to bring back recommendations on a community engagement program at a future meeting, whether as an Ordinance or other directive. Councilwoman Dolbow noted that she had discussed with Ms. Mojer possibilities regarding the City website.
Ms. Mojer returned to the podium and acknowledged the concerns, she felt that the Charter provisions' value lay in precisely in the commitment it represents, that even if specific mechanisms evolve, the Charter enshrines the City's obligation to proactively engage its community. She compared it to other provisions that were being advanced despite uncertainty about implementation details.
Councilwoman Dolbow proposed adding the community engagement language to the Charter ordinance. City Attorney Rollins specified that the motion should be to include the provision in Ordinance 2026-O-18.
Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Avenue, addressed the data center topic and warned that data centers heavily strain local water resources and create noise comparable to an air conditioning unit running inside.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Mayor DePew, to deny Resolution No. 2026-R-26. The motion failed by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Bridgette Vaissiere, Finance Director, presented the Resolution, explaining that it incorporates all information reviewed at the June 25, 2026 budget workshop and utility rate review, and also includes statutorily required updates to building permit fees. The last update had been August 18, 2025. Staff recommended approval with an effective date of October 1, 2026.
Cindy Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, opposed the rate approval, stating around 60% of residents don't use recycling yet still pay for it. She highlighted significant rate hikes in storm water, water base and reclaimed water charges.
Candise Gress, 1101 Regent Street, argued that the utility rate increase and the data center agenda items were interrelated and should have been discussed together rather than placed at opposite ends of the agenda. She expressed frustration that the City was raising utility bills while simultaneously entertaining data centers, which would further burden the water and electricity system.
Mayor Depew was not in favor of the utility rate increase but acknowledged the need to address capital projects, he felt that there were other funding sources that have not been fully explored yet. He cited poor management decisions in the past, specifically the construction of the Public Works facility, as the root cause of the current funding shortfall. He expressed concerns about continuing to raise rates without pursuing alternatives.
Councilwoman Dolbow acknowledged the difficulty of the situation and questioned where the alternative funding would come from. She referenced the 11 infrastructure projects that had been deferred two-to-five years at the last budget cycle, arguing that continued deferral increases long-term costs. She presented the Council's options as a stair-stepped increase of approximately 4.5% per year over five (5) years versus a potential 30% increase at the end of five (5) years if nothing is done now.
City Manager Mahoney confirmed that the five-year plan calls for 4.5% annual increases. He noted that staff had reduced the capital improvement plan to only critical needs projects, and that value engineering of the wastewater treatment plant had already reduced an initial estimate of approximately $90 million by around $20 million. He acknowledged that the City faces additional fiscal uncertainty due to potential State tax reform, with a year-one deficit estimated at $3.5 million and a combined two-year deficit of $5 million if the property tax reform passes. He encouraged the public to review the budget workshop materials to understand the relationship between rates and impact fees, noting that capital projects in the plan are necessary to support impact fee calculations for new development.
Councilman Rainbird raised the pending question of a ballot measure on recycling, noting that if recycling is eliminated, at a savings of approximately $8 per month per household, it would largely offset the proposed rate increase, resulting in roughly a flat bill or only a $1-$2 increase. City Manager Mahoney confirmed that was accurate and noted a future possibility of shifting the storm water fee to property tax bills to reduce the burden on renters.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed dissatisfaction with water quality, stating she was not comfortable raising rates for what she felt was unchanged or poor-quality service, including green-tinted water. Councilwoman Dolbow acknowledged the water quality concerns and noted that improving clarity would require a separate, costly capital improvement project.
City Attorney Sabatini confirmed that a motion to deny the Resolution was legally permissible.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve Ordinance No. 2026-O-14. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, presented the request and explained that the parcel is within the City's interlocal service boundary agreement (ISBA), is contiguous to the City boundary, and is being annexed solely to allow for a road access easement. The access easement is required because Volusia County traffic engineering requested the driveway entrance align with Edgewater Canal Road rather than being located on the parcel to the south, as originally planned. The application provides access to two (2) 5-acre tracts.

Robert Clinton, 4210 Liza Clinton Road, expressed hope that lawyers would resolve the Clinton Cemetery Road maintenance matter promptly so he would not need to return in a few years with the same complaint.
Mayor Depew stated that he was comfortable with the annexation as it brings the parcel under City control. He noted the parcel is currently in unincorporated Volusia County.
Mayor Depew closed the public hearing.
After the motion and vote, City Manager Mahoney provided an update on Clinton Cemetery Road. He confirmed that Clinton Cemetery Road is not a platted roadway and is private property. He stated that he held personal conversations with Mr. Clinton and was working with Volusia County and the City Attorney's office to research the historical records. He indicated that the matter should be resolved soon and that if the City has legal authority to maintain the road, it will do so, noting that taxpayer money cannot be expended on private property without proper legal authority.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve Ordinance No. 2026-O-15. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, presented this item as concurrent with the annexation. The applicant requests a change from County Urban Low Intensity to City of Edgewater Low Density Residential with Conservation Overlay, consistent with adjacent parcels already in the City. A key feature of this minor three-lot subdivision is that City staff negotiated a 1.3-acre storm water easement over the Gabordy Canal along the full property boundary, providing the City with future legal access to maintain or expand the canal by 20 to 25 feet.
Mr. Solstice noted that the original proposal for this area had involved 17 lots. The current application reduces development to 3 lots of 5 acres each. By right under current future land use, the property could support up to approximately 60 units, or realistically 17 lots accounting for wetlands. The comparison of 3 lots versus 17 was emphasized as a meaningful reduction in density and impervious surface.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed concern about nearby residents who had raised flooding issues, therefore she was not comfortable with the project.
Mayor Depew asked what the applicant would be permitted to build without any City approval. Mr. Solstice confirmed that a single-family home is buildable by right in the County, and that the full entitlement in the City could theoretically support far greater density.
Councilwoman Dolbow acknowledged the trade-off, noting three (3) lots versus 16-17 is a meaningful reduction and less traffic.
Councilman Rainbird highlighted the significance of the 1.3-acre storm water easement obtained through this process, as well as the additional easement from Daytona State College addressed later in the agenda.
Mr. Solstice also noted that the G2/G11 canal project, a $16 million project currently underway, is expected to substantially reduce flooding in the broader area.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-O-15 - Request for a small scale comprehensive plan map amendment for a parcel located on the east side of Tatum Boulevard, South of Josephine Street from County Urban Low Intensity to City of Edgewater Low Density Residential with Conservation Overlay, Parcel ID: 7430-04-12-0070.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve Ordinance No. 2026-O-16. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, presented the rezoning as concurrent with the annexation and comprehensive plan amendment, bringing the parcel into City zoning to reflect the approved land use designation.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Avenue, asked whether the rezoning would allow houses to be built and what the flooding impact would be on surrounding properties, given new construction elevation requirements.
Mayor Depew explained that the City's stormwater master plan model provides predictive data on how development affects flood levels during 100-year and 200-year storm events, and that the model incorporates surrounding homes. He acknowledged that any concrete or fill can have flooding implications but directed residents to the stormwater master plan for detailed information.
Councilman Rainbird emphasized that the developer is legally entitled to build something and that negotiating from 17 lots to three (3) while securing the Gabordy Canal easement represents a better outcome for the City. Mr. Solstice clarified that 5-acre single-family lots are unlikely to be extensively filled due to the prohibitive cost, and that construction will likely be limited to a small building footprint or stem-wall construction.
Mayor Depew closed the public hearing.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to approve Ordinance No. 2026-O-21 - a permanent moratorium on the acceptance, processing, review, approval, and issuance of development orders, development permits, and related land use approvals for data centers, hyperscale data centers, artificial intelligence data centers, cryptocurrency mining facilities, and other high-energy data processing facilities. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
City Manager Mahoney confirmed that this Ordinance was brought forward following Council consensus at the July 20, 2026 meeting and deferred to the City Attorney for any legal context.
Cindy Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, highlighted Elon Musks' AI power centers in Texas, noting their operation as independent power facilities that produce noise and emit acid rain. She mentioned federal restrictions on local government bans for these operations and urged the Council to understand the differences between conventional data centers and these standalone AI power installations.
Candise Gress, 1101 Regent Street, stated her opposition to data enters and argued that they misrepresent the benefits of building them. She mentioned they would damage the environment, strain water and electric systems, and warned Council to be aware of the environmental impacts before acting on any proposals.
Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Ave, shared his personal experience of driving near data centers and reiterated concerns about noise and infrastructure burdens. He argued that data centers should not receive taxpayer-funded utility infrastructure and should be located in less populated areas.
Linda Mojer, 319 Leaning Oaks Drive, commended the Council for taking a two-pronged approach in both the Charter amendment and the moratorium, calling it proactive and meaningful. She did have concerns about NDA's potentially being used to conceal development contracts.
Councilman Rainbird felt that Edgewater does not have the power grid capacity to support a large-scale data center in any case, noting these facilities require enormous energy infrastructure not available in Florida.
Councilwoman Gillis requested Council consensus to amend the Ordinance from a temporary moratorium to a permanent one, effectively banning data centers altogether.
City Attorney Sabatini confirmed the modification is legally permissible as it does not change the Ordinance's purpose.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-O-21 - Permanent Moratorium on the Acceptance, Processing, Review, Approval, and Issuance of Development Orders, Development Permits, Building Permits, and Related Land Use Approvals for Data Centers, Hyperscale Data Centers, Artificial Intelligence Data Centers, Cryptocurrency Mining Facilities, and Other High-Energy Data Processing Facilities

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve Resolution No. 2026-R-27. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:

This easement allows the City to maintain the canal, potentially expand it and reshape banks to reduce erosion and maintenance costs. The City will also reach out to Onyx Corporation in Parktown for an additional easement, aiming to create a continuous corridor along the canal.

Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Avenue, asked whether the easement was near the newly proposed townhomes across from New Smyrna Beach High School, Mr. Solstice clarified that the easement is on the Daytona State College and that the new development is in New Smyrna Beach, a completely separate jurisdiction.
Councilwoman Dolbow expressed strong support, noting that combined with the 1.3-acre easement obtained through the Tatum Boulevard application, the City is making meaningful progress in the right direction for stormwater maintenance.
Mr. Solstice confirmed that the Gabordy Canal borders both the City of Edgewater and the City of New Smyrna Beach, and that the County currently holds the only legal access. This easement would give the City legal access to respond to issues within the canal.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve the request for Major Site Plan Approval for the Edgewater River Oaks Dry Stack Boat Storage, Marina, and Restaurant. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, presented the request for major site plan approval for the eastern portion of the Edgewater River Oaks MUPUD, consisting of a 71,550-square foot dry stack boat storage facility with 338 dry slips, a 10-wet-slip marina, and a 14,400-square-foot restaurant with 400 seats on 18.8 acres. The applicant does not include the entitled hotel component. The applicant has undergone seven Technical Review Committee reviews, including a third-party engineering review, and staff confirmed the project meets all requirements of the MUPUD agreement, City comprehensive plan, and land development code with zero outstanding comments.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Mark Watts, Cobb & Cole, 231 N Woodland Boulevard, Deland, representing the applicant, provided a summary presentation confirming the application proposes no variances, waivers, deviations, rezoning, or changes to the MUPUD or comprehensive plan. He noted the approximately 20 months of review, thanked City staff for their work, and offered to answer any questions.
Theresa David, 1015 Regent Street, requested confirmation that the applicant remains committed to mangrove preservation, including maintenance against invasive species, given the site's proximity to the river.
Mr. Watts confirmed that invasive removal is part of the approved plan; areas where prior clearing occurred will be replanted with mangroves in coordination with Riverside Conservancy; and the applicant is exploring the addition of oyster beds as part of the marina development.
Mayor Depew had concerns about the impact of the MUPUD on the City's boat slip allocation from the Volusia County Manatee Protection Plan. He noted that the development has consumed a portion of the City's allocated wet slips, which has limited slips for the planned public boat ramp near Boston Whaler, affecting grant eligibility including ECHO and Port Authority grants. He emphasized that it is not the developer's or current staff's fault, but a result of previous city management's negotiations, placing the matter on public record.
City Manager Mahoney confirmed that the new public boat ramp project had been scaled back but expressed optimism about the project moving forward with available grant funding.
Councilman Rainbird sought to clarify whether the developer had stayed below the originally allocated slip numbers, which was confirmed, the applicant had allocated fewer wet slips than originally entitled, with some being released back to the City's allocation.The Manatee Protection Plan does get updated every 15-20 years.
Council also confirmed that this was a quasi-judicial matter involving compliance with existing PUD standards.
title: SP-2412: Request for Major Site Plan approval for the Edgewater River Oaks Dry Stack Boat Storage, Marina, and Restaurant for the property located at 161 Jones Fish Camp Road.

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve HT-2602 - Request for permission to Remove Three Historic Trees at 300 Base Leg Drive, as requested. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
attachments: Tree Removal Plan w/ Site Plan Overlay
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, presented the application by Williams Development Company to remove three (3) Virginia live oak trees located at 300 Base Leg Drive within Parktown. Under section 21-5503(b) of the Land Development Code, Council was presented with the following options:
1. Determine the trees are hazardous and allow removal with no replacement
2. Require replacement at a 1-inch-to-1-inch diameter ratio, totaling 119.5 DBH inches or 48 trees at a minimum 2.5-inch DBH.
3. Require a tree fund fee of $25 per square inch, totaling $93,463.94.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Taylor Huddleston, 811 S Cooper Street, New Smyrna Beach, representing Williams Development Company intends to build a light industrial facility consistent with existing Parktown development. He stated that the historic trees are centered on the lot, obstructing building construction. The trees have a current elevation of 7-feet, while construction regulations require fill to 11 feet, making their survival unlikely. The Parktown PUD and storm retention pond were designed for 80% impervious coverage across lots. Additionally, he offered to convey a sewer lift station, currently on the property without a formal easement, to the City at no cost as an act of goodwill.
Chris Collins, 123 Via Capri, New Smyrna Beach, also representing Williams Development, assured that the lift station conveyance is not contingent on the tree removal, it will be provided either way. He noted that the company is a long-term investor with four (4) Edgewater properties. He requested the three historic trees be handled with the specimen tree fee, totaling roughly $115,000 for all site trees, instead of adding a $93,000 extra charge for historic trees. He felt the historic tree fee cost is too costly for the project.
Mr. Solstice explained that Parktown allows for 80% impervious surface across all lots and that the development agreement already accounts for specimen tree clearing fees, with the five (5) remaining Parktown lots currently under review.
Councilwoman Gillis expressed concern about the total number of trees being removed from the site, approximately 55 trees total on the clearing, and felt the clear cutting needed to stop.
Mayor Depew acknowledged the frustration but noted that the Parktown PUD was established prior to this Council and the clearing is contractually permitted. He also noted that denying the application could expose the City to legal challenge under SB 180.
City Attorney Sabatini noted that the historic tree Ordinance predates SB 180 and would not automatically expose the City to a SB 180 lawsuit, though the denial could still carry legal risk. He suggested postponing the item to the next meeting to facilitate a workshop discussion on the tree Ordinance pricing structure and the lift station easement matter.
Councilwoman Dolbow preferred to move forward with the original options as presented and noted that the PUD's clear-cutting provisions were established long before the current Council.
title: HT-2602: Request for permission to remove three (3) historic trees at 300 Base Leg Drive.

action_text: A motion was made by Mayor DePew, second by Councilwoman Dolbow, to waive the Hawks Park fees for a period of six (6) months for the Edgewater Community Group LLC to operate a community market at Hawks Park. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Ryan Solstice, Development Services Director, presented the request from Megan Schmidt of the Edgewater Community Group LLC to host a weekly community market at Hawks Park. The City's Land Development Code limits special activities to three (3) events every six (6) months, requiring a formal agreement for more frequent use. Staff recommended an amended fee of $750 per month rather than $750 per event.
Mayor Depew opened the public hearing.
Megan Schmidt, 2713 Woodland Drive, the market organizer and a local small business owner, described how the market originated as a way to promote her own business before growing into a community driven event.
She requested three modifications: waive first-term fees, extend the monthly agreement through December 2027, and add one Friday night market monthly. She also would like the City's assistance with promotional things like marquis ads and social media. Ms. Schmidt assured that she held liability coverage and offered to cover additional event utility costs. She noted that she had volunteered hundreds of hours without profit and had prioritized highlighting community engagement through initiatives like school supply collections.
Heather Schwegler, 2425 Travelers Palm Drive, submitted a letter requesting that the Council reconsider the $750 fee. As a vendor at the Halifax River Tiki Dock market in Port Orange, she noted that these markets attract visitors from all over, even out of state. She believes that the Edgewater Community Market could achieve similar success. She felt the fee is a barrier to early--stage community events and suggested that directing resources toward advertising and entertainment that would benefit the City over time.
Cindy Black, Umbrella Tree Drive, expressed support for the market but cautioned against the weekly frequency as she was concerned it would cause burnout.
Mayor Depew expressed strong support, noting that market had good attendance despite poor weather at its first event. He indicated that the City would assist with advertising as it would with any community partner. He asked Mr. O'Keefe about labor costs to the City, staff confirmed there had been no overtime generated and minimal City labor has been involved.
Councilwoman Dolbow praised the market and relayed tips from the New Smyrna Beach Farmers Market president, including best practices regarding scales calibration, vendor rules (no franchises, no MLMS, no China-made products), handicap access, and nonprofit space. She suggested that the City develop a community market Ordinance for long-term structure.
City Manager Mahoney recommended the Council authorize a fee waiver for a three-month period while staff works with Ms. Schmidt to finalize a formal agreement that addresses all details. Mayor Depew proposed a six-month waiver instead, which he moved on.
title: AR-2026-0229: Request to consider an agreement to utilize Hawks Park on a weekly basis for a Community Market.

The Board reviewed the executive summary of the draft Turnbull Creek-Old Mission Regional Resilience Corridor white paper. The initiative is intended to develop a coordinated, long-term regional approach involving Edgewater, New Smyrna Beach, Volusia County, and other partners rather than addressing roadway, drainage, and development issues independently.
Discussion focused on infrastructure, flood protection, water quality, transportation safety, emergency access, and economic development. The Board discussed recurring flooding along Old Mission Road, the lack of shoulders and roadway drop-offs, accident-related closures, use of Old Mission Road as an alternate route when Interstate 95 is closed, increased truck traffic, and projected traffic associated with residential and industrial growth.
The Board also discussed untreated stormwater flowing toward Turnbull Creek and the Intracoastal Waterway, the need for stormwater facilities and possible right-of-way or land acquisition, and opportunities to coordinate grant funding. Members noted New Smyrna Beach's Turnbull Creek Preservation Board and prior land-acquisition and water-management efforts as examples of work that could be expanded through regional coordination.
The white paper was described as a multi-year, phased planning effort intended to align infrastructure and resiliency projects among participating jurisdictions. The Board was advised that the document was being updated with comments from the County and other partners in preparation for the Southeast Volusia Chamber economic summit scheduled for October 14, 2026, at the Brannon Center.

attachments: FY27 Budget Presentation August 10 2026 as of 08.10.2026
minutes_note:
Finance Director Vaissiere presented an update and City-wide recap of the proposed Fiscal Year 2026-2027 budget. She stated that the presentation summarized the June and July budget workshops and reflected several significant changes. The budget remained a work in progress, with minor adjustments possible before the September public hearings. Staff was awaiting final results from the compensation and classification study; preliminary estimates had been incorporated into the budget model. Management was also reviewing the potential effects of proposed property-tax reform legislation and taking proactive measures during the current fiscal year. Ms. Vaissiere reported that the proposed homestead tax reforms could reduce the City's ad valorem revenue by approximately $5 million during the first two years of implementation, consisting of an estimated $3.5 million reduction in Fiscal Year 2027-2028 and $1.5 million in Fiscal Year 2028-2029, with additional reductions in subsequent years. Potential responses within the City's control included increasing the residential fire assessment from approximately $50 to approximately $300 per home, which could generate about $3 million; increasing the operating millage from 6.33 mills to 6.83 mills for non-homestead property, which could generate approximately $650,000; reducing service and staffing levels; allowing wages to fall below the compensation study recommendations; and reducing capital and equipment purchases.
The proposed General Fund budget was balanced using the current operating millage rate of 6.33 mills. Estimated ad valorem revenue was $14,192,630, approximately 42% of recurring General Fund revenue. The proposed fire assessment was based on $50 per residential unit, with square-footage rates for commercial, industrial, and institutional property, and was expected to generate $641,771. No new positions were included, and vacant positions would be reviewed individually before being filled. Preliminary compensation-study estimates represented an estimated 9.1% General Fund impact, and health and dental insurance costs were estimated to increase by 7%. Personnel costs represented approximately 64% of General Fund expenditures, operating costs approximately 24.47%, with debt service, transfers, and capital purchases comprising the balance.
Proposed General Fund capital outlay totaled $559,480 and included vehicles and equipment for Economic Development, Development Services, Fire, Streets, Parks and Recreation, Information Technology, and Police. General Fund reserves as of September 30, 2025, were reported at $17,833,178. The required 15% minimum reserve was approximately $4.6 million. The proposed reserve designations included $1.2 million for Fiscal Year 2027 budget use, $300,000 for a fire ladder truck, $1 million for an interfund loan to be repaid with impact fees, $3 million for tax-reform transition planning, $2 million for major stormwater-grant cash flow, and approximately $5.2 million for two months of operating reserves. An additional $489,133 remained designated for City Hall. Ms. Vaissiere reviewed General Fund capital projects totaling approximately $11.5 million. Projects included paving, dirt-road reduction, sidewalks and trails, park improvements, and a boat-ramp project anticipated to be funded with grants and impact fees. She also reviewed the special-revenue funds. Mobility impact fees had an estimated $1.5 million available, with Jones Fish Camp Road and the Silver Palm sidewalk identified as anticipated uses. Police impact fees had approximately $410,000 available, with a training station and equipment identified as possible uses. Fire impact fees included an additional $350,000 proposed to be reserved for a future fire truck. Recreation impact fees had approximately $32,000 available, and an additional approximately $132,000 in impact fee collections was reserved for a related project. Governmental impact fees had approximately $184,000 available.
The Community Redevelopment Agency budget included approximately $886,000 in estimated revenue for land acquisition and streetscape projects. The Tree Mitigation Fund had approximately $7,599 remaining after Council allocated approximately $180,000 during the current fiscal year for projects including City Hall and Public Works landscaping. The scholarship fund had approximately $5,000 available, and the Edgewater Police Volunteers Association settlement fund had approximately $80,000 available. Grant funds included $1 million reserved as a City match for recreation, spur, and related projects and approximately $1.079 million reserved for the Canal Road Community Development Block Grant project. The Economic Development Fund had approximately $704,730 available.
Ms. Vaissiere reviewed the enterprise funds. The Water and Sewer Fund reflected the rate resolution approved on August 3, 2026, and proposed a 4.5% water and sewer rate increase for Fiscal Year 2027. The fund included approximately $42.4 million in debt for the wastewater treatment plant and approximately $10 million for water-line and other projects. Fiscal Year 2029 charges for service were projected to increase by approximately $1.2 million, primarily from new accounts. Proposed Water and Sewer capital equipment totaled $435,749, and proposed projects totaled approximately $12.765 million, including approximately $6.6 million for wastewater treatment plant design and approximately $1.5 million for sewer lining.
The Solid Waste Fund proposed a 3% residential refuse rate increase from $29.71 to $30.60 per month, producing an estimated $333,965 increase in charges for service, including revenue from new accounts. Recycling was proposed to remain at $8 per month, subject to the November ballot question concerning continuation of recycling service. Solid Waste capital outlay included two refuse trucks totaling $611,600, and outstanding Solid Waste debt was approximately $4.5 million.
The Stormwater Fund proposed a $5.03 monthly residential increase from the current $14.15 rate, generating approximately $1 million in additional charges for service. Staff had revised the five-year Stormwater Capital Improvement Program after determining that design, engineering, and construction should be divided into achievable phases. The five-year program was reduced from approximately $103 million to approximately $37 million. The Fiscal Year 2027 proposed rate remained unchanged from the previous presentation, while increases in the following four years were approximately half of the amounts previously recommended. The proposed stormwater impact fee was revised from approximately $14,150 to approximately $8,700. Proposed Stormwater capital outlay totaled $771,820 and included a walking excavator, compact track loader, and trailer. Fiscal Year 2027 projects totaled approximately $6.8 million and included design work for Mango Pond and Queens Pond, 27th Street, 18th Street canal improvements, Fisherman's Pond/Mango No. 12, and other stormwater infrastructure upgrades. Outstanding Stormwater debt was approximately $3.4 million.
Ms. Vaissiere reviewed the City's internal service funds, including Information Technology, property and liability insurance, health insurance, and workers' compensation. She concluded that the proposed budget was based on maintaining the 6.33 operating millage rate, with a voted debt-service millage rate of 0.1050 for GO for Parks. The proposed all-funds balanced budget was $128,179,325. The total included approximately $42.19 million in the General Fund, $1.9 million in special-revenue funds, $396,000 in debt service, $10.674 million in capital-project funds, $64 million in enterprise funds, and $8.6 million in internal-service funds. Minor adjustments were expected before the budget public hearings scheduled for September 14 and September 28 at 6:00 p.m.
Councilman Rainbird asked about the revised five-year Stormwater Capital Improvement Program and the time needed to complete the projects. Ms. Vaissiere explained that design and engineering for some projects would begin during the next fiscal year while construction would occur in later years; Mango Pond construction, for example, was scheduled for approximately Fiscal Year 2030. The schedule had been extended to make the program realistic and achievable. Councilman Rainbird then asked about the Tree Mitigation Fund and the projects funded during the current year. Ms. Vaissiere confirmed that the fund had previously contained approximately $180,000 and that Council had allocated most of the balance to City-wide projects, including future City Hall landscaping, landscaping at Public Works, and additional landscaping projects. Approximately $7,599 remained available. Councilman Rainbird then asked what would occur if Council had not approved the utility-rate increases. Finance Director Vaissiere stated that, without the increases, staff would have needed to substantially revise the enterprise-fund budgets. For Stormwater, most projects in the capital improvement program would have to be removed. Water and Sewer capital projects would also require review, and employee compensation, operating costs, and service levels could be affected.
Councilman Rainbird inquired whether insufficient revenue and reserves could affect the City's ability to obtain grants or financing. Ms. Vaissiere confirmed that grantors and lenders review reserve balances and revenue streams; weakening those measures could reduce financing opportunities or result in higher interest rates. She explained that City debt was used primarily for major, long-lived capital assets rather than ongoing operations. Spreading the cost of infrastructure over its useful life could support rate stability, provided that borrowing remained affordable and sustainable.
In response to Councilman Rainbird's questions regarding interest rates and lenders, Ms. Vaissiere explained that the City pursued competitive financing with assistance from its financial advisor. State revolving-fund programs for water and sewer projects could offer interest rates of approximately 1 to 2 percent and could include principal forgiveness. Staff was pursuing approximately $19 million in principal forgiveness for the wastewater treatment plant project. Other governmental borrowing was generally in the range of approximately 3 to 5%, depending on economic conditions, the financing structure, City revenues, and reserve levels. Council thanked Finance staff and complimented the City's financial management.
No formal action was taken.

Tiffany Sudakis and Crystal Weipert of the Recreation and Cultural Services Board explained the Edgewater Butterfly Wing Art Project, stemming from the Hawks Park Butterfly Garden. Student from K-12 were invited to design butterfly wings for a mural. With hundreds of entries, two (2) winning designs were chosen: a larger one for adults and a smaller one for children and/or pets. The larger design will be painted by a professional muralist, while the smaller will be a community paint-by-number project. The muralists haven't been chosen yet.
The two winning students were recognized: Wyatt Lavender, who submitted his design as a second grader at Samsula Academy and is now a 7th grader at Creekside Middle School, and Jada Morrell, who submitted her design as a 9th grader at New Smyrna Beach Middle School and is now in 11th grade. Each recipient received four (4) tickets to the Crayola Experience in Orlando, gift cards from local businesses, and will have their names permanently inscribed on the mural wall with the words: "Wings Inspired By."

agenda_note: This is the time for the public to come forward with any comments they may have. Citizen comments relating to any agenda matter may be made at the time the matter is before Council. Please state your name and address, and please limit your comments to three (3) minutes or less.
minutes_note:
Art Slack, 3031 Umbrella Tree Drive, commended the Edgewater Wings Butterfly Mural Project and suggested that the City consider commissioning murals on utility control cabinets throughout the City, particularly those that have been tagged with graffiti, noting he had seen this done effectively in other communities.
Anna Hoffman, 3104 Orange Tree Drive, requested a change to the City Ordinance for Florida Shores to allow residents to continue using drainage easements for overflow parking and debris placement, as they have historically done. She highlighted that these areas sit over unobstructed water flow, driveways are closely spaced, and yard debris at driveway ends create traffic hazards.
Sheila Bernard, 3109 Orange Tree Drive, supported Ms. Hoffman's request and asked Councilmembers to drive through Florida Shores to observe the conditions firsthand before making a decision.
Tanya Plaut, 403 Wildwood Drive, Edgewater 32132, expressed concern about the condition of stormwater infrastructure in the Wildwood subdivision. She noted she pays approximately $14–$15 per month for stormwater maintenance on her water bill, yet the catch basin near the confluence of Cherrywood Drive and Wildwood Drive has not been maintained by the city, residents have been maintaining it themselves. She reported the basin is clogged with weeds and requested that someone from the city contact her regarding a maintenance plan. Mayor DePew directed her to leave her contact information with staff and indicated that City Manager and Jeff Lariscy of Public Works would follow up.
Brandon Wiley, Northwest Lineman College, 501 Fulman Road, Parktown Industrial Park, introduced himself as Service Campus President of Northwest Lineman College (NLC), a lineman training college founded in 1993 with five campuses nationwide. He noted the Edgewater campus opened in 2016 and offers pre-apprenticeship and apprenticeship programs, and announced plans to expand into regional workforce development and transmission apprenticeship training. He expressed a desire to partner more actively with the city and engage local high schools. Mayor DePew encouraged the college to hold community events and increase its social media presence to raise awareness.
Jim McGinnis, 2607 Willow Oak Drive, raised concerns about the repeated placement of political campaign signs in violation of city and county regulations by the same individual. He argued that the repeated cycle of removal and replacement constitutes an ongoing cost to taxpayers in the form of employee time, fuel, and administrative resources, and asked the city council, city management, code enforcement, and city attorney to review available legal remedies, including fines, penalties, and administrative costs, for habitual violations. He emphasized that he was asking for equal enforcement applied consistently to all candidates.
Gary Taylor, Edgewater Fitness Center and Edgewater CrossFit, announced a community-wide fitness challenge beginning the following week called "Fitness Through the Decades," featuring themed nights, team participation opportunities, and sign-up available online. He encouraged council members to participate and help spread the word.
title: CITIZEN COMMENTS

minutes_note:
Councilwoman Gillis reported on the following: attended the YMCA's end-of-year summer program celebration; observed the first phase of River Cycling Services' oyster restoration and seagrass project at Veterans Park; spoke at the Southeast Volusia Chamber Leadership Program government day; attended the September 11th ceremony at Fire Station 55; and proposed that the Council begin a process to select a Veteran of the Year to be honored at the November meeting, gathering nominations in October. Council consensus was in favor of moving forward with this process.
Councilman Rainbird commented on the importance of the lineman trade and Northwest Lineman College; expressed support for the oyster restoration project, noting local resident and professor Bob Chew is overseeing a freshwater-resilient seagrass planting effort; noted that Edgewater's Sergeant Castellano received the Officer of the Year award at the Crime Stoppers dinner, recognizing his work in establishing standard operating procedures; acknowledged the 25th anniversary of September 11th on a personal note as a former New York area resident; congratulated Mayor DePew; and acknowledged ongoing work to address the city's flooding issues, noting that while progress is being made, it will take time.
Councilwoman Dolbow reported on several recent community activities, including a local summer program celebration, participation in the Southeast Volusia Leadership Program, and the City’s September 11 remembrance ceremony. She highlighted the Leadership Program’s focus on areas such as local government, economic development, education and workforce development, public safety, human services, agriculture, and nonprofit organizations. She also thanked those involved in organizing and participating in the September 11 ceremony.
Mayor DePew thanked Edgewater residents, acknowledged the ongoing political attacks in the community, reported attending the September 11th ceremony, the Southeast Volusia Chamber of Commerce Leadership Class, and the Crime Stoppers dinner; expressed a desire to honor Sergeant Castellano at a council meeting; reported attending a Florida League of Cities event with seminars on home rule; raised concerns about parking and debris overflow in Florida Shores and proposed that the council move forward with an ordinance creating a "common space area" designation allowing residents to utilize drainage easement areas for overflow parking of up to two vehicles and debris placement, while fully protecting stormwater management access.
Council discussion on the parking ordinance topic was broad, with Councilman Rainbird corroborating the safety hazard created by vehicles parked adjacent to driveways, and Councilman Thomas noting the issue with lawn maintenance vehicles blocking roads in Florida Shores and suggesting that a permitting or notification requirement be considered for such services.
At this point in the meeting, State Senator Tom Wright was recognized to speak regarding license plate reader (Flock) cameras. Senator Wright advised the council not to rush into removing the cameras, noting their value to law enforcement in solving crimes throughout Volusia County. He explained that the cameras read license plates only, not facial features, and feed into the county's VC3 facility. He noted that cameras have been in use for nearly 30 years and that the Fourth Amendment concerns raised by some have never been upheld in court. He cautioned that at least one Florida city faces a $90,000 lawsuit for breaching its contract with the camera vendor and urged the council to consult with legal counsel before taking further action. Mayor DePew thanked Senator Wright for his public service and attendance.

minutes_note:
Finance Director Bridgette Vaissiere presented Resolution 2026-R-29. The City Council first approved the fire services assessment in FY 2023 and has reimposed it annually since. Staff recommended continuation for FY 2027. The residential fee remains $50 per unit. Commercial, industrial, and institutional rates are based on square footage capped at 97,000 square feet, at rates of $0.03, $0.01, and $0.05 per square foot respectively. Estimated gross revenue for FY 2026–2027 is $731,570, with an estimated net realized revenue of $641,771 after exemptions and collection costs.

Councilman Thomas noted that, for context, he was initially unaware of how the fire assessment was used, but has since come to appreciate that it funds necessary equipment and that Edgewater's $50 rate compares favorably to other communities charging as much as $250. action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Gillis, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve Ordinance No. 2026-O-21. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Staff presented the second reading.
Council received the second reading of Ordinance 2026-O-21. The ordinance was described as a response to resident concerns about data center development in the city. Staff and city attorney noted the ordinance broadly covers nearly any type of applicable application, with "data center" defined as a facility whose primary purpose is housing computer systems, servers, telecommunications, data storage, or cloud computing infrastructure, meaning incidental residential use such as individual cryptocurrency mining would not be captured.
Councilman Rainbird raised a concern about the vagueness of terms such as "hyperscale," suggesting that measurable thresholds (e.g., wattage) would strengthen the ordinance. City Attorney acknowledged it was a valid concern, stated the language is already quite broad and discouraging to applicants, and committed to monitoring and strengthening definitions going forward. Councilwoman GIllis and Mayor DePew both noted that the ordinance is also expected to go to the ballot in November for inclusion in the city charter. Councilman Rainbird further noted the urgency of the permanent moratorium, referencing how a prior delayed moratorium on building resulted in a flood of applications being filed during the delay period.
The public hearing was opened and closed. No citizen comments were received.
title: 2nd Reading - Ordinance No. 2026-O-21 - Permanent Moratorium on the Acceptance, Processing, Review, Approval, and Issuance of Development Orders, Development Permits, Building Permits, and Related Land Use Approvals for Data Centers, Hyperscale Data Centers, Artificial Intelligence Data Centers, Cryptocurrency Mining Facilities, and Other High-Energy Data Processing Facilities

action_text: A motion was made by Councilwoman Dolbow, second by Councilman Rainbird, to approve SP-2605. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Planning staff reported that applicant Joseph Hopkins first submitted for site plan approval on March 27, 2026. The application underwent three reviews by the Technical Review Committee and third-party engineers. Staff found the plan in compliance with the city's comprehensive plan, land development code, and the mixed-use planned unit development agreement. The development includes indoor pickleball courts, a yoga studio, outdoor seating, required landscape buffers along Air Park Road and West Park Avenue, a 50-by-50-foot right-of-way triangle dedication for future intersection improvements, and a trail extension along Air Park Road.
Regarding stormwater, staff confirmed the site drains to the adjacent canal in both pre- and post-development conditions, but the post-development runoff is reduced from 8.86 CFS to 7.99 CFS in the 100-year storm, with the applicant retaining approximately 355,000 gallons on-site. Staff also noted the applicant was required to make a net cut of approximately 500 cubic feet on the site to offset any fill brought in.
Council noted the development is preferable to what could have been built on the formerly light-industrial-zoned land, that the site is already cleared, and that the project ties into the city's trail system.
title: SP-2605: Request for Major Site Plan approval to construct a 28,320 square foot indoor/outdoor pickleball recreation facility with a yoga studio and related site improvements for the property located at 2945 West Park Avenue.

minutes_note:

The city first received a preliminary plat and construction plans on April 27, 2023. The applicant's last submission was November 26, 2024. The applicant failed to submit a required updated transportation impact analysis and proportionate fair-share agreement. Staff sent certified letters to the property owner on June 22 and August 24, 2026, with no response received. Staff recommended revocation.
Council and planning staff discussed the long-term opportunity the property presents given that it is approximately 80% wetlands and constitutes the headwaters of Turnbull Creek. Staff noted that revocation of the existing PUD would require any future applicant to renegotiate with staff and meet the council's current goals and objectives. Council identified potential for future collaboration between the City of Edgewater, City of New Smyrna Beach, and Volusia County on stormwater retention and environmental preservation for this parcel.

City Manager Mahoney recognized Parks and Recreation Deputy Director Chris Love as the September Team Member of the Month. Councilman Thomas commented that he had personally observed a Parks and Recreation employee continue working in the rain during hurricane weather and expressed pride in the City's workforce.
Upcoming Weather/Storm Preparedness: City Manager Mahoney reported that Public Works and Utilities had begun stormwater inspections and debris clearing ahead of expected rainfall. He said crews are on call 24/7 for localized flooding response and that severe impacts were not anticipated.
Stormwater Fee Assessment: City Manager Mahoney said the next Council meeting will include a presentation on converting the stormwater fee to a non ad valorem assessment. agenda_note: This is the time for the public to come forward with any comments they may have. Citizen comments relating to any agenda matter may be made at the time the matter is before Council. Please state your name and address, and please limit your comments to three (3) minutes or less.
minutes_note:
Laura London, 2632 Woodland Avenue, addressed the Council about commercial and political signs posted on public property and rights of way in violation of County and City Ordinances, raised concerns about enforcement and possible selective enforcement, and requested that illegal signs be removed.
Kim Long, 3312 Mango Tree Drive, raised concern about Park Avenue sidewalks and shade trees, recycling on the ballot, drainage capacity for future development, and returning the City Hall property deed to the public. Mayor Depew advised that the new sidewalks are ADA compliant.
Robert DeVoe, 232 N Ridgewood Avenue, expressed concern about resident confusion over Amendment 3 and asked for a public forum on its fiscal impact; Mayor Depew advised that the issue had been discussed during budget meetings, related information is available on the City website, and the City estimates a loss of about $5 million.
Linda Mojer, 319 Leaning Oak Drive, president of the Majestic Oaks Phase 1 and 2 Homeowners Association, said a revised site plan would limit US 1 access to right in only, routing oversized commercial traffic through Oak Branch Drive and the neighborhood canopy, and asked the Council to pursue restoration of full right in/right out access.
title: CITIZEN COMMENTS

minutes_note:
Mayor Depew said the City has three (3) Code Enforcement staff, sign enforcement is largely complaint driven, and candidate materials should more clearly explain sign placement rules. He also noted some of his signs had been removed in error and that staff had addressed the issue through retraining.
City Manager Mahoney reported that, as of that morning, Code Enforcement had removed 16 political signs from the right of way, and in the prior week had collected approximately 60 signs in total. He confirmed that Code Enforcement efforts are unbiased, acknowledged the error involving the Mayors signs, and stated that weekend staffing would be added to increase sign removal efforts. He also noted that the City could potentially strengthen its sign ordinance and consider disposing of confiscated signs rather than holding them.
Councilman Thomas suggested forming a committee to develop strong sign enforcement measures, and stated that candidates should be held responsible for signs placed on public property. City Manager Mahoney noted that with the election approaching, there would soon be an opportunity to review and potentially strengthen the sign ordinance for future election cycles.
Councilwoman Dolbow reported attending the State of the City, the DAR well dedication, and volunteer dinners at the Elks Lodge. She also met with residents and businesses, and clarified that Senator Tom Wright's recent Council appearance followed her invitation and coordination with his staff, and was only intended to share information.
City Manager Mahoney clarified for the record that while there was correspondence with Senator Wrights staff regarding possible meeting dates, the Senator's office never formally confirmed his appearance for that evening.
Mayor Depew noted that going forward, the City Clerk or City Manager should alert him as chair if a guest speaker is expected, so that proper notification can be provided.
Councilman Rainbird asked the community to keep Wayne McCloskey in their thoughts and prayers and thanked him for running for Mayor. He said that the Volusia Young Marines are seeking a new local meeting space, with Hawks Park and Rotary Park considered and another option under review. He also said that if he runs again, he will keep his campaign signs to a minimum, and expressed regret over concerns raised about his prior "fight the flooding" signs.
Mayor Depew congratulated City Manager Mahoney on his one year anniversary, thanked the DAR and Jennifer Fox for the restored well project, and noted his attendance at the State of the City with the Chamber of commerce.
Councilwoman Gillis reported attending several community and regional events, including the Crime Stoppers Award Ceremony, business ribbon cuttings, a Habitat for Humanity home dedication, a school board meeting, Mayor's Fitness Challenge events, and the Fund Coast Foundation fundraiser. She recognized Parks and Recreation staff for their work on the old flow well restoration, shared that she would relay FDOT safety information on e bikes to the City Manager, thanked Jeff Lariscy for assisting residents with water issues, and noting upcoming TPO and Florida League committee meetings.

action_text: A motion was made by Mayor DePew, second by Councilman Rainbird, to nominate Jim McGinnis and Rick Wollet for Veterans of the Year 2026. The MOTION was APPROVED by the following vote:
minutes_note:
Before discussing the Veteran of the Year nominees, Council agreed by unanimous consensus to recognize Sara and David Owen, leaders of the Volusia County Young Marines, as the first honorees under the new Veteran Organization of the year program at the November Council meeting.
Regarding the Veteran of the Year nominees, Councilwoman Dolbow nominated Rick Wollet, describing him as a behind-the-scenes contributor who volunteers every Thursday at Gifts of Love, is active at both the American Legion and the AMVETS, and consistently shows up without recognition.
Councilman Rainbird also nominated Rick Wollet, noting his 20-plus years of veteran community involvement, his charter membership in AMVETS Post 2, his ongoing presence at events, and his selfless service to the veteran community.
Mayor Depew nominated Jim McGinnis, describing him as a longtime Edgewater resident who served as a drill sergeant, a life member of the American Legion and Disabled American Veterans, a participant in the American Legion Legacy Ride, and a familiar presence in the community who volunteers at food banks, serves with his church, and plays Santa Claus in the annual Christmas parade.
Councilwoman Gillis noted that she had been debating between both nominees and proposed, consistent with last year, that the Council move forward with honoring both nominees as Veterans of the Year.
Mayor Depew agreed and suggested updating the program language from Veteran to Veterans to formally accommodate multiple honorees on an ongoing basis.
